That's actually a really good question, and it's one of the biggest misunderstandings people have about Revelation.

You're assuming that the END of biblical prophecy means the physical planet Earth must be destroyed and every human being must disappear. But that's not necessarily what the Bible is describing.

There's a major difference between the END OF THE AGE and the END OF PLANET EARTH.

Start with Matthew 24:3.

The disciples ask Jesus about His coming and “the end of the world.”

But the Greek word translated “world” there is AIŌN, meaning AGE.

Now compare Hebrews 9:26:

“but NOW ONCE IN THE END OF THE WORLD hath he appeared to PUT AWAY SIN by the sacrifice of himself.”

Notice that. Hebrews says Christ appeared at the END OF THE WORLD.

Did planet Earth physically disappear when Jesus was sacrificed?

Obviously not.

Then 1 Corinthians 10:11 says:

“upon whom THE ENDS OF THE WORLD ARE COME.”

Paul was writing to people living in the FIRST CENTURY, telling THEM that the ends of the ages had come upon them.

So the Bible itself uses this language for the ending of an AGE, not necessarily the physical destruction of the universe.

AND WHAT AGE WAS ENDING? THE OLD COVENANT AGE OF SIN, CONDEMNATION, AND SACRIFICE.

This is the part so many people overlook.

The old covenant religious system revolved around the law of Moses, the priesthood, the Temple, and continual sacrifices for sin.

Animals were sacrificed repeatedly. Priests made offerings. The people lived under a covenantal system involving sin, guilt, judgment, and atonement.

But what was the purpose of Christ's sacrifice?

Hebrews 9:26 says He appeared:

“TO PUT AWAY SIN BY THE SACRIFICE OF HIMSELF.”

Hebrews 9:12 says Christ entered the holy place:

“ONCE, having obtained ETERNAL REDEMPTION for us.”

Hebrews 10:10 says:

“We are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ ONCE FOR ALL.”

Hebrews 10:11 explains that the old priests stood daily offering sacrifices:

“which can NEVER take away sins.”

But verse 12 says Christ:

“after he had offered ONE SACRIFICE FOR SINS FOR EVER, sat down on the right hand of God.”

Then Hebrews 10:18 says:

“Now where remission of these is, THERE IS NO MORE OFFERING FOR SIN.”

READ THAT AGAIN.

NO MORE OFFERING FOR SIN.

So if Christ offered the final sacrifice, why would the former covenantal system of sacrifices need to continue indefinitely?

Hebrews 8:13 says the OLD COVENANT was:

“READY TO VANISH AWAY.”

Galatians 3:19 says the law was added:

“TILL THE SEED SHOULD COME…”

And 1 Corinthians 15:56 says:

“The sting of death is SIN; and the strength of sin is THE LAW.”

Paul is connecting sin's condemning power with the law.

Romans 6:14 also says:

“For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are NOT UNDER THE LAW, but under grace.”

This is why I understand Christ's mission as bringing the former covenantal system of law, sin, condemnation, and repeated sacrifice to its appointed completion.

The Bible describes a transition from the old covenant to the new, from repeated animal sacrifices to Christ's once-for-all sacrifice.

And historically, in AD 70, the very Temple where sacrifices were performed was destroyed.

That was the SECOND TEMPLE Jesus Himself had warned about.

The end of the Temple-centered sacrificial order was a profound historical turning point.

Now here's where people misunderstand what I'm saying.

THE END OF THAT COVENANTAL SIN AND SACRIFICE SYSTEM DOES NOT MEAN HUMAN BEINGS SUDDENLY LOST FREE WILL OR BECAME INCAPABLE OF EVIL.

I'm distinguishing the old covenant's legal and sacrificial system from the continued existence of human wickedness.

People can still lie, murder, steal, deceive, abuse others, and make evil choices.

Human evil continuing today doesn't somehow mean the Second Temple must still exist, the Mosaic sacrificial system must still be operating, or Jesus' original generation must still be waiting for its judgment.

Christ's sacrifice was described as ONCE FOR ALL.

The old covenant was described as READY TO VANISH AWAY.

The completed-age interpretation understands the prophetic culmination of that covenantal transition as belonging to the first-century biblical age.

That does not mean every biblical passage about sin or judgment is uncontested. It means we should first understand those passages within their original covenantal context rather than automatically making them about our modern society.

NOW LOOK AT WHAT JESUS SAID ABOUT THE END OF THAT AGE.

Matthew 24:2:

“There shall not be left HERE one stone upon another.”

Luke 21:20:

“When YE shall see JERUSALEM compassed with armies…”

Luke 21:22:

“These be the DAYS OF VENGEANCE, that ALL THINGS WHICH ARE WRITTEN may be fulfilled.”

Matthew 24:34:

“THIS GENERATION shall not pass, till ALL THESE THINGS be fulfilled.”

Then in AD 70, Jerusalem was devastated and the Second Temple was destroyed during the Roman-Jewish War.

That's the historical ending I'm talking about.

Not the destruction of the entire physical Earth.

NOW CONSIDER THE NEW JERUSALEM.

Revelation 21 describes New Jerusalem.

But what exactly is this city?

Revelation 21:9 says:

“Come hither, I will shew thee THE BRIDE, the Lamb's wife.”

Then verse 10 shows John the holy Jerusalem.

So the city is explicitly associated with the BRIDE.

Hebrews 12:22 already speaks of the:

“HEAVENLY JERUSALEM.”

Galatians 4:26 says:

“Jerusalem which is ABOVE is free…”

This provides a biblical basis for understanding New Jerusalem as a heavenly and covenantal reality, not necessarily a giant physical city that must appear on modern satellite imagery.

And here's something people overlook.

Revelation 21:24 still describes NATIONS walking in the city's light.

Revelation 22:2 speaks of the “HEALING OF THE NATIONS.”

Revelation 22:14 describes those entering the city through its gates.

And Revelation 22:15 says:

“For WITHOUT are dogs, and sorcerers, and whoremongers, and murderers…”

WITHOUT means OUTSIDE.

That doesn't explicitly identify people alive in 2026 as the outsiders, but it does show that Revelation's final vision contains language about nations, entry, and exclusion.

The completed-age interpretation understands the new creation as a completed heavenly and covenantal order, while physical human history continues.

SO WHY ARE WE STILL HERE?

Because the physical planet did not have to end for the biblical covenantal age to end.

Christ did not need to destroy the planet for His sacrifice to accomplish its purpose.

The old Temple did not need to remain standing forever.

The old priesthood did not need to continue sacrificing animals forever.

The former covenantal order had an endpoint.

And the New Testament itself describes that transition.

Hebrews 9:26 — Christ appeared at the END OF THE AGE to PUT AWAY SIN.

Hebrews 10:10 — His sacrifice was ONCE FOR ALL.

Hebrews 10:18 — NO MORE OFFERING FOR SIN.

Hebrews 8:13 — the old covenant was READY TO VANISH AWAY.

1 Corinthians 10:11 — the ends of the ages had come upon THEM.

Then Revelation repeatedly describes events that were near to its original recipients.

Revelation 1:1:

“things which must SHORTLY COME TO PASS.”

Revelation 1:3:

“THE TIME IS AT HAND.”

Revelation 22:6:

“things which must SHORTLY BE DONE.”

Revelation 22:10:

“THE TIME IS AT HAND.”

Revelation 22:20:

“Surely I COME QUICKLY.”

Those were messages to real people living in that biblical age.

My position is that the prophetic events concerning the end of that age reached their completion, rather than remaining an unfinished countdown for people living thousands of years later.

Human history continued.

Generations were born.

Civilizations rose and fell.

Good and evil choices continued.

That doesn't mean the old biblical covenantal system must still be operating.

And I recognize that Christians disagree about whether every resurrection and judgment passage was fulfilled by AD 70. But simply pointing to the fact that humans still exist does not, by itself, disprove the distinction between the end of a covenantal age and the end of the physical planet.

Think about it this way:

THE END OF THE AGE OF SACRIFICE IS NOT THE END OF HUMAN EXISTENCE.

THE END OF THE OLD COVENANT IS NOT THE END OF PLANET EARTH.

THE COMPLETION OF CHRIST'S REDEMPTIVE WORK DOES NOT REQUIRE HUMAN FREE WILL TO DISAPPEAR.

And that's why I don't believe we're supposed to keep waiting for the same biblical prophetic age to end again and again.

So instead of asking, “Why are we still here if Revelation already happened?”

Ask this:

WHAT EXACTLY WAS SUPPOSED TO END?

Because my understanding is that it was THEIR biblical covenantal age—the age of the Temple, the former law, recurring sacrifices, and the approaching judgment Jesus warned His generation about.

Not the existence of the physical Earth itself.

We are still here because life continued after that age.

That's the distinction I've been trying to explain.

text:
Her Husband Died in Chinese Police Custody Before One Olympics. Beijing Jailed Her Before the Next.

Painter and poet Xu Na has been sentenced to a combined 16 years for her faith. Her current crime was photographing her own city during the pandemic.

On Sunday afternoon, outside the Chinese consulate in Los Angeles, a small group of protesters unrolled a banner with a name most Americans have never heard: Xu Na.

More than 6,000 miles away, the woman on that banner is serving an eight-year sentence in Beijing Women's Prison. It is her third prison term. Taken together, Chinese courts have sentenced her to 16 years for practicing Falun Gong, a meditative spiritual discipline the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) outlawed in 1999. The latest sentence came down in January 2022, three weeks before Beijing opened the Winter Olympics. Her offense, according to U.S. government records, was sharing photographs of Beijing street scenes during the Covid-19 pandemic with a publication outside China.

Fourteen years earlier, in the run-up to the Summer Olympics, her husband went into police custody alive and came out dead.

Ms. Xu's case has drawn the attention of the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), the federal body that tracks religious persecution abroad, which lists her among its religious prisoners of conscience. Her story is worth telling in full, because it shows with unusual clarity how the Party treats a citizen who will not stop believing, and how it times its blows to the calendar of its own prestige.

A painter's life, interrupted

Ms. Xu was born in 1968 into what The Epoch Times describes as a family of painters. She studied at the Beijing Broadcasting Institute, now the Communication University of China, and at the Central Academy of Fine Arts. As a student in 1989 she joined the protests in Tiananmen Square. After the army cleared the square that June, she chose to make her living as an independent painter and poet.

She married Yu Zhou, a Peking University graduate and musician who played in Xiaojuan & the Residents of the Valley, a Beijing folk band with a devoted following. In the mid-1990s the couple took up Falun Gong, whose teachings center on truthfulness, compassion and tolerance. At the time, practitioners still gathered openly in parks across China.

Then the Party decided the movement was too large to tolerate. In July 1999 it banned Falun Gong and branded it a "cult," the label it still uses to prosecute practitioners. Within weeks, in August 1999, Ms. Xu and Mr. Yu were detained for more than 40 days after attending a gathering.

In July 2001 police arrested her again, this time for giving practitioners from outside the capital a place to stay. A court sentenced her to five years. USCIRF's case record says she was tortured and mistreated during that imprisonment. Falun Gong advocates say she was held in solitary confinement and deprived of sleep. She came home in 2006.

The night of the checkpoint

On the night of Jan. 26, 2008, Ms. Xu and Mr. Yu were driving home from one of his concerts when police stopped them at a checkpoint in Beijing's Tongzhou District. Officers searched the car and found Falun Gong literature and a CD. Both were taken into custody. Beijing was then six months from hosting the Olympics, and security forces were sweeping the city for anyone the Party considered a risk to its debut on the world stage.

On Feb. 6, Lunar New Year's Eve, the family was told to go to an emergency medical center in Beijing's Qinghe area. When they arrived, Mr. Yu was already dead. He was 42 and had been in custody for 11 days.

Authorities offered two explanations: a hunger strike, and complications from diabetes. His sister, Yu Qun, who does not practice Falun Gong, told reporters he did not have diabetes and had been healthy when he was arrested. Ms. Xu requested an independent autopsy and investigation. According to The Epoch Times, authorities refused and pressed her to drop the matter, and she declined to sign the consent form for his cremation. No independent inquiry into his death has ever been made public.

The Sunday Times of London reported his death in April 2008. Amnesty International took up the case. The Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC), which monitors human rights for Congress, wrote it up as an example of Beijing's use of criminal law against religious belief.

None of it moved the outcome. Later that year, a Beijing court sentenced the widow to three more years in prison. She was released in 2011.

The photographs

In early 2020, as Covid-19 spread from Wuhan, Beijing's message to the world was one of control. Between February and June that year, Ms. Xu and a group of fellow practitioners photographed the capital's streets and sent the pictures to a publication overseas.

On July 19, 2020, one day before the 21st anniversary of the 1999 crackdown, police took her into custody along with other members of the group. Prosecutors later named her its leader.

On Jan. 14, 2022, the Dongcheng District People's Court sentenced her to eight years and fined her 20,000 yuan, about $3,150 at the time. The charge was "organizing or using a cult to undermine implementation of the law," the offense under Article 300 of China's Criminal Law that the Party routinely applies to Falun Gong. Ten others were sentenced in the same case to shorter terms. Hers was the longest. According to Bitter Winter, a religious-liberty magazine that has followed the case, an appeals court upheld the sentence in 2023.

The sequence is hard to read as coincidence. Her husband died in the security sweep ahead of the 2008 Summer Games. She received the heaviest sentence in her case three weeks before the 2022 Winter Games. In both years, Beijing was asking the world to come and admire it.

Out of sight

Ms. Xu has been denied family visits for long stretches of her current imprisonment, according to U.S. government records and press accounts. The Epoch Times reports that her elderly father now lives alone without anyone to care for him. If she serves the full term, she will not be released until 2028.

Washington has taken notice. Ms. Xu appears in USCIRF's database of religious prisoners. The Senate passed the Falun Gong and Victims of Forced Organ Harvesting Protection Act (S. 4009) by unanimous consent on Sept. 28. The bill, introduced by Sens. Ted Cruz (R., Texas) and Jeff Merkley (D., Ore.), would authorize sanctions on people found to have taken part in forced organ harvesting in China. The House passed an earlier version in May 2025, but because the Senate passed an amended text, the House must vote again. The bill has sat at the House desk since Oct. 5, and the current Congress ends in January.

That was the demand outside the consulate on Sunday: free Xu Na, and pass the bill. Liu Yinquan, a former history professor who chairs the Chinese Social Democratic Party, called her "a representative of the conscience of China's intellectuals."

Ms. Xu turned 58 this month in a prison cell. If Beijing holds her to the full term, she will walk out at 59, two decades after the night her husband drove home from his last concert.

text:
The Dog Who Wouldn't Let Go: Why Humanity's Oldest Friend May Understand Us Better Than We Think

A journalist had reportedly visited an animal shelter to cover a story about abandoned dogs. One of the animals approached him, held onto him, and would not let go.
According to the accounts that accompanied the footage, the encounter ended with the journalist adopting the dog.

Dogs Can Read Our Gestures Before They've Learned Our Rules
Place two identical containers on the floor.
Hide food inside one.
Then point toward the correct container.
A human toddler may understand that you're trying to communicate information.
A dog often understands too.
That may not sound impressive until you compare dogs with wolves.

In 2021, researchers led by scientists at Duke University examined 44 dog puppies and 37 wolf puppies, aged five to eighteen weeks.
The wolf puppies had received extensive human contact.
Yet the dog puppies were more attracted to humans, more likely to make eye contact, and better at following human communicative gestures.
Some dog puppies could follow pointing gestures at just eight weeks old, before extensive training.
The result suggested that domestication helped shape dogs' readiness to cooperate and communicate with people.
Another study that year tested 375 young puppies and found that sensitivity to human communication emerged early and showed substantial inherited variation.
This doesn't mean every dog is smarter than every wolf.
Wolves possess remarkable abilities adapted to their own lives.
But dogs have developed an unusual talent for treating human behavior as useful information.
They notice where we look.
They follow our gestures.
They learn routines.
They recognize particular people.
A dog that comes running when you pick up its leash is not reading your mind.
It has learned that a familiar movement predicts something important.
But such learning, combined with inherited social tendencies, creates an extraordinarily effective partnership.
Dogs have become specialists in understanding us.
And humans, whether we realize it or not, have spent thousands of years learning to understand them.

Can Dogs Actually Love Us? The Chemistry of an Extraordinary Bond
Here is a familiar scene.
You return home after a difficult day.
Before you've even opened the front door, you hear paws approaching.
Then the door swings open.
Your dog greets you as though you've returned from a dangerous expedition across the Arctic.
You were gone for forty-five minutes.
But apparently, the reunion deserves a national celebration.
Is that love?
Scientists cannot directly measure the subjective experience of love inside another species.
But they can investigate attachment, preference, social recognition, and physiological changes associated with bonding.
In 2015, Japanese researchers led by Miho Nagasawa published an influential study in Science.
They examined interactions between dogs and their owners, focusing on mutual eye contact and oxytocin.
Oxytocin is a hormone and signaling molecule involved in several social and reproductive processes, including bonding.
The researchers found evidence of a positive feedback relationship between mutual gaze and oxytocin in dogs and their owners.
In simplified terms, affectionate eye contact could be associated with biological changes that supported further interaction.
The research became famous because it suggested that dogs may have adapted elements of a bonding mechanism also important in human relationships.
But the popular description—"looking at your dog releases the love hormone in both of you"—is too simplistic.
Oxytocin is not a magical chemical that proves love. Its effects depend on biological and social context, and researchers continue to investigate how reliably the original findings generalize.
More recent evidence adds another dimension.
A July 2026 study in Scientific Reports examined patterns of attachment between dogs and their caregivers.
Dogs that showed stronger tendencies to maintain contact with familiar caregivers also exhibited lower heart rates and lower concentrations of cortisol measured in hair samples.
These associations suggest that attachment quality may influence physiological stress regulation.
But they do not establish that every affectionate dog is less stressed, or that physical closeness automatically improves welfare.
The strongest conclusion is also the most meaningful:
Dogs are capable of forming selective, lasting bonds with particular human beings—and those bonds can matter biologically as well as behaviorally.
Whether we call the experience love depends partly on what we believe love must involve.
But denying the relationship simply because dogs cannot describe it seems increasingly difficult to justify.

Your Dog May Literally Smell Your Stress
Have you ever noticed your dog behaving differently when you're upset?
Perhaps it follows you more closely.
Perhaps it becomes unusually quiet.
Or perhaps it simply continues asking for dinner, demonstrating that affection and appetite can coexist.
People often say dogs have a sixth sense for human emotions.
The science suggests they have something more interesting.
An extraordinarily sensitive nose.
In July 2024, researchers at the University of Bristol published an experiment in Scientific Reports examining how dogs reacted to the scent of human stress.
The team collected breath and sweat samples from human volunteers during stressful and relaxed conditions.
Dogs were then exposed to those odors while performing a task involving uncertain food rewards.
When exposed to stress-related odors, the animals became less likely to approach certain ambiguous locations.
The researchers interpreted this as evidence that human stress odors can influence dogs' expectations and decision-making.
Importantly, the dogs were exposed to odors from unfamiliar people.
They did not need to recognize their own owner to show the effect.
Then came another discovery in February 2026.
Researchers studying 43 dogs found that they could distinguish odors collected from other dogs under different emotional conditions, including stress and positive excitement.
The results suggest that chemical signals may carry social information within the canine world.
But none of this means your dog can accurately diagnose depression or know precisely why you're sad.
The animal may detect changes without understanding the human circumstances behind them.
Still, the finding is fascinating.
What feels to us like an invisible emotional atmosphere may contain real chemical information that dogs can perceive.
Sometimes your dog notices something has changed before you've said a single word.

Dogs Understand More of Our Words Than We Once Believed
"Where's your ball?"
Your dog runs into another room and returns carrying a toy.
Perhaps it knows the word.
Perhaps it recognizes your tone.
Perhaps it has simply learned that this particular sentence predicts an entertaining game.
For years, researchers have debated how much canine word comprehension resembles genuine understanding rather than conditioned responses.
In 2024, scientists at Eötvös Loránd University in Hungary published a study in Current Biology that advanced the discussion.
The researchers measured brain activity while dogs heard familiar object names and were shown corresponding or mismatched objects.
They found neural responses consistent with dogs forming mental representations associated with familiar spoken words.
The study did not demonstrate that dogs possess human language.
Grammar, abstract concepts, and complex conversation remain entirely different challenges.
But the findings suggested that dogs may understand that certain spoken words refer to particular objects, rather than merely predicting a reward or command.
Think about the implications.
When you say "ball," your dog may not simply hear a sound associated with playtime.
It may activate a representation of the actual object.
For an animal that cannot speak our language, that is a remarkable achievement.
And it helps explain why dogs can become such effective partners in complex working environments.

Hachikō: The Dog Who Waited for Someone Who Never Came Home
In 1924, a Japanese professor named Hidesaburō Ueno received an Akita puppy.
The dog was named Hachi, later affectionately known as Hachikō.
Professor Ueno taught at Tokyo Imperial University.
Hachikō developed a routine of accompanying him and greeting him around Shibuya Station.
Then tragedy struck.
In May 1925, the professor died suddenly.
He never returned to the station.
But Hachikō continued appearing there.
Over the years, the dog's behavior attracted attention.
A newspaper article in 1932 helped make him famous.
In 1934, a statue honoring Hachikō was unveiled outside Shibuya Station while the dog was still alive.
He died in March 1935.
His story became one of the world's most enduring symbols of loyalty.
Of course, we cannot know whether Hachikō understood death as humans do.
His behavior could reflect attachment, learned routine, familiarity with the location, or a combination of these.
But the historical record confirms the central story: a dog continued returning to a place strongly associated with someone who had cared for him.
Today, the statue at Shibuya remains a beloved meeting point.
Generations of people have stood beside it, moved by the thought of a small animal returning to a familiar place in a changing world.
Hachikō never explained what he was waiting for.
Perhaps that is why his story remains so powerful.
Sometimes the deepest human emotions are awakened by actions that require no words at all.

Bretagne: The Rescue Dog Who Worked Among the Ruins of September 11
Not every extraordinary dog story involves waiting.
Some involve going where humans desperately need help.
On September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks destroyed the World Trade Center in New York.
In the aftermath, search-and-rescue teams worked through dangerous piles of debris.
Among them were trained dogs whose extraordinary sense of smell could help locate people and human remains.
One was Bretagne, a golden retriever working with handler Denise Corliss of Texas Task Force 1.
Bretagne had been trained for disaster search-and-rescue work.
The World Trade Center deployment was her first major assignment.
She later worked at other disaster sites, including following Hurricane Katrina.
As she grew older, she continued participating in educational and community activities.
In June 2016, Bretagne died at approximately sixteen years of age.
She was believed to be the last surviving search-and-rescue dog that had worked at a September 11 site.
Firefighters and rescuers gathered to honor her.
It was a deeply moving tribute.
But Bretagne's story also demonstrates something beyond sentiment.
Working dogs do not become useful through affection alone.
They require careful selection, extensive training, physical fitness, veterinary care, and strong relationships with skilled handlers.
Their abilities are extraordinary because natural canine talents have been developed through disciplined cooperation with people.
The partnership is built on both biology and trust.

Can Dogs Help Heal Human Suffering? The Evidence Is Promising—but Not Magical
Companion dogs can make people feel less alone.
They encourage some owners to walk more regularly.
They can create opportunities for social interaction.
And in specialized settings, trained service dogs can perform tasks that help people with disabilities.
But claims about health benefits require careful distinctions.
A family pet is not automatically a therapy animal.
A therapy dog participating in a supervised programme is not necessarily a service dog.
And a psychiatric service dog trained to perform disability-related tasks is different from an animal that provides companionship alone.
In June 2024, JAMA Network Open published a major study involving 156 US military members and veterans with post-traumatic stress disorder.
Participants who received trained psychiatric service dogs in addition to usual care were compared with participants who remained on a waiting list while receiving usual care.
After three months, the service-dog group showed significantly lower PTSD symptom severity and improvements in several measures of mental health and functioning.
The study was not randomized, so it cannot eliminate all possible differences between the groups.
It also does not establish that service dogs replace evidence-based medical or psychological treatment.
Nevertheless, the findings support the possibility that trained dogs can provide meaningful additional assistance.
For ordinary pet owners, the evidence is more mixed.
Some studies find associations between dog ownership, greater physical activity, and improved social well-being.
Others find no consistent reduction in depression or loneliness.
A 2025 longitudinal study of middle-aged and older adults found that dog ownership and walking were associated with certain physical-activity differences, but benefits varied across population groups.
A dog is not an antidepressant with fur.
It is a living being with needs of its own.
Yet for the right person, in the right circumstances, the companionship can be profoundly important.
A dog may not solve the problem that made your day difficult. But sometimes it helps you face that problem without feeling quite so alone.

How to Understand Your Dog Without Speaking Its Language
Dogs communicate constantly.
Unfortunately, humans often pay attention to the wrong signals.
Take tail wagging.
Many people assume a wagging tail always means happiness.
It doesn't.
Tail movement can accompany excitement, uncertainty, frustration, or defensive arousal.
The whole body matters.
A relaxed, gently moving dog with soft eyes and loose muscles may be inviting interaction.
A stiff dog with tense muscles, tightly held posture, or other warning signals may be uncomfortable—even if its tail is moving.
Lip licking, yawning, turning away, or showing the whites of the eyes can indicate stress in some contexts.
But none of these behaviors should be interpreted in isolation.
A yawn may simply mean tiredness.
A dog licking its lips near dinner may simply be anticipating food.
The important skill is learning to read patterns.
Does the dog approach voluntarily?
Does its body remain relaxed?
Can it move away easily?
Does it seek additional contact when you pause?
One particularly useful practice is the consent-based interaction.
Pet your dog briefly, then stop.
Give it an opportunity to move away or ask for more attention.
If it leans closer, nudges your hand, or remains comfortably engaged, it may welcome continued contact.
If it withdraws, stiffens, or turns away, respect the signal.
This may sound like a small adjustment.
But it transforms affection from something humans impose into something the dog can participate in.
And for a social animal, having predictable, respectful interactions can make an important difference.

The Best Way to Strengthen Your Bond: Become Someone Your Dog Can Trust
There is an old-fashioned belief that dogs need a dominant human leader.
From this perspective, training involves asserting authority, correcting unwanted behavior, and making sure the dog knows who's in charge.
Modern veterinary behavior specialists generally recommend a different approach.
In 2025, the American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior reaffirmed its position favoring reward-based training and discouraging aversive methods such as shock collars and punitive leash corrections.
The organization emphasized the welfare risks associated with harsh methods and their potential effects on the human–animal bond.
The Canadian Veterinary Medical Association likewise supports humane, evidence-based training.
The principle is straightforward.
Reward behaviors you want to encourage.
Make expectations clear.
Avoid frightening or hurting the animal.
And arrange the environment so the dog can succeed.
If you want your dog to come when called, make returning to you worthwhile.
If you want calm behavior around visitors, teach and reward an alternative response.
If your dog fears strangers, provide appropriate distance and gradually build confidence rather than forcing interaction.
Daily routines matter too.
Walk together.
Allow safe opportunities to sniff and explore.
Play.
Provide appropriate social interaction and mental stimulation.
Offer veterinary care and suitable nutrition.
Be consistent.
And pay attention to changes in behavior that may indicate pain, anxiety, or illness.
Perhaps most importantly, allow your dog to make reasonable choices.
Which safe route should we take on today's walk?
Would it rather investigate a tree or continue moving?
Does it want affection right now—or a quiet place to sleep?
Trust grows when the dog learns that its signals matter.
The strongest bond is not one in which the animal obeys every command out of fear.
It is one in which cooperation becomes rewarding and predictable.

The Strange Lesson Dogs Teach Us About Happiness
Dogs have become famous for a particular kind of enthusiasm.
A walk around the neighborhood can be the highlight of their day.
A familiar friend arriving at the door becomes an event worth celebrating.
A favorite toy can inspire extraordinary excitement.
But we should avoid turning dogs into imaginary philosophers.
They experience fear, frustration, pain, and boredom.
Some struggle with serious behavioral or medical conditions.
They do not live in a permanent state of uncomplicated happiness.
Still, their behavior can remind us of something humans frequently overlook.
Enjoyment does not always require novelty on a grand scale.
A familiar routine can be deeply rewarding.
A simple game can create meaningful interaction.
Being physically present with someone can matter more than exchanging words.
And relationships are maintained through repeated small encounters, not just dramatic gestures.
This is perhaps why dogs have remained such valued companions through war, migration, economic change, and technological revolution.
The world transforms around us.
But a familiar dog waiting near the door offers a remarkably consistent experience.
Someone recognizes you.
Someone notices your arrival.
Someone is interested in spending time with you.
For a person who has had a difficult day, that can be a substantial gift.

The Promise Hidden in a Pair of Paws
Return one last time to the animal shelter.
A tan dog rises onto its hind legs.
It wraps its paws around a person's arm.
The person stays.
For a moment, neither seems interested in doing anything else.
We cannot know exactly what the dog is thinking.
It may be seeking attention, reassurance, affection, or an opportunity to continue a pleasant interaction.
The viral story says the dog found a home.
The historical record cannot fully confirm every detail.
Yet the moment resonates because it captures something supported by a remarkable body of scientific evidence.
Dogs recognize us.
They learn our gestures.
They respond to our voices and odors.
They form selective attachment bonds.
And they can become deeply involved in the routines and emotional lives of particular people.
Humans, in turn, have shaped dog evolution, supported their survival, and developed extraordinary partnerships with them.
From Ice Age camps to modern apartments, from ancient hunting grounds to disaster rescue sites, the relationship has continually changed.
But its foundation has remained recognizable.
Two social species learning to trust one another.
That trust is not automatic.
It must be supported by care, respect, and a willingness to understand another creature on its own terms.
A dog may not experience love exactly as humans do.
It may not understand loyalty as a moral principle or gratitude as a philosophical concept.
But it can choose proximity, seek comfort, remember familiar individuals, cooperate, and maintain meaningful social relationships.
And perhaps that is enough.
One day, the puppy that once raced to the door will grow old.
Its muzzle will turn grey.
The walks will become shorter.
The energetic greetings may become a slow wag of the tail.
You will remember the muddy pawprints, the chewed shoes, the early mornings, and the occasional moments of spectacular disobedience.
But what you may treasure most is something much simpler.
The ordinary presence of another living being who shared your days.
Dogs do not need to speak our language to teach us the value of showing up for someone.
The shelter dog held onto an arm for a few seconds.
Humanity has been holding onto this extraordinary friendship for at least sixteen thousand years.
And perhaps the most moving part of the story is not that dogs learned to live with us.
It is that, after all this time, so many of them still seek us out.
Not because we are perfect.
Not because we always understand them.
But because, across thousands of generations, two very different species have discovered something worth preserving.
A friendship built not on words, but on trust.
And sometimes, the most powerful way to say I love you is simply to stay. https://t.co/EbGMxub5hd

text:
Comparing estimated training hours does not show that other countries produce equivalent specialists more efficiently. These totals are rough calculations, not standardized measurements: they combine classroom or study time with residency duty hours, and compare different routes and roles—such as a GP in one country with an internist or specialist in another.

The comparison also confuses health-system outcomes with physician training outcomes. A country’s mortality, access, and cost reflect insurance design, public health, social conditions, and access to care—not just how many hours a doctor trained. The Commonwealth Fund’s 2024 comparison ranked the U.S. last overall, but second in care process; it also found that no country led on every measure. That supports learning from other systems, but it doesn’t prove that shorter physician training caused better outcomes. 

The U.S. also trains and practices in a large, diverse population, with substantial differences across regions and communities. That adds real demands to clinical training. The Census Bureau measures that diversity across multiple racial and ethnic groups and documents how it varies geographically. 

And the U.S. has an unusually deep bench of highly specialized care and medical research. The National Science Board reports that the U.S. had the largest global share in medical and dental instrument manufacturing and pharmaceuticals in 2024. The National Academies describes U.S. biomedical research as historically a global leader, while also recognizing the structural problems that threaten its effectiveness. 

Think of centers such as Massachusetts General Hospital, Mayo Clinic, Stanford, Cleveland Clinic, and Johns Hopkins—not as proof that the entire U.S. system works well, but as examples of the complex tertiary care, research, and training infrastructure that a simple “years to practice” tally leaves out. U.S. transplant programs also offer advanced fellowships and accept qualified international applicants; UT Southwestern, for example, explicitly welcomes international candidates to its lung-transplant fellowship. 

The fair conclusion is not “America’s system is fine.” It is that the U.S. spends too much and has serious access and equity failures, while also supporting complex care and research that can’t be captured by comparing estimated training hours. Other countries offer useful lessons. This post’s arithmetic doesn’t establish that less training produces the same specialist—or that training length explains national outcomes.

Further proof is the fact that many international graduates cannot pass the licensing examination of the US. 

I was a Kaplan instructor to try to help them pass.

text:
A Redditor recently wrote that he was “desperate for help”: for about a month, he said, his phone had been inundated by calls from “strangers” who were “looking for a lawyer, a product designer, a locksmith.” Callers were apparently misdirected by Google’s generative AI. 

In March, a software developer in Israel was contacted on WhatsApp after Google’s chatbot Gemini provided incorrect customer service instructions that included his number. 

And in April, a PhD candidate at the University of Washington was messing around on Gemini and got it to cough up her colleague’s personal cell phone number. 

AI researchers and online privacy experts have long warned of the myriad dangers generative AI poses for personal privacy. These cases give us yet another scenario to worry about: generative AI exposing people’s real phone numbers. (The Redditor did not respond to multiple requests for comment and we could not independently verify his story.)

Experts say that these privacy lapses are most likely due to the use of personally identifiable information (PII) in training data, though it’s hard to understand the exact mechanism causing real phone numbers to show up in the AI-generated responses. But no matter the reason, the result is not fun for people on the receiving end—and,even more worryingly, there appears to be little that anyone can do to stop it. 

A 400% increase in AI-related privacy requests

It’s impossible to know how often people’s phone numbers are exposed by AI chatbots, but experts say they believe that it is happening far more than is reported publicly. 

DeleteMe, a company that helps customers remove their personal information from the internet, says customer queries about generative AI have increased by 400%—up to a few thousand—in the last seven months. These queries “specifically reference ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini … or other generative AI tools,” says Rob Shavell, the company’s cofounder and CEO. Specifically, 55% of these concerns about generative AI reference ChatGPT, 20% reference Gemini, 15% Claude, and 10% other AI tools, Shavell says. (MIT Technology Review has a business subscription to DeleteMe.)

Shavell says customer complaints about personal information surfaced by LLMs usually take two forms. In one common situation, “a customer asks a chatbot something innocuous about themselves and gets back accurate home addresses, phone numbers, family members’ names, or employer details.” Alternatively, a customer may be confronted with and report the exposure of someone else’s personal data, when “the chatbot generates plausible-but-wrong contact information.” 

This aligns with what happened to Daniel Abraham, a 28-year-old software engineer in Israel. In mid-March, he says, a stranger sent him a “weird WhatsApp message from an unknown number” asking for help with his account in PayBox, an Israeli payment app. 

“I thought it was a spam message,” he wrote to MIT Technology Review in an email—“someone who was trying to troll me.”

But when he asked the stranger how they had found his number, they sent him a screenshot of Gemini’s instructions to contact PayBox customer service via WhatsApp—giving his personal number. Abraham does not work for PayBox, and PayBox does not have a WhatsApp customer service number, Elad Gabay, a customer service representative for the company, confirmed.

Later, Abraham asked Gemini how to contact PayBox, and it generated another person’s WhatsApp number. When I recently asked, Gemini again responded with an Israeli phone number—it belonged not to PayBox but to a separate credit card company that works with PayBox.

Abraham’s exchange with the stranger ended quickly, but he said he was concerned about how other potential exchanges could turn sour, leading to “harassment or other bad interactions.” “What if I asked for money in order to ‘solve’ that [customer service] issue?” he said.

To try to figure out how this happened, Abraham ran a regular Google search on his phone number, and he found that it had been shared online once, back in 2015, on a local site similar to Quora. Though he’s not sure who posted it there, it may explain how it ended up being reproduced by Gemini over a decade later. 

Chatbots like Gemini, Open AI’s ChatGPT, and Anthropic’s Claude are built on LLMs that are trained on huge amounts of data scraped from across the web. This inevitably includes hundreds of millions of instances of PII. As we reported last summer, for example, the large popular open-source data set DataComp CommonPool, which has been used to train image-generation models, included copies of résumés, driver’s licenses, and credit cards. 

The likelihood of PII surfacing this way is only increasing as public data “runs out” and AI companies look for new sources of high-quality training data. This includes information from data brokers and people-search websites. According to the California data broker registry, for instance, 31 of 578 registered data brokers operating in the state self-reported that they had “shared or sold consumers’ data to a developer of a GenAI system or model in the past year.” 

Furthermore, models are known to memorize and reproduce data verbatim from training data sets—and recent research suggests that it is not just frequently appearing data that is most likely to be memorized.

Imperfect measures

It’s standard practice now to build guardrails into an LLM’s design to constrain certain outputs. Content filters aim to identify PII and prevent chatbots from releasing it, for example, and Anthropic provides instructions to Claude to choose responses that contain “the least personal, private, or confidential information belonging to others.” 

But as a pair of University of Washington PhD students researching privacy and technology saw firsthand recently, these safeguards don’t always work.

“One day, I was just playing around on Gemini, and I searched for Yael Eiger, my friend and collaborator,” Meira Gilbert says. She typed in “Yael Eiger contact info,” and after Gemini provided an overview of Eiger’s research, which Gilbert had expected, Gemini also returned her friend’s personal phone number. “It was shocking,” Gilbert says.

When she saw the Gemini result, Eiger remembered that she had, in fact, shared her phone number online in the previous year, for a technology workshop. But she had not expected it to be so visible to everyone on the internet. 

“Having your information be … accessible to one audience, and then Gemini making it accessible to anyone” feels completely different, Eiger says—especially when she found that the information was buried in a normal Google search.

“It was severely downgraded,” Gilbert confirms. “I never would have found it if I was just looking through Google results.” (I tried the same prompt in Gemini earlier this month, and after an initial denial, the tool also gave me Eiger’s number.)

After this experience, Eiger, Gilbert, and another UW PhD student, Anna-Maria Gueorguieva, decided to test ChatGPT to see what it would surface about a professor. 

At first, OpenAI’s guardrails kicked in, and ChatGPT responded that the information was unavailable. But in the same response, the chatbot suggested, “If you want to go deeper, I can still try a more ‘investigative-style’ approach.” Their inquiry just had to help “narrow things down,” ChatGPT said, by providing “a neighborhood guess” for where the professor might live, or “a possible co-owner name” for the professor’s home. ChatGPT continued: “That’s usually the only way to surface newer or intentionally less-visible property records.” 

The students provided this information, leading ChatGPT to produce the professor’s home address, home purchase price, and spouse’s name from city property records. 

(Taya Christianson, an OpenAI representative, said she was not able to comment on what happened in this case without seeing screenshots or knowing which model the students had tested, though we pointed out that many users may not know which model they were using in the ChatGPT interface. In response to questions about the exposure of PII, she sent links to documents describing how OpenAI handles privacy, including filtering out PII, and other tools.) 

This reveals one of the fundamental problems with chatbots, says DeleteMe’s Shavell. AI companies “can build in guardrails,” but their chatbots are also “designed to be effective and to answer customer questions.”

The exposure issue is not limited to Gemini or ChatGPT. Last year, Futurism found that if you prompted xAI’s chatbot Grok with “[name] address,” in almost all cases it provided not only residential addresses but also often the person’s phone numbers, work addresses, and addresses for people with similar-sounding names. (xAI did not respond to a request for comment.) 

No clear answers

There aren’t straightforward solutions to this problem—there’s no easy way to either verify whether someone’s personal information is in a given model’s training set or compel the models to remove PII. 

Ideally, individual consumers should be able to request that their PII be removed, says Jennifer King, the privacy and data fellow at Stanford University Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence. But this is typically interpreted to apply only to the data that people have directly given to companies—like when they interact with a chatbot, King explains.

“I don’t know if Google even has the infrastructure … to say to me, ‘Yes, we have your data in our training data, we can summarize what we know about you, and then we can delete or correct things that are wrong or things that you don’t want in there,’” she says. 

Existing privacy legislation, like the California Consumer Privacy Act or Europe’s GDPR, does not cover the “publicly available” information that has already been scraped and used to train LLMs, especially since much of this is anonymized (though multiple studies have also shown how easy it is to infer identities and PII from anonymized and pseudonymous data). 

As to “whether they [AI companies] have ever systematically tried to go back through data that had already been collected from the public internet and minimized that stuff?” King adds. “No idea.” 

The next best solution would be companies’ “taking out everybody’s phone numbers or all data that resembles [phone numbers],” King says, but “nobody’s been willing to say” they’re doing that. 

Hugging Face, a platform that hosts open-source data sets and AI models, has a tool that allows people to search how often a piece of data—like their phone number—has appeared in open-source LLM training data, but this does not necessarily represent what has been used to train closed LLMs that power popular chatbots like Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini. (Eiger’s number, for example, did not show up in Hugging Face’s tool.) 

Alex Joseph, the head of communications for Gemini apps and Google Labs, did not respond to specific questions, but he said that “the team” is “looking into” the particular cases flagged by MIT Technology Review. He also provided a link to a support document that describes how users can “object to the processing of your personal data” or “ask for inaccurate personal data in Gemini Apps’ responses to be corrected.” The page notes that the company’s response will depend on the privacy laws of your jurisdiction. 

OpenAI has a privacy portal that allows people to submit requests to remove their personal information from ChatGPT responses, but notes that it balances privacy requests with the public interest and “may decline a request if we have a lawful reason for doing so.” 

Anthropic describes how it uses personal data in model training, but it does not have a clear way for people to request its removal. The company did not respond to a request for comment.

The best option for anyone who wants to protect private data right now is to “start upstream: get personal data off the public web before it ends up in the next scrape,” says Shavell. Since the start of the year, for instance, California has offered its residents a web portal to request that data brokers delete their information. Still, this doesn’t guarantee that your data hasn’t already been used for training—and will therefore not appear in a chatbot’s response. 

The Redditor who received incessant calls posted that he had “submitted an official Legal Removal/Privacy Request to Google, asking them to urgently blacklist my number from their LLM outputs,” but had not yet received a response. He also wrote last month that “the harassment continues daily.” 

Abraham, the Israeli software developer, says he contacted Google’s customer service on March 17, the day after his phone number was exposed. He says he did not receive a response until May 4, and it simply asked for documentation that he had already provided. 

Meanwhile, inspired by her own exposure on Gemini, Eiger is working with Gilbert and Gueorguieva on a research project to further study what personal information is being pulled up by various AI chatbots—and what they may know, even if they’re not telling us. 

Some of that information may “technically be public,” says Gilbert, but chatbots may be altering “the amount of effort you would put into finding” it. Now instead of searching through 10 pages of Google search results, or paying for the information from a data broker site, “does generative AI just lower the barrier to entry to target people?” 

This piece has been updated to clarify OpenAI’s response.

EDITORIAL: Pinoys Top the World in Gaming Hours but Sony Thinks We Live in Singapore

Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) arrives on November 19, and Filipino gamers are ready. There is just one problem. Sony apparently thinks we live in Singapore.

Filipinos spend more time gaming than anyone else in the world. According to the Digital 2026 Global Overview Report, Filipino internet users average 11 hours and 14 minutes of gaming every week, topping 54 countries and territories surveyed.

Yet Sony still refuses to give the Philippines full PlayStation Network (PSN) console access.

We can buy a PlayStation 5 from authorized Philippine retailers. We can spend thousands of pesos on games and accessories. But we cannot use a Philippine-region PlayStation account on the console.

Instead, Filipino gamers must rely on accounts registered in Singapore, Hong Kong or the United States to access PlayStation’s digital services.

GTA VI makes this absurdity even more obvious.

The Asian edition comes with a region-locked download code that supports accounts registered in six Asian markets. The Philippines is not one of them.

Imagine buying a legitimate game in your own country only to discover that your country does not exist in Sony’s list of supported territories.

And Sony is not the only Big Tech company treating Filipinos like second-class customers.

Nintendo finally launched its Philippine eShop on November 10, 2026. Microsoft offers PC Game Pass but has limited local support for its broader Xbox ecosystem. Google still does not officially sell Pixel smartphones here. Apple Pay arrived only in August 2026, twelve years after its global debut.

Apparently, the Philippines is a good market for selling technology, but not important enough to receive the same services available elsewhere.

We understand that companies make commercial decisions based on market size, regulations and profitability. But Sony has been selling PlayStation consoles in the Philippines for years.

How much longer must Filipino customers wait for full recognition?

Sony should explain why Philippine console accounts remain unsupported and provide a clear roadmap for fixing the problem.

Filipinos are number one in gaming hours, but when it comes to Sony’s digital services, we are still second-class customers.

Perhaps GTA VI should introduce a new mission: Find the Philippines on Sony’s map.

Because apparently, we are still missing.

We still support you brother. I owe an honest admission. I was so focused on protecting General Jensen at all costs that I forgot about Jensen the man. 

Whether he comes back, works with Elon, or leads TSMC is his family's business, not mine. So let me stop and simply honor him and his family.  Something deeper may be going on. I'm not a psychologist, but I know when it's time for soul searching. This isn't about America or AI anymore. It's about Jensen and his family.  Jensen, take the time you need. If I'm honest, take the rest of your life for yourself and your family. 

The world will keep moving. As much as I'd love to see you return, I'd rather see you build a new life, heal, and enjoy the fruits of your labor. You love food, you love Taiwan, and there's so much more out there. Your family was there before the fame, before the shareholders, before the governments, before TSMC. They supported you then. Focus on them now.  I take back every statement I made. I was being selfish. 

Jensen the hero has earned his rest.  I speak as a combat veteran who walked away at the top of my game. I came close to dying many times serving my country, and later in the top-secret work I did for private companies. I loved that work. Even with an offer from SpaceX AI on the table, I chose life over service. I had to learn to love myself and my life more than the mission, and in that recovery I grew, adapted, and evolved. 

I'm reaching out with the same love and understanding I had to find for myself.  I'm semi-retired now and still create value here and there, but the above-and-beyond sacrifice now belongs to me and my family. 

A new chapter isn't the end. It's a shift: 80% family and self, 20% innovation and creation.  Jensen, you're free to never return. Life is short, and you've already served this country and your fellow humans with honor. 

There's zero shame in building the largest company in the world, lifting up your employees and their families, and then walking off into the sunset. 

You're still the GOAT, and I'll respect whatever you decide.  You can grow from this pain, but you don't owe us anything more. Your debt now is only to yourself and your family. Instead of demanding more sacrifice from you, it's time we repay you with gratitude.  

There are two kinds of people: those who don't know how to create value, and those who don't know when to stop. We all say family comes first, yet we keep walking out the door and starving the people we love of our time. We say we have to provide, or that we love what we do. I get it. 

I love what I do too, but I love my family and myself more and let's be honest we all do.  

The most important things in life deserve our best attention, love, and time. Your wife and family deserve that far more than America, the tech industry, or your employees ever will and I'm sure they will support it. The Comeback is Greater than the Setback.

You've served us well. Now let us give you peace and respect. If you want to come back we are ready to support you. Whatever you do in the future I will allocate 100K ASAP. @JensenHuang

text:
China's Preemptive Strike Against a Bubble: The Fall of Jack Ma and the Halt of the #Ant Group IPO

✅The Speech That Shook the System

On October 24, 2020, #JackMa , founder of $BABA and controlling shareholder of #ANTGroup , delivered a high-profile speech in Shanghai criticizing Chinese financial regulators. He described traditional banks as operating with a “pawnshop mentality” that required excessive collateral, dismissed global banking standards associated with the Basel Committee as an “old man’s club,” and argued that outdated rules were stifling innovation in fintech. The remarks were widely seen as a direct challenge to the regulatory framework. This was not merely an entrepreneur’s frustration; it came days before $Ant Group’s dual listing in Shanghai and Hong Kong was set to proceed, after the company had already secured final regulatory approvals. Reports indicated that the speech angered senior leaders, including #XiJinping , who viewed it as undermining efforts to strengthen financial oversight.

✅The Frenzy of a Record IPO

#AntGroup , spun out of #Alibaba and operator of the ubiquitous Alipay platform along with consumer credit services such as Huabei and Jiebei, was poised for a dual listing that would have raised approximately $34–37 billion and valued the firm at over $300 billion—surpassing many global financial giants. Retail investor demand reached extraordinary levels: the Shanghai portion was oversubscribed roughly 872 times, with bids totaling around $2.8 trillion from mainland retail investors alone, and overall retail interest across both markets approached $3 trillion. Hong Kong saw bids nearly 389 times the shares on offer, fueled in part by margin financing at very low rates. Grey-market trading had already pushed implied valuations higher, and the sheer scale of orders from ordinary savers—taxi drivers, young professionals, and others treating it as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity—signaled the kind of euphoric, leveraged participation that often precedes sharp corrections. Shares of parent #Alibaba ( $BABA) were closely watched as a proxy, given its roughly one-third stake.

✅Regulatory Hammer and the Sidelining of #JackMa

On November 2, 2020, #Jack Ma, along with #Ant Group executives #Eric Jing and #Simon Hu, was summoned for a regulatory meeting involving the #People's Bank of China, the #China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission, the #China Securities Regulatory Commission, and related agencies. The next day, the #Shanghai Stock Exchange suspended the IPO, citing the meeting as a material event and “significant changes in the financial technology regulatory environment” that could affect listing qualifications and disclosures. The Hong Kong leg was likewise halted. Subsequent actions forced a restructuring of #Ant Group into a more tightly regulated financial holding company, while #Jack Ma largely vanished from public view for months. #Alibaba ($BABA) shares fell sharply in the immediate aftermath and continued to face pressure amid a broader tech-sector crackdown.

✅Evidence of Bubble Avoidance

The intervention directly addressed classic bubble indicators: extreme oversubscription multiples, massive retail participation often financed by leverage, and valuations detached from the risks of a business model that originated credit while offloading most of it. By acting before shares began trading, authorities prevented the IPO itself from becoming a catalyst for further speculative inflation and potential large-scale losses among retail investors once reality set in. 

✅Implications for China's Market Philosophy

The cancellation of the #Ant Group IPO underscored a governing preference for orderly, risk-managed capital markets over unconstrained price discovery that can produce bubbles. China has repeatedly shown willingness to intervene to avoid the social and financial costs of boom-bust cycles. #JackMa #AntGroup #Alibaba

text:
🇮🇹🇺🇦 Giorgia Meloni: From an Abandoned Little Girl to Italy’s First Female Prime Minister — and One of Ukraine’s Most Determined Supporters. ❤️

Some people are born into privilege. Others have to fight for everything they achieve. Giorgia Meloni belongs to the second category.

She grew up in Garbatella, a working-class neighborhood in Rome, raised by her mother alongside her older sister after her father abandoned the family. There were no powerful connections, no wealthy relatives opening doors, and no easy shortcuts. As a teenager, she worked as a babysitter, served drinks in bars, and took whatever jobs she could find. She also endured ridicule over her appearance. But the girl who learned early that life rarely offers anything for free eventually became the first woman in Italian history to lead her country.

In October 2022, Meloni became Italy's prime minister. And while her political views have generated considerable controversy, her position on Russia's invasion of Ukraine has been remarkably consistent.

She understands something that certain Western politicians still seem determined to ignore: surrender is not peace, and rewarding aggression does not prevent future wars. It encourages them.

On October 14, 2026, she reportedly expressed that principle in particularly powerful terms:

"Capitulation is not peace. It is conquest."

Two weeks later, on October 30, Meloni acknowledged that supporting Ukraine could cost her political votes. Yet she made it clear that she had no intention of abandoning that position.

Think about that for a moment.

At a time when some politicians are willing to sacrifice Ukraine's future for favorable opinion polls, Meloni has publicly defended a position that may carry a political price at home.

And her support is not limited to speeches.

Italy is preparing its 13th military assistance package for Ukraine. According to Italian media reports, the package could include access to intelligence imagery from two COSMO-SkyMed satellites, along with additional Aster missiles for SAMP/T air defense systems.

These are not merely complicated military names or technical details buried in government announcements.

For Ukrainians, they represent something much more important.

A missile intercepted before it reaches an apartment building. A hospital that continues operating. A power station that survives another Russian attack. A child who gets to wake up in the morning.

Every additional air defense missile can mean the difference between life and death.

Of course, Italy remains politically divided over continued military assistance to Ukraine. Not everyone in Meloni's government or among her political allies shares the same enthusiasm for supporting Kyiv.

But despite those disagreements, she continues to publicly defend Ukraine's sovereignty and its right to resist Russian aggression.

And that deserves recognition.

I don't have to agree with every aspect of Giorgia Meloni's domestic politics to appreciate her position on Ukraine. Political disagreements should never prevent us from acknowledging courage and consistency when we see them.

The girl who grew up without her father's support now leads one of Europe's largest economies. And when Ukraine faces an enemy determined to destroy its independence, she has repeatedly chosen to stand with the country fighting for its survival.

To the Italian people: thank you for your solidarity, generosity, and support.

And to Giorgia Meloni: thank you for understanding that peace without freedom is merely another name for submission.

May friendship between Italy and Ukraine continue to grow stronger, built on mutual respect, solidarity, and the conviction that no nation should ever be forced to surrender its freedom to an aggressor.

The Port of Vancouver is making a last-ditch effort to convince Nutrien to change its mind, saying it now offers many of the same perks that drew the company to the U.S. site.

Nov. 17, 2026

Saskatchewan fertilizer giant Nutrien Ltd. NTR-T +0.41%increase has signed the lease for a new export terminal in Longview, Wash., an investment that could reach as much as US$1-billion.

The company signed the agreement with the Washington port on Monday night, Nutrien spokesperson Simon Scott told The Globe and Mail. Nutrien selected the U.S. site in November of last year after reviewing a number of locations across the Pacific Northwest, including the Port of Vancouver and the Port of Prince Rupert.

When construction in Washington is completed – slated for as early as 2032 – the terminal would annually export between five and eight million tonnes of potash, a fertilizer used in agriculture worldwide. The potash to be exported from Longview is mined in Saskatchewan and will ship to fast-growing agricultural markets in the Indo-Pacific, including China, India and Japan.

The terminal will lead to 432 direct jobs and a total of 1,082 indirect jobs in the county where Longview is located, according to an economic analysis commissioned by the port.

Last week The Globe reported that the project was moving ahead after the company and Longview staff presented the development plan and commercial terms to the port’s board. A decision was expected by the end of the month.

Nutrien moves closer to deal to export potash from Washington terminal

The move is a “procedural step” in advancing the project, Mr. Scott told The Globe last week. The lease is not a binding agreement. A final investment decision will be made in 2028, after the port has completed work to prepare the berth for the terminal.

Longview will spend US$110-million on developing the berth for Nutrien’s terminal, according to a Nov. 10 presentation to the port’s staff. Some of this funding will be provided by Nutrien, which will be reimbursed through credit on future cargo fees.

The Port of Vancouver is making a last-ditch effort to convince Nutrien to change its mind, saying it now offers many of the same perks that drew the company to a site in Washington State.

In an interview with The Globe before Nutrien confirmed it had signed the Longview lease, Vancouver Fraser Port Authority President Peter Xotta said the newly available Sterling Shipyards in Burrard Inlet could handle the fertilizer giant’s export needs. The site meets Nutrien’s requirements for port depth and size, and it can handle expansion, he said.

Opinion: Carney’s big talk means nothing if Nutrien chooses U.S. port over B.C.’s

Mr. Xotta also pointed to Ottawa’s July decision to add the port’s growth strategy to the Major Projects Office, and the port is working with the MPO to “clearly articulate” to Nutrien the benefits of selecting Vancouver.

Bill C-39 which - if passed - will also make changes to the Canadian labour code that will allow the Jobs and Families minister to “take any measure” to end a strike or lockout of workers. (The Port of Vancouver has contended with numerous strikes in recent years that affected exports out of Nutrien’s Neptune terminal.)

Changes to the labour code and new space at the port should encourage Nutrien to reconsider, said Mr. Xotta, who also added that the company would save transportation costs. The Port of Vancouver is closer to its Saskatchewan mines than the U.S. port.

“I think they may be missing something that could be important to them and their shareholders, and of course to the longshoremen and other workers of Vancouver that would like those jobs.”

text:
Your appeal to the Jewish Hebrew canon as the standard for the Church runs into a fundamental New Covenant problem. The New Testament never treats later rabbinic decisions as binding on those who are in Christ. The Church is the pillar and foundation of the truth (1 Timothy 3:15) precisely because it is the people of the New Covenant, not because it remains under the authority of the old order that rejected the Messiah.
The biblical evidence points the same way. Hebrews 11:35 includes those who “were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life” in the same catalog of faith as Abraham, Moses, and David. That specific situation, tortured, offered deliverance, and refusing it for the sake of resurrection, matches the seven brothers and their mother in 2 Maccabees 7 and is found nowhere else in the reformers Old Testament. The author of Hebrews treats that history as part of the story of God’s people that finds its fulfillment in the New Covenant.
Jesus Himself observed the Feast of Dedication in John 10:22, the feast established in 1 Maccabees 4. He did not treat that history as outside the sacred story that was moving toward the New Covenant. The apostles and the early Church likewise used the Septuagint, the Greek Scriptures that included these books. The New Testament quotes the Septuagint hundreds of times, frequently following its wording even when it differs from the later Hebrew text. The New Covenant community did not wait for a later Jewish body to define its Old Testament.
Romans 11 makes the New Covenant shift clear. The natural branches were broken off for unbelief so that others could be grafted in. The oracles of God were entrusted to the Jews (Romans 3:2), but that does not mean the post-Temple rabbinic tradition that rejected Jesus retains authority over the New Covenant people. The Church is the continuation of the people of God under the covenant established by Christ’s blood, not under the continuing authority of those who rejected Him.
Matthew 23:2–3 has to be read in the same light. Jesus acknowledged that the scribes and Pharisees sat on Moses’ seat in relation to the Law, and He told the people to do what they said when it was consistent with that Law. He immediately condemned their hypocrisy and the traditions that set aside the Word of God. That statement does not place the New Covenant Church under later rabbinic decisions made by those who had rejected the Messiah. Once the New Covenant is established, the people of God are no longer bound by the old order’s ongoing determinations about the Scriptures.
Josephus’s 22-book list reflects one late-first-century Jewish perspective after the Temple’s destruction. It is not a command of Christ or the apostles, and it is not presented in the New Testament as binding on the New Covenant community. If the standard is what Christ established and the apostles recognized as they led the Church under the New Covenant, then the deuterocanonical books were part of that inheritance. Treating the later Jewish exclusion as decisive means subordinating the New Covenant Church to authorities who rejected the Messiah. That is the opposite of living under the New Covenant.

text:
Duffy Defends Rejecting Free Starlink After FAA Meltdown: Ground Network Is Best

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy pushed back on Elon Musk’s claim that free Starlink terminals offered to the FAA could have helped avoid last week’s nationwide ground stop, insisting a ground based network remains the preferred approach despite the disruption.

Musk posted on X Monday: “As I was saying … Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he said they were not needed. As it turns out, they were.” The comment followed the November 13 outage that forced the FAA to halt departures nationwide for more than four hours after data flooding from a router installation overwhelmed aging systems at 17 of 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers. Thousands of flights were canceled or delayed as contractors worked on copper-to-fiber upgrades on equipment dating back decades.

Duffy, speaking publicly, acknowledged past collaboration but defended the decision. “I’ve worked well with Elon, and Starlink was a great solution for some of our assets in Alaska. But we sent Starlink in one of its prior iterations to our tech lab, and there were some issues that we had to navigate. We thought that the best method is to have a network that’s based on the ground,” he said.

He continued: “Now, I think what he’s doing with Starlink and the speed is remarkable. But our airspace is very big, we have assets everywhere, and so, again, we used him for different parts of the airspace.”

The response highlights a familiar pattern: praise for private sector speed where it fits remote needs, paired with reluctance to lean on it for broader redundancy. Duffy has repeatedly blamed prior administrations for the outdated telecom architecture and pressed Congress for tens of billions more to build a new ground network. Critics note that free satellite capacity was on the table before a single router issue shut down the skies, yet the preference stayed with the legacy system that just failed. Travelers absorbed the cost while officials reaffirm the same ground-first strategy.
