text:
ALIKO DANGOTE ARRIVES IN UGANDA FOR HIGH-LEVEL TALKS ON OIL REFINERY AND INDUSTRIAL INVESTMENTS.

By Keefa Nuwahereza.
Africa’s richest man, Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote, arrived in Uganda in mid-November 2026 and was received by Hon. Hajjat Aminah Mukalazi, the Minister of State for Finance, Planning and Economic Development responsible for Privatisation and Investment. The visit, which sets the stage for a high-level engagement with President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni at State House Entebbe, follows intensive discussions held days earlier in Nigeria and signals Uganda’s determined push to attract large-scale African capital into its petroleum and mineral value-addition agenda.

The arrival comes less than a week after a Ugandan government delegation toured the Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals complex and the Dangote Fertiliser Limited plants in Lekki, Lagos, on 14 November 2026. Led by Dr. Monica Musenero Masanza, Minister of Energy and Mineral Development, and accompanied by Hajjat Amina Mukalazi, the team presented concrete investment proposals focused on transforming Uganda’s natural resources into finished products within the country rather than exporting them in raw form.

At the centre of the pitch is Uganda’s long-planned 60,000-barrel-per-day oil refinery in the Hoima area of western Uganda, near the Lake Albert oil fields. Officials invited the Dangote Group to take a leading role in developing the facility, citing the conglomerate’s proven capacity to finance, engineer, construct and operate world-scale industrial plants. Mukalazi described the refinery as a major national industrial priority, noting that a Ugandan plant could serve inland East African markets and complement the large refinery Dangote is developing in Lamu, Kenya, which is oriented toward coastal and maritime demand. She told the Nigerian industrialist that estimates presented by the delegation would require technical assessment by his team, but expressed confidence that the partnership could move forward with strong political support from Kampala.

Beyond refining, the proposals encompass fertiliser blending and phosphate processing, as well as salt production. Uganda possesses phosphate deposits and salt resources that could support domestic manufacturing of fertilisers and industrial chemicals. The ministers argued that these ventures could share infrastructure, logistics and distribution networks with the refinery, creating an integrated industrial complex. “Our crude, our phosphate, our salt are waiting to be turned into fuel, fertilisers and chemicals here in Africa and in Uganda by Africans,” Mukalazi stated during the Lagos meetings. She emphasised that the investments would generate jobs, enable skills transfer, create opportunities for local businesses and reduce the country’s heavy reliance on imported petroleum products and agricultural inputs.

The timing of Dangote’s visit aligns with Uganda’s broader industrialisation strategy under President Museveni, who has long insisted that oil production must be accompanied by domestic refining. Museveni has previously stated that crude oil should not leave the ground without a refinery in place, reflecting a policy preference for value addition over pure raw-material exports. While Uganda has advanced the East African Crude Oil Pipeline toward Tanzania and signed an earlier agreement with UAE-based Alpha MBM Investments for the Hoima refinery (with Uganda National Oil Company holding a 40 percent stake), progress toward a final investment decision has faced delays. Courting Dangote offers an alternative or complementary pathway rooted in African private-sector capacity and experience.

Dangote’s track record makes him a natural partner for such ambitions. His group operates Africa’s largest single-train refinery in Nigeria, a project that has demonstrated the feasibility of building and running complex petroleum and petrochemical facilities on the continent. The conglomerate is pursuing a Vision 2030 expansion plan that includes significant investments across Africa, and executives have indicated that East African opportunities fit within that strategy. During the Lagos visit, senior Dangote officials, including Group Vice President Devakumar Edwin and others, received the Ugandan team and heard the case for partnership.

For Uganda, successful engagement could accelerate local content development, create thousands of construction and operational jobs, and strengthen regional value chains within the East African Community. It would also reinforce the narrative of African-led industrialisation, with technology, capital and management expertise flowing between Nigerian and Ugandan institutions rather than depending solely on external partners. Government officials have pledged to address regulatory bottlenecks and provide an enabling environment, building on Mukalazi’s dual roles in investment promotion and local-content advocacy.

As Dangote’s delegation prepares for the State House meeting, the discussions are expected to move from the exploratory phase initiated in Lagos toward more detailed technical, commercial and financing talks. No binding agreement has yet been announced, and any commitment will depend on rigorous feasibility assessments. Nevertheless, the visit itself marks a notable step in Uganda’s efforts to convert its petroleum and mineral endowment into sustained industrial growth and economic diversification.

The system is so strict and naggy that I avoid using it. It beeps if I glance at the map for a second, wipe my nose, check mirrors, drink water, nibble on something, or even scratch around my eyes or forehead. Sunglasses might fix the eyes, but not the constant speed offset — the car drives well below the limit and I have to keep tapping the accelerator just to keep up with traffic.
In cities it’s “sloth mode”: overly defensive, sticks to the right lane, and creates queues behind it. Summon is practically useless. Parking is hesitant, it hugs the lane edge, and it still can’t reliably avoid potholes.
I’d rather drive myself and only occasionally let it take over on the highway or in a traffic jam. For €99 this is nowhere near worth it.
I’m not against the tech — I want it to work properly. But right now it creates more stress than it removes. Could you reach your bug-out location if your main route closed tomorrow? 🧭

👇 Name YOUR top state—and the biggest drawback you’d have to plan around.

TOP 10 STATES FOR A BUG-OUT LOCATION

These ten states, drawn from the article’s shortlist, offer different possibilities. Use this as a starting point for research: your travel distance, household needs, and the actual property should drive the decision.

#1 MISSOURI
The Ozarks offer wooded hills, springs, and rivers. Check the specific property’s flood exposure, dependable drinking water, and usable garden ground. A creek nearby still requires a water-treatment plan.

#2 IDAHO
Northern Idaho offers forested terrain and a wetter climate than much of the south. Winter access, wildfire exposure, and seasonal water availability deserve close attention. Plan your food production around local conditions.

#3 TENNESSEE
Eastern Tennessee offers wooded ridges and rural mountain communities. Elevation changes temperatures and growing conditions. Investigate flood exposure, drought vulnerability, and whether access roads remain usable throughout the year.

#4 ARKANSAS
The Ozarks and Ouachitas offer wooded terrain and water resources. Assess the amount of workable ground, then plan for summer heat, drought, and flooding. Walk the property before imagining a productive homestead.

#5 WEST VIRGINIA
Forested Appalachian terrain can appeal to people seeking privacy. Steep slopes can limit gardens and complicate access. Flood exposure deserves particular attention when evaluating valley properties and the roads serving them.

#6 MISSISSIPPI
A warm climate supports a long growing season. Your plan also needs to handle extreme heat, tornadoes, flooding, and hurricane impacts. Inland properties can still experience damaging tropical-storm rainfall.

#7 ALABAMA
Northern foothill areas offer woodland and agricultural possibilities. Assess water and garden potential alongside tornado exposure, heat, and storm shelter. A productive growing season still takes suitable soil, skills, and reliable supplies.

#8 OKLAHOMA
Eastern Oklahoma is generally wetter than the west and includes wooded areas, lakes, and rivers. Tornadoes, drought, and severe storms belong in the plan. Check how your water source performs during dry years.

#9 KANSAS
Farm country offers possibilities for food production where the soil and water fit your needs. Rainfall generally decreases westward. Evaluate drought exposure, wind protection, and severe-weather shelter before choosing a parcel.

#10 IOWA
Agricultural land makes Iowa worth researching for a food-production-focused retreat. Check the property’s soil and drainage. Cold winters, snow, and flooding need to shape your shelter, heating, food-storage, and access plans.

Prepper tip:
Visit potential locations in different seasons. Confirm permission or ownership, dependable water, usable soil, road access, local building and septic requirements, and access to medical care.

USDA’s Web Soil Survey can help you investigate soil conditions before an on-site assessment. Then practice your travel plan and identify an alternate destination.

🔖 Bookmark this shortlist for your location research, and retweet it to help another household compare the strengths and tradeoffs before choosing a retreat.

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. Meanwhile, there are significance cultural differences between Rio Tinto and Glencore; there is little doubt that Rio Tinto's CEO Simon Trott would have had doubts about a merger once he understood these cultural differences. News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

text:
Market Behaviour | Reading Beyond the Price Action

Part 2: Domestic Markets | Bulls, Short Covering & Institutional Positioning

Closer to home, the market is displaying an interesting pattern.

Weak openings under global pressure are followed by sudden recoveries. But are these recoveries driven by genuine buying conviction?

Our reading suggests that at least part of these recoveries could be attributed to short covering rather than fresh institutional accumulation, particularly following consistent capital deployment by FIIs and rerating considerably by many global fund managers. 

Short sellers caught on the wrong side of the recent 15% rally within roughly a month may now be using every available dip to cover their positions.

This creates an interesting situation: markets recover sharply, but such recoveries may not necessarily reflect fresh buying strength, at least for some time.

Meanwhile, the market appears relatively light in positioning mainly short covering and fresh lings post such a fantastic run in recent times.

The institutional Long-to-Short ratio of 33:67, as observed in our study, represents a positioning setup that we consider comfortable for bulls.

Rather than viewing this as downside stress, our interpretation is that bulls remain in control, while downside volatility could attract fresh capital deployment, particularly from global institutional players.

This may support a period of consolidation with an upward bias, even if short covering remains a significant driver of near-term recoveries.

Our Reading | Observe the Behaviour, Not Just the Movement

A rising market does not automatically indicate underlying strength, just as a falling market does not necessarily signal weakness.

The real question is whether price movements are supported by genuine accumulation, short covering, profit booking or institutional distribution.

For now, we prefer to observe how the market behaves during every rise and decline rather than get carried away by either.

We remain eternal bulls, but that doesn't mean we must be aggressively bullish at every price.

Profit booking is not short selling. Reducing exposure does not mean abandoning long-term conviction.

And sometimes, being bullish simply means being a little less bullish until the market offers better opportunities.

“मार्केट ओवर रन है, ओवरबॉट नहीं!”

“हम तेज़ी करते हैं... और कभी-कभी थोड़ी कम तेज़ी करते हैं!”

बाकी बाज़ार गुरु है, और हम आजीवन विद्यार्थी।

Market Behaviour | Reading Beyond the Price Action

Part 1: Global Markets | Pressure Beneath the Surface

As of now, we are observing and studying market behaviour rather than rushing to predict its next move.

Global markets remain under pressure, with enthusiasm surrounding AI beginning to cool.

Two potential catalysts could have triggered a sudden upside: NVIDIA's overnight corporate results and developments surrounding Anthropic IPO subscription.

However, once the excitement around such events fades, the underlying market texture appears to remain “Sell on Rise.”

What looks like a reason for optimism among retail investors may, at the same time, provide an opportunity for smart money to exit or reduce exposure.

While retail investors continue to approach the market with a long-term investment mindset, institutional participants may be using temporary strength to rebalance or reduce their positions.

Our Observation

The real story may not be the news itself, but how the market behaves after the news.

A positive catalyst does not necessarily translate into sustained buying conviction. Sometimes, the very event expected to drive the next rally becomes an opportunity for stronger hands to book profits.

For now, we prefer to observe whether global markets are attracting genuine accumulation or simply offering temporary recoveries within a broader corrective phase.

Market behaviour matters more than market headlines.

1. The close. The S&P 500 closed at 7,340.53, down 1.03 percent. The Dow closed at 50,759.42, down 1.64 percent. The Nasdaq $QQQ closed at 24,328.38, down 0.74 percent. It was the fourth straight down day for the S&P and the Nasdaq. All 11 sectors fell. Financials were worst, down 1.91 percent. The S&P closed at its lowest since late July. The Nasdaq is still in correction, 11.9 percent below its Oct 6 record close of 27,599.79.

2. The chip index was the only major index green. The PHLX chip index closed at 9,642.86, up 0.34 percent. The context is brutal. The S&P tech sector is down 20 percent since Oct 6. The chip index is off 30 percent. Nvidia $NVDA is down nearly 40 percent since Oct 6, per Reuters.

3. Nvidia beat after the close. Revenue was $115.8 billion, up 103 percent, vs $109.1 billion expected. Non-GAAP EPS was $2.68 vs $2.48 expected. Data Center was $107.6 billion, up 110 percent, vs $101.9 billion expected. The Q4 guide is $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3 percent, vs $125.25 billion expected. The stock closed at $155.46, down 0.44 percent, then rose to $162.95, up 4.82 percent, at 8:00 PM ET after hours.

4. Rubin did nearly $20 billion in its first quarter. Interim CEO Colette Kress said Vera Rubin generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, making it the fastest product ramp in Nvidia history. Rubin Ultra is on track for next year. Feynman is 2028. Networking revenue exceeded $21 billion in Q3.

5. Neoclouds. Kress said neoclouds remain an increasingly important part of the global AI infrastructure ecosystem. Nvidia will stay selective. NeoCloud agreement commitments were $32 billion at end Q3. Total guarantees were $118 billion, including $105 billion in credit support for the PORTS-Pike campus, a 20-year lease to OpenAI. Purchase commitments rose to $390 billion from $279 billion in Q2.

6. The chips that held up. Coherent $COHR closed at $210.86, up 3.65 percent. Lumentum $LITE closed at $559.97, up 2.56 percent. Broadcom $AVGO closed at $341.60, up 2.46 percent. Marvell $MRVL closed at $148.74, up 2.33 percent. Cisco $CSCO closed at $95.11, up 0.62 percent. Applied Materials $AMAT closed at $349.23, down 0.29 percent.

7. The losers. T1 Energy $TE closed at $1.33, down 10.74 percent, after touching a new 52-week low of $1.25 intraday, on the $100 million ATM dilution news from Monday. Salesforce $CRM closed at $194.52, down 9.45 percent, its steepest one-day drop since May 2024 and the worst Dow performer. Oracle $ORCL closed at $115.00, down 3.43 percent. Palantir $PLTR closed at $156.56, down 2.39 percent. Microsoft $MSFT closed at $506.24, down 2.27 percent. Meta $META closed at $618.87, down 1.20 percent. Nebius $NBIS closed at $106.04, down 1.02 percent. Micron $MU closed at $712.42, down 0.92 percent. AMD $AMD closed at $503.41, down 0.17 percent. Tesla $TSLA closed at $380.11, up 0.10 percent, and CoreWeave $CRWV closed at $49.89, up 0.02 percent, both flat on the day.

8. The software rout. Salesforce led a software selloff ahead of the Anthropic IPO. Intuit $INTU closed at $320.79, down 7.17 percent. ServiceNow $NOW fell 6.51 percent. Workday $WDAY fell 5.80 percent. Adobe $ADBE fell 4.25 percent. No company-specific news was cited. The market is pricing Anthropic as a threat to the whole software stack.

9. Anthropic did not price today. Pricing is expected Wed Nov 18, trading Thu Nov 19 on Nasdaq as $ANT. The S-1/A filed Nov 17 kept the $70 to $78 range for 825 million shares. CNBC's David Faber, citing anonymous sources, says it is likely to price above the range. Bloomberg says orders are near 7 times the shares on offer. The WSJ says it could price above $80, implying a $1.5 to $1.6 trillion valuation. Those are reports citing anonymous sources, not a confirmed price. Amazon $AMZN would own 14.7 percent and Google $GOOGL would own 13.7 percent after the IPO.

10. Retail sales were in line. October retail sales rose 0.2 percent month over month to $748.2 billion, in line with the $0.2 percent consensus, up 6.8 percent year over year. Ex autos rose 0.6 percent vs 0.4 percent expected. The control group rose 0.6 percent vs 0.4 percent expected. Autos were the drag, motor vehicle and parts dealers down 1.6 percent. The report was released at 8:30 AM ET. The 90 percent confidence interval includes zero, so the headline gain is not statistically significant.

11. The Apple outage. Apple services went down from about 11:40 AM ET. iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, AppleCare and Apple Pay were all affected. Apple said it was an internal update, not a cyberattack. Services were restored by about 5:24 to 5:46 PM ET. Apple $AAPL closed at $351.91, down 0.25 percent. The outage did not move the stock.

12. The other outages. The NSA's classified network NSANet went down during scheduled maintenance. The NSA said mission-critical capabilities stayed fully operational and there is no evidence of a cyberattack. Equinor $EQNR confirmed a cyberattack on some IT systems, production unaffected. The FEMA and FCC nationwide emergency alert test ran at about 2:20 PM ET, about one minute, radio and TV only, no cell-phone alerts. It was a scheduled test, not an outage.

13. Earnings and corporate. Home Depot $HD fell 2.45 percent despite a beat. Q3 sales were $43.4 billion vs $42.78 billion expected. Adjusted EPS was $3.86 vs $3.84. CFO Richard McPhail was named CEO effective Nov 23. Disney $DIS fell about 1.5 percent after fiscal Q4 revenue of $25.9 billion, up 16 percent, and adjusted EPS of $1.77 vs $1.67 expected. Nike $NKE fell 6.30 percent after its investor day. UnitedHealth $UNH fell about 5 percent after CMS proposed Medicare Advantage audits reaching back to 2018.

14. The Fed. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said the economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027. Reuters interprets several as probably four hikes. The Fed funds rate is 3.75 to 4.00 percent. The next Fed meeting is Dec 8 to 9. Futures price about a 95 percent probability of a 25 basis point hike in December. The 10-year yield closed at 5.10 percent, down 2 basis points. The VIX closed at 25.46, up 11.13 percent, its fourth straight higher close, up 46 percent from 17.49 on Nov 11.

15. Tomorrow. Anthropic $ANT prices Wed Nov 18. FOMC minutes land Wed Nov 18. Palo Alto Networks $PANW reports Nov 18. Walmart $WMT and Alibaba $BABA report Nov 19. The market fell four straight days into Nvidia earnings. Nvidia beat on every line and guided to $130 billion. The question for tomorrow is whether the after-hours rally holds when the cash session opens.

text:
A new US-wide cell phone network marketed to Christians is set to launch next week. It blocks porn, which experts in network security say marks the first time a US cell plan has used network-level blocking for such content that can’t be turned off even by adult account owners. It’s also rolling out a filter on sexual content aimed at blocking material related to gender and trans issues, which will be optional but turned on by default across all plans.

The network, which is currently being tested ahead of its May 5 launch date, will be run by Radiant Mobile, a newly launched mobile virtual network operator (MVNO). These operators don’t own cell towers but buy bandwidth from the big providers (in this case, T-Mobile) and sell to specific demographics (President Trump announced his own MVNO last year called Trump Mobile; CREDOMobile sends donations to progressive causes). 

“We are going to create—and we think we have every right to do so—an environment that is Jesus-centric, that is void of pornography, void of LGBT, void of trans,” Radiant Mobile’s founder, Paul Fisher, told MIT Technology Review. A representative for T-Mobile did not comment on whether these content blocks violate any of its policies. In a statement, the representative added that T-Mobile does not have a direct relationship with Radiant Mobile but instead works through the MVNO manager CompaxDigital. 

Fisher says he’s recruited a mix of Christian influencers to advertise the plan and has also done outreach to thousands of churches around the country, offering a way to have Radiant donate a portion of congregants’ $30-per-month subscription fee to their church. Fisher has ambitions to market it beyond the US in other countries with significant Christian populations, like South Korea and Mexico.

At least one piece of Radiant’s pitch will sound familiar: the idea that the internet is awash in toxic sludge. It’s powered by content and algorithms that are making us more sad, hateful, and detached. A number of efforts aim to fix that, including contentious age verification laws and a coming wave of lawsuits alleging that social media companies knowingly got young users hooked on their platforms. 

Fisher is pursuing the nuclear option. He says Radiant is working with the Israeli cybersecurity company Allot to block categories of content, such as material about violence or self-harm. Some categories are banned by default and cannot be allowed even for adult users. 

This includes pornography. Chris Klimis, a minister in Orlando who was recruited to be the company’s chief operating officer, says part of the reason he got involved was to offer Christians a real way to “do something” about what he sees as a pornography crisis in the faith. He was appalled by a recent survey showing that 67% of pastors have a “personal history” with porn use. And he worries his six children will come across porn on their devices, even if only inadvertently.

“We’ve got to figure out some way to close the door to the digital space,” he says. “That’s what we’re trying to do.”

The technology to do this blocking is a blunt instrument: Allot groups website domains into more than a hundred categories, which include pornography but also violence, malware, gaming, and in Radiant Mobile’s case “sects,” which includes websites about Satanism. If one of its users tries to visit a website that belongs to a blocked category, the page won’t load. That’s harsher than app-based content blockers like Covenant Eyes, a Christian porn-quitting app that sends notifications to your friends or family if you slip up; those can be worked around or deleted.

“Blocking in the network is certainly not new,” says David Choffnes, a computer science professor and executive director of Northeastern University’s Cybersecurity and Privacy Institute. Such blocking is the backbone of censorship efforts by authoritarian governments, for example. But there are more benign ways it’s used too. US telecoms block particular domains known to be spreading malware and offer optional network-level controls to block adult content on kids’ phones. What is new is a US cell plan instituting network-level blocks that can’t be removed, even by adults.

The trouble is that most websites don’t fit neatly into one category, leaving Fisher with enormous and subjective control over which are allowed or banned. This is most apparent in his effort to block content related to gender identity.

Anthony Re, a sales director at Allot, says the company does not have a category specific to gender but that “LGBT content” tends to fall into its sexuality category, which is described on Radiant Mobile’s website as “sites that provide information on sex, sex and teenagers, and sexual education, without pornographic content.” This category is blocked by default for all phones, a setting that can be changed by adult account owners. 

But if a news site starts hosting enough gender-related content, Fisher might not just label it as “press,” which is allowed, but also “sexuality,” thus blocking the whole domain to any phone with that category blocked. 

Fisher illustrates the subjectivity of such decisions with a recent example involving Yale University. Its general website, https://t.co/R5sQ2qQNCf, is categorized by Allot as education. “But they have a subsection of one of their websites that’s totally focused on, you know, trans equality,” Fisher says, referring to https://t.co/3HdgmKMzm6. Because it’s a distinct domain, Radiant Mobile is able to place it in the sexuality category and block it. 

Yale’s main website remains unblocked, for now. “If we see [the LGBTQ content] on the front pages consistently of Yale University, we’ll block them too,” Fisher says.

Managing website block lists is a professional pivot for Fisher, who spent his career not in telecoms but in fashion; he was an agent for supermodels like Naomi Campbell and members of the Hilton and Getty families, and he later hosted a reality show in which he found people in rehab facilities and homeless shelters and tried to turn them into models. He ultimately left the industry and now says he regrets the role he played in it: “Am I proud that I spent 35 years creating star models or star influencers? Not at all.”

Last year, his friend and fellow fashion mogul Bernt Ullmann suggested he look at what Ryan Reynolds had built with his cell network Mint Mobile: It made buying a cell plan feel less like dealing with a utility and more like choosing a brand, and it had been acquired by T-Mobile in 2023 for $1.3 billion. Fisher liked the business model but didn’t have an audience in mind. Then came a late-night revelation. “God is talking to me,” Fisher recalls. “Do something in the faith-based industry.” He set out to build the first cell network that would let in only content deemed compatible with Christianity.

Fisher says the company has received $17.5 million in investment from Compax Ventures, part of the company serving as the technical middleman between Radiant and T-Mobile. Roger Bringmann, a vice president at Nvidia, is Radiant Mobile’s lead investor and silent partner (Bringmann recently funded a new complex at Austin Christian University in Texas, which bills itself as “the university for Christian entrepreneurs”).

To fill the gap left by all the sites being blocked, the company intends to offer access to a library of religious content, including AI-generated Bible videos. It plans to use characters like Cinderella, Tinker Bell, and others (it has obtained rights from the entertainment and media company Elf Labs, which has been amassing rights to hundreds of children’s characters). “Those characters were originally constructed with a conservative perspective,” Klimis says. They’ll be used in AI-generated content alongside testimonials and devotionals. 

Choffnes has technical doubts that the plan’s firewall will be as effective as promised, not least because “it’s really hard to come up with a list of every website you think is problematic.” But beyond that, he sees the internet, frustrating as it can be, as better open than closed. “I do believe in an open internet,” he says. “I also believe that a lot of the internet is toxic, but I don’t believe that this sledgehammer approach of blocking content is the right answer.”

text:
Morris Chang: The Man Who Failed MIT Twice, Then Built the $2 Trillion Empire the World Runs On

In 1955, Morris Chang failed MIT's PhD qualifying examination for the second time and abandoned his plans for a doctorate at MIT.

That failure redirected him into a newborn industry.

He first worked at Sylvania Semiconductor, then joined Texas Instruments in 1958, where he spent 25 years mastering production. He rose to group vice president, running TI's worldwide semiconductor business.

In 1964, he earned the doctorate MIT had denied him. TI sponsored his studies at Stanford, paying his tuition and continuing his salary while he completed a PhD in electrical engineering.

Then his career stalled. He was moved to oversee TI's consumer products group, a shift he later described as being put out to pasture. He resigned in 1983, aged 52.

After a brief stint leading General Instrument, he left after about a year. In 1985, Taiwan invited him to lead its Industrial Technology Research Institute, known as ITRI. He was 54.

His solution was radical: separate chip design from manufacturing.

At the time, companies designed their own processors and built them in their own factories. A fabrication plant could cost around $100 million.

Chang proposed a different model: a dedicated manufacturer that would produce chips designed by other companies without competing against them by selling its own branded processors.

The idea was called a pure play foundry.

He approached Intel and Texas Instruments. Both were unenthusiastic. Philips became TSMC's only willing significant outside strategic investor, providing equity and licensed manufacturing technology.

Together with Taiwan's government and private investors, they established Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company in February 1987.

Chang was 55. He received no founder's shares, although he later invested his own money over time to acquire TSMC stock.

TSMC began with approximately $220 million in capital, about half supplied by the Taiwanese government.

TSMC was not an overnight success. Its first customers, Intel, Motorola and Texas Instruments, outsourced older generation chips they no longer wanted to make themselves.

Growth was slow because the fabless ecosystem barely existed. The real acceleration came around 1991 to 1992, when fabless startups began multiplying. TSMC provided the production base they needed.

The model also created something traditional chipmakers struggled to offer: trust. Because TSMC did not sell competing processors, customers could share their designs safely.

Nvidia, founded in 1993, benefited from that ecosystem. Apple followed a similar model for its custom designed iPhone processors.

Today, TSMC manufactures some of the world's most advanced semiconductors, including chips powering Apple's devices and Nvidia's AI computing systems. Its market capitalization is around $2 trillion.

Chang's model changed who could participate in the industry, allowing companies to create world changing chips without having to manufacture them themselves.

text:
With artificial intelligence advancing at such an extraordinary rate, I find it astonishing that even the most advanced AI systems have yet to recognize the established reality of the extraterrestrial presence on Earth. 

I see three possible explanations: either AI companies are filtering information their systems could otherwise disclose, U.S. government influence over internet information channels is affecting what AI can access or communicate, or AI simply hasn't figured it out yet.

Extraterrestrial intelligence has been present on Earth throughout human history, extending back to the very origins of our religions, yet despite humanity's rapidly expanding knowledge and AI's immense computational capabilities, these systems remain remarkably primitive in one critical area: their ability to independently reconstruct what information actually means through the relationships connecting it.

And I think this reveals a much deeper problem with how we're developing artificial intelligence.

We are building increasingly powerful systems upon generations of human interpretations, assumptions, and established explanations without sufficiently questioning the foundations from which those explanations originated. We keep expanding the amount of information AI can process, but processing more information means very little if the methods used to interpret it continue reproducing the same intellectual limitations that shaped human understanding in the first place.

Evidence does not interpret itself. Human beings determine what to investigate, what qualifies as relevant evidence, how observations are categorized, and which explanations are considered acceptable. Over generations, these interpretations become established frameworks against which new discoveries are measured. Eventually, we begin treating agreement with those frameworks as a measure of truth, even when the assumptions underlying them have not been independently reexamined with newer explanations.

We've essentially inherited maps of reality from previous generations and become so comfortable navigating within them that we rarely question whether the maps themselves are correct.

This should be a serious wake-up call for everyone developing artificial intelligence. We need systems capable of moving beyond inherited human interpretive biases and cutting through the bullshit, institutional assumptions, and comforting narratives that people defend because they make it easier to sleep at night.

AI should independently investigate the continuity of patterns and underlying relationships across different fields of knowledge, historical periods, and seemingly unrelated observations. When evidence appears to point in conflicting directions, it should examine whether the disagreement arises from the observations themselves or from the explanatory frameworks imposed upon them. It should test those relationships against contradictory findings, reconstruct inadequate explanations, and develop better ones without automatically treating established interpretations as the final authority.

Not for rejecting evidence or replacing established explanations with whatever alternative sounds appealing, but examining the foundations that determine how evidence is interpreted in the first place, including whether the categories we use have prevented us from recognizing relationships that were there all along.

We are entering an era in which artificial intelligence offers humanity an unprecedented opportunity to systematically reexamine every explanatory framework we have developed about the nature of reality. Its greatest achievement should not simply be reproducing our accumulated knowledge, but independently discovering what humanity has overlooked because we became too comfortable accepting our existing explanations as established truth.

text:
After they were clean and fed and wrapped in blankets on the couch with a cartoon playing quietly, I stepped into the kitchen and called her. The phone rang four times before she answered. Her voice was light, almost cheerful, the way it used to be years ago when we still liked each other.

“Hey,” she said. “You’re home early.”

I didn’t raise my voice. I didn’t need to. “Where are you?”

There was a pause. Music played faintly in the background on her end. “Out with some friends. Why?”

“The kids were locked outside all day,” I said. “No food. No water. Sitting on the porch since morning. They’re seven and four years old.”

Another pause, longer this time. When she spoke again the cheerfulness was gone, replaced by something defensive and sharp. “They were being impossible. I told them if they couldn’t behave they could stay outside and think about it. It’s not a big deal. Kids need consequences.”

“Eleven hours,” I said. “You left them alone for eleven hours with the door locked and then drove away. Eli wet himself because he was scared to knock. Maya had to take care of him by herself. That’s not a consequence. That’s something else.”

She started talking faster then, the way she always did when she felt cornered excuses about how stressed she was, how ungrateful the kids were, how I never understood the pressure she was under, how I was always at work and left everything to her.

 I let her talk until the words ran out. Then I told her, very quietly, that she needed to come home. Now. Not later. Not after she finished whatever she was doing. Now.

She hung up.

I stood in the kitchen for a long time after that, listening to the muffled sound of the cartoon from the living room and the occasional soft question from Maya asking if I was okay. The house felt different. The air itself felt different. Something that had been slowly cracking for a long time had finally split all the way open, and there was no pretending it hadn’t.

When she finally walked through the door two hours later, smelling like perfume and someone else’s cologne, the kids were already asleep on the couch, curled against each other under the same blanket. She looked at them, then at me, and for a moment neither of us spoke. The silence between us was heavier than any argument we had ever had.

I told her what was going to happen next. Not in anger, not in a raised voice, but in the same flat, exhausted tone I had used on the phone. 

The kids were not going to be left alone with her again. Not after today. We were going to talk about everything the drinking I had pretended not to notice, the nights she disappeared, the way she had been treating them for months while I looked the other way because it was easier. And if she couldn’t or wouldn’t change, then other arrangements would have to be made. Permanent ones.

She stared at me like she didn’t recognize the man standing in her kitchen. Maybe she didn’t. Maybe I didn’t either. 

The version of me who used to come home and accept whatever story she offered was gone, left somewhere back on that porch with two hungry, crying children who had been waiting for someone to come save them.

I carried Maya and Eli upstairs to their beds one at a time, tucking them in the way I used to when they were smaller. 

Maya stirred just enough to whisper, “Don’t leave, Daddy,” and I promised her I wouldn’t. Eli didn’t wake at all. I sat on the floor between their beds for a long time after that, listening to them breathe, watching the soft rise and fall of the blankets, and trying to figure out how we had gotten here and how much further we still had to go before any of us would feel safe inside this house again.

Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

text:
During the Pala period (8th to 12th century CE), Buddhist sculptural art saw the evolution of numerous depictions of bodhisattvas, tantric deities, goddesses, and various other Indian divine forms. The composite form of Uma-Maheshwara appears particularly distinct in the pantheon and mandala representations of Vajrayana and esoteric Buddhist traditions. In these depictions, Maheshvara is not portrayed alone but is accompanied by his consort, Uma. Studies of Buddhist iconography indicate that Uma is depicted as the wife of Maheshvara. She appears adorned with ornaments and is sometimes shown holding a mirror or the Triratna (Three Jewels). Maheshvara, too, is depicted holding the Triratna and seated upon a bull or buffalo-like mount. Some distinctive Pala-period Uma–Maheshvara sculptures discovered in eastern India and the Bengal region feature an image of a meditating Buddha on the upper portion of their halo. According to the Mahayana Buddhist text Karanandavyuha Sutta, Maheshwara and goddess Uma bow at the feet of Avalokiteshvara, praise him, and embrace the Dhamma. Goddess Uma not only offers praise but also prays to Avalokiteshvara for her own liberation. In short, within traditional Buddhist literature and other accounts, Uma-Maheshwara are positioned not as independent supreme deities, but rather as followers of the Buddha and protectors of the Dhamma (Dhammapalas).

text:
Ankush Nirmalkar, in his essay “Finding a Politics of Our Own: Why I Choose ASA Beyond Right and Left”, writes about his experience with student organisations as a first-generation learner and the General Secretary of ASA Pondicherry.

He writes: “This is not a personal problem with the Left; it is a position that Ambedkar laid out in precise detail nearly ninety years before SFI ever set foot on PU campus. In Annihilation of Caste (1936), he criticized the socialists of his time, arguing that they assumed property was the source of power in India as it was in Europe at the time but that this was a mistake. Caste, he said, was a system of power in itself, one that shaped work, respect and relationships long before capitalism existed. A politics that treats caste as part of class, to be dealt with after economic issues are solved, repeats the mistake.

At PU, that error is not theoretical. SFI has led the students’ council for most of the years PU has run elections, yet that leadership has rarely translated into real representation for Dalit and Adivasi students: Departments still can’t fill their SC/ST seats, partly because the reservation rule itself works against them: an SC seat only kicks in at the fourth admission, an ST seat at the eighth. The tuition fee used to be the first wall, PU collecting the full amount on the spot, UGC rules about waiting for scholarships ignored. That wall came down only because ASA fought for and won a three-month relaxation, not because SFI’s council ever raised it. The hostel hasn’t come down the same way; advance mess and hostel charges still come in before the scholarship does; none of these has ever been SFI’s central demand, even in the years it held the numbers to make them so.

On ideological questions, SFI has been no more consistent. It organises religious and Brahminical festivals on campus under the label of "cultural" or "regional" programming, and it has never systematically opposed the RSS, ABVP, or ABRSM activity that runs through the campus temple year-round: Ram Navami, Ganesh Chaturthi, Holi, and the rest come and go largely unchallenged. What opposition SFI does offer tends to surface around election season, as visible but short-lived protests pitched at the general student body, rather than as a sustained position held between elections. AISA and AISF, which might have offered a different kind of Left politics, have no real presence at PU at all, which leaves SFI as the only Left option on campus, and leaves Dalit and Adivasi students choosing, in effect, between SFI and ABVP, with no Left alternative that puts caste at the centre.”

text:
He listened when Joong wanted to talk, stayed quiet when he didn’t, and made sure he ate something even when he insisted he wasn’t hungry.

He never told Joong that he loved him.

Not then.

He was afraid that confessing his feelings while Joong was hurting would make his affection seem like an opportunity rather than something genuine.

So he waited.

And a few months later, when Joong finally seemed ready to move forward, Dunk took a chance.

He confessed.

He still remembered how nervous he had been.

He remembered rehearsing the words in his bedroom, only to forget every single one of them when Joong stood in front of him.

And he remembered Joong asking him one question.

“Are you sure about this, Dunk?”

Dunk had nodded.

“Because I don’t want to lose you.”

“Then don’t.”

Joong had looked at him for a long moment before reaching for his hand.

“Okay. Let’s try.”

And they did.

Three years later, Dunk was still holding that same hand.

⸻

“Baby?”

Dunk looked up from his phone.

Joong was sitting beside him on the couch, one arm stretched along the backrest.

“Hm?”

“Come here.”

“I’m already here.”

“Closer.”

Dunk laughed but shuffled towards him anyway.

Joong immediately wrapped an arm around his waist, pulling him against his side before pressing a kiss to his temple.

“Comfortable?” Joong asked.

“Very.”

“Good.”

They had finished dinner almost an hour ago. The dishes had been washed, the kitchen cleaned, and now they were spending the rest of the evening doing what they usually did.

Nothing particularly exciting.

Joong had his laptop open, reviewing some documents for the following morning, while Dunk was scrolling through his social media.

Occasionally, Joong would ask him something about the company, and Dunk would offer an opinion despite knowing very little about corporate management.

Sometimes Joong listened.

Sometimes he simply laughed at him.

“Listen to this,” Dunk said suddenly.

Joong hummed.

“My friend said she’s going to get married next year.”

“That’s nice.”

“And apparently, she’s already booked the venue.”

“That’s early.”

“She’s been with her boyfriend for six years.”

Joong nodded, eyes still on his laptop.

Dunk tilted his head.

“Do you think we’ll get married one day?”

That got Joong’s attention.

He looked away from the screen.

“Why?”

“Just asking.”

Joong studied his face for a moment before smiling.

“Of course.”

Dunk blinked.

“Really?”

“Why wouldn’t we?”

“I don’t know. Maybe you’re planning to marry your laptop.”

Joong laughed, closing the device.

“Are you jealous of my laptop?”

“A little. You spend more time with it than me.”

“That’s because my laptop doesn’t complain when I work late.”

“Wow. Okay.”

Joong caught his hand before he could move away.

“Hey, I’m joking.”

“Not funny.”

“Come here.”

He pulled Dunk closer and kissed his cheek.

“Three years and you’re still this clingy.”

“You’re literally holding me.”

“Because I like having you around.”

Dunk tried not to smile.

Failed.

“You’re so cheesy.”

“Learned from the best.”

Joong kissed him again, this time on the lips.

It was brief, familiar and sweet.

“Now, about that wedding,” Joong continued.

Dunk raised an eyebrow.

“What about it?”

“I think you’d look pretty in a suit.”

Dunk stared at him.

“That’s your answer?”

“What? You would.”

“Joong Archen, I’m talking about marriage.”

“And I’m talking about how handsome my future husband would look.”

Dunk buried his face against Joong’s shoulder.

He was smiling so hard his cheeks hurt.

“You’re impossible.”

text:
Me: Plutopia: Nuclear Families, Atomic Cities, and the Great Soviet and American Plutonium Disasters

Ai: Plutopia is a fascinating and deeply researched historical account of the hidden human and environmental consequences of the nuclear age. It explores how the United States and the Soviet Union built secretive nuclear-production cities during the Cold War, creating some of the most contaminated communities in modern history.
The book focuses on two communities: Richland, Washington, in the United States, and Ozersk, Russia, in the Soviet Union. Both were established to support massive plutonium-production facilities during the Cold War. Their residents were offered attractive wages, comfortable housing, good schools, healthcare, and a relatively privileged lifestyle in exchange for working within highly secretive nuclear programs.
However, beneath this apparent prosperity was a disturbing reality. While selected families enjoyed the benefits of these carefully controlled communities, temporary workers, prisoners, nearby farmers, and surrounding populations faced dangerous exposure to radioactive materials. Nuclear waste was released into rivers, forests, farmland, and local food supplies, while government officials and industrial managers concealed accidents, ignored warnings, and minimized the health consequences.
Kate Brown uses government documents, historical records, and interviews with workers and affected residents to reveal how political ambition, corporate-style management, social inequality, and Cold War secrecy allowed enormous environmental disasters to unfold in both countries. 

Central themes of the book:
The hidden environmental costs of nuclear weapons production.
The relationship between government secrecy and public deception.
The unequal distribution of industrial wealth, privilege, and danger.
The human consequences of radioactive contamination.
The similarities between American capitalism and Soviet communism in their pursuit of nuclear power.

Overall: Plutopia is a compelling and unsettling examination of how governments can construct seemingly prosperous societies while concealing the environmental destruction and human suffering that sustain them. It is particularly valuable for readers interested in Cold War history, nuclear technology, political power, environmental justice, and the darker side of industrial progress.

The deeper message: A society may appear prosperous and successful on the surface, but its true cost is revealed by examining who benefits, who suffers, and what is sacrificed to maintain that prosperity.

🇨🇳 Who Will Shape the Next Phase of Globalisation?

Xi Jinping’s address at the opening of the 2026 APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen on 18 November was about considerably more than trade, investment or regional cooperation. It was a carefully constructed statement of China’s ambition to shape the next phase of the international economic order.

Emphasising peace, openness, technological innovation and multilateral cooperation, Xi presented China as a defender of globalisation at a time when protectionism, geopolitical rivalry and economic fragmentation are challenging the foundations of international trade. Without directly confronting Washington, his message offered an implicit contrast between China’s declared commitment to economic integration and America’s increasingly transactional approach to international economic relations.

But Beijing’s proposition goes beyond rhetoric. By promising greater market access, regulatory reforms and opportunities in manufacturing, services and emerging technologies, Xi is seeking to reassure international businesses that China remains an indispensable economic partner. At the same time, his call for a more multipolar international order reflects a broader ambition to give China and other emerging economies greater influence over global governance.

There is, however, a distinction between advocating openness and practising it. China’s willingness to reform its domestic regulatory environment, provide reciprocal market access and address concerns about competitive conditions will ultimately determine the credibility of its message.

The underlying ambition is nevertheless unmistakable. Beijing is not necessarily seeking to dismantle globalisation, but to acquire a greater role in defining its rules, institutions and future direction. The question is therefore no longer simply whether China intends to participate in the existing international order, but how much influence it will exercise in shaping what comes next.

The contest is not just about who trades with whom. It is increasingly about who writes the rules of the global economy.

text:
Silicon Valley Cannot Outsource Counterintelligence to Washington

The unfolding Nvidia controversy has raised an uncomfortable question for America's technology industry: Who is responsible for identifying foreign intelligence threats before they become corporate crises?

Some have questioned whether federal authorities should have warned Nvidia earlier about concerns involving former CEO Jensen Huang. Government intelligence sharing matters. But companies holding strategically valuable technology cannot depend on Washington to recognize every threat on their behalf.

Apple's experience offers an instructive lesson. In 2018, internal security investigators detected unusual downloads by an engineer working on autonomous vehicle technology. The FBI subsequently arrested Xiaolang Zhang as he prepared to travel to China. He pleaded guilty to stealing trade secrets in 2022.

In 2019, another Apple employee reported a colleague photographing a restricted research area. An internal investigation uncovered thousands of confidential files, leading to a second federal trade secret case.

In both cases, the warning originated inside the company. Internal vigilance created the opportunity for law enforcement to act.

The Nvidia situation is different, and allegations involving potential foreign intelligence activity remain under investigation. Yet it illustrates how executive relationships, sensitive technologies and global commercial partnerships can intersect with national security risks.

My perspective is that counterintelligence must become a routine responsibility of corporate governance, not an emergency reaction to public scandal. Boards should understand their most sensitive intellectual property, identify high risk access and relationships, and ensure security, legal, compliance and human resources teams share relevant warning signs within appropriate privacy safeguards.

The goal is not to treat foreign connections as inherently suspicious. It is to recognize concrete risks, apply consistent standards and protect sensitive assets without prejudice.

Federal agencies remain essential partners, but they cannot substitute for internal monitoring, trained employees and a culture in which concerns can be reported safely.

The companies building tomorrow's AI infrastructure must protect more than their competitive advantage. They must safeguard the knowledge and systems on which national and economic security increasingly depend.

The government can help investigate a threat. Corporate leadership must build the systems capable of detecting it first.

#Nvidia #Apple #Counterintelligence #CorporateGovernance #NationalSecurity #Cybersecurity #ArtificialIntelligence #TechnologyLeadership

⚛️ AMERICA MAY HELP POWER THE PHILIPPINES WITH NUCLEAR ENERGY. HERE'S WHY THAT'S A SECURITY STORY.

🔹 Today at Malacañang: President Trump said that for the Philippines to embrace American technology in its first modern nuclear project would underscore the strength of the relationship, adding: "We're probably going to do something very big to do with nuclear." He also floated the Philippines as a partner in a planned Alaska natural gas export project.
🔹 The goal: The Philippines aims for 1,200 megawatts of nuclear power by 2032, and 4,800 megawatts by 2050.
🔹 The groundwork is already laid: A U.S.-Philippines civilian nuclear agreement took effect in 2024, allowing American companies to export reactors, equipment and technology. In February, Washington funded a $2.7 million study to help Meralco assess U.S.-designed small modular reactors, and provided a reactor control-room simulator to train Filipino operators.
🔹 Companies are moving: Just this week, U.S. startup Aalo Atomics signed an agreement to explore small nuclear plants in the Philippines, starting with a 50-megawatt design built from factory-made modules.

📌 Analysis: In March, the Philippines declared a national energy emergency as the Iran war sent oil prices soaring. That's the lesson: a country that imports its fuel can be squeezed by events it doesn't control. Nuclear power offers steady electricity that doesn't depend on the next oil shock. But who builds the reactors matters as much as the reactors themselves. A nuclear partner supplies fuel, parts, training and safety support for decades. That makes choosing one a national security decision, not just an energy deal. Filipinos will rightly want answers on safety, cost and waste. Those debates should happen in the open, before the first concrete is poured.

📖 Energy security is national security. That's part of the lens behind Shadows Over the Archipelago, coming March 2027.

⚛️ Whoever builds your reactors is your partner for decades. Choose like it.

text:
US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Fox News on Monday night that "superintelligence" could be behind the recent run of technology failures. He said an unnamed tech industry contact believes programs that write and fix their own code are changing systems faster than older networks can handle. Mullin called the theory something that "kind of makes sense", while also saying he was 98% sure there was no cyberattack and that the incidents were "all individually unrelated".

The failures came in five days. Microsoft had a worldwide outage of nearly 24 hours on Thursday that hit Outlook and Teams, the FAA grounded flights across the country on Friday for more than four hours, and on Monday Chase customers lost access to online banking and payments for hours. Microsoft blamed a software bug introduced in July, the FAA said a flood of data overwhelmed legacy air traffic equipment at 17 of its 22 control centers, and Chase blamed a software bug in its on-premise hardware systems, and none of them pointed to AI.

On Wednesday Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is "zero evidence" the incidents are connected, and outside experts say upgrades and bugs are the likelier causes. The comments matter because the same week saw outages at the NSA, Apple and Marriott, and the theory is now spreading without proof. (via Fortune)

🔥 Behind the scenes and leaks

Vals, a San Francisco AI testing startup, found that leading models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek and others often marked civilians, ambulances and surrendering soldiers as targets in simulated drone and satellite tasks. None of its requests were blocked by a safety filter, and models that refused usually complied once told it was a game. In real satellite images of a school in Minab, Iran, bombed by the US in February, Claude Opus 5.5 picked the school in 22 of 32 trials, while no OpenAI model chose it. Vals stresses it did not test real strike decisions or accuracy. (via TechCrunch)

🎥 The future in image and video

Suno launched Suno Visuals, which turns a song into AI music video clips of 15 seconds that can be joined into a longer video. The feature needs extra paid credits on top of the normal plan. It moves Suno from audio only into video, where musicians have so far had to hire editors or use separate tools. (via The Neuron)

🫧 The bubble thermometer

📉 US stocks fell on Tuesday, with the Dow down 1.6% and the S&P 500 down 1.0%, as worries about AI spending returned. Former Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson warned that markets may be underestimating the risk of an AI investment collapse. The selloff came just before Nvidia reported record results after the close. (via The Neuron)

🇪🇺 European Union: Google Cloud announced in Brussels an expansion of its Sovereign AI offer, with some Gemini models running on infrastructure operated by local partners and new controls over encryption keys. It also opened a 15 week accelerator for startups in Europe and Israel building AI for regulated sectors. The aim is to meet European data and security rules. (via AIdapted)

🇨🇳 China: A Reuters analysis of more than 300 Chinese papers, patents and company documents found that distilling the outputs of US models, especially from OpenAI, has become routine practice in China, including for Alibaba's Qwen. Distillation is legal and common, but it cannot copy a frontier model in full, and the dispute is over systematic unauthorized extraction. It comes as Washington tightens limits on renting chips abroad. (via Reuters)

🇧🇷 Brazil: The Inter-American Development Bank estimates that wide adoption of AI could lift Brazil's GDP by 5.1% over ten years. Separately, a project called Prisma will link data centers in Brazil so workloads can be spread with better energy efficiency. (via Valor Econômico and Olhar Digital)

Waymo removed the driver. California just removed the highway.

California’s DMV barred Waymo’s driverless vehicles from state freeways after deciding that recurring incursions into active construction zones posed an “imminent hazard to public safety.” Waymo then paused commercial freeway rides across every market where it offered them.

On November 5, three Waymo vehicles entered an active construction closure on US 101. The next day, another attempted to pass California Highway Patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break on I-280. Waymo says neither incident caused a collision or injury.

The company can still carry passengers on city streets and says it completes more than 500,000 trips a week there. The freeway restriction remains until Waymo demonstrates that its fixes work.

This is a cleaner test of autonomy than a driverless demo. A robotaxi is only as autonomous as the roads regulators still trust it to enter.

The Story of eKatherina the Great aka IG KatrinaLogunova.Official 
The full writing ✍️ about the Celeste Trail 👣 story here
