text:
🧭 KALEİÇİ | TRAVEL ESSENTIALS
📍 Getting There

Located in central Antalya, Kaleiçi is accessible from Antalya Airport via the AntRay tram. Get off at İsmetpaşa and walk into the old town. Taxis are another option, particularly with luggage.

🗺️ What to Explore

Begin at Hadrian’s Gate, follow the historic lanes toward Hıdırlık Tower, and descend to the Old Harbour. For a different perspective, consider a coastal boat trip. History enthusiasts can add the Yivli Minaret complex and local museums.

⏱️ Time Needed

Allow 2–4 hours for a walking exploration, or half a day with museum visits and waterfront stops. Staying overnight in a restored historic house offers more time to experience the neighbourhood beyond its busiest hours.

🌤️ When to Visit

Spring and autumn generally offer more comfortable walking conditions. During summer, early mornings and late afternoons are preferable to the midday heat.

💰 Costs & Local Insight

Exploring Kaleiçi’s public streets requires no admission ticket. Museums and boat excursions may charge separately. The harbour sits below the upper streets, so plan for sloping lanes and steps when choosing your route.

India and the Philippines are advancing discussions on a wider defence partnership beyond the existing BrahMos deal. Manila is examining at least six additional BrahMos supersonic cruise missile batteries, more than five regiments of Akash air-defence systems for the Army, Navy, Air Force and Marines, and multiple batteries of Pinaka multi-barrel rocket launchers for the Army.

Financial terms remain under discussion, including the standard advance payment requirement. India has also offered to examine integration of BrahMos on Philippine naval vessels. In parallel, Indian firm MKU is setting up a manufacturing facility in the Philippines for bullet-proof jackets after a ₹1,400 crore order, while exploratory talks cover helicopter acquisitions.

On the space front, India has proposed establishing observation stations in multiple Philippine locations to provide access to Indian satellite imagery for maritime domain awareness in the South China Sea. The two sides are also negotiating a Visiting Forces Agreement to create a legal framework for Indian military personnel participating in joint exercises and other engagements. Cadet training exchanges at India’s National Defence Academy and Indian Military Academy are expanding.

These steps form part of Manila’s ongoing modernisation and diversification of suppliers amid South China Sea tensions, while positioning Indian systems across strike, air defence and rocket artillery domains.

text:
👻 100 FACTS ABOUT GHOST TOWNS AROUND THE WORLD (PRIPYAT TO KOLMANSKOP)

☢️ PRIPYAT & THE CHERNOBYL ZONE 🇺🇦
𝟏. Pripyat was founded in 1970 to house workers of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant

𝟐. It was granted city status in 1979

𝟑. About 49,000 people lived there in 1986

𝟒. Reactor No. 4 exploded at 1:23 a.m. on 26 April 1986

𝟓. The evacuation began about 36 hours later, on the afternoon of 27 April

𝟔. Residents were told to pack for roughly three days; almost none ever returned

𝟕. Reportedly around 1,200 buses were used to move the population out

𝟖. The amusement park's yellow Ferris wheel was reportedly due to open for May Day 1986 and never officially ran

𝟗. The average age of residents was said to be only about 26

𝟏𝟎. The Chernobyl Exclusion Zone covers roughly 2,600 km²

𝟏𝟏. Wolves, elk, lynx and reintroduced Przewalski's horses now roam the zone

𝟏𝟐. The nearby 'Red Forest' got its name when its pines turned reddish-brown and died from radiation

𝟏𝟑. Some elderly villagers, known as 'samosely' (self-settlers), moved back into the zone despite the ban

𝟏𝟒. Ukraine officially opened the zone to tourists in 2011

𝟏𝟓. In 2016 the giant New Safe Confinement arch was slid over the ruined reactor

🏜️ KOLMANSKOP & THE DIAMOND DESERT 🇳🇦
𝟏𝟔. Kolmanskop lies in the Namib Desert, about 10 km inland from the port of Lüderitz, Namibia

𝟏𝟕. In 1908 railway worker Zacharias Lewala found a diamond there and showed it to his supervisor, August Stauch

𝟏𝟖. At the time, Namibia was the German colony of German South West Africa

𝟏𝟗. A diamond rush followed, and the authorities fenced off a huge 'Sperrgebiet', or forbidden zone

𝟐𝟎. The town grew into a German-style settlement with a ballroom, theatre, school, bakery and skittle alley

𝟐𝟏. Its hospital reportedly had the first X-ray machine in the Southern Hemisphere, partly to catch diamond smugglers

𝟐𝟐. An ice factory supplied residents with blocks of ice for their iceboxes

𝟐𝟑. Fresh water was scarce and had to be brought in from far away, reportedly by ship from Cape Town

𝟐𝟒. After World War I, richer diamond fields to the south drew miners away

𝟐𝟓. The last residents left in 1956

𝟐𝟔. Today desert dunes pour through doorways and fill rooms knee-deep with sand

𝟐𝟕. Photographers can buy special permits to shoot inside at sunrise and sunset

𝟐𝟖. Elizabeth Bay and Pomona are other abandoned diamond towns inside the Sperrgebiet

🤠 THE AMERICAN WEST & BEYOND 🇺🇸
𝟐𝟗. Bodie, California, began after gold was found in 1859 by a prospector usually named as W. S. Bodey

𝟑𝟎. At its peak around 1879-1880, Bodie had an estimated 7,000 to 10,000 people

𝟑𝟏. Bodie became a California State Historic Park in 1962

𝟑𝟐. It is kept in 'arrested decay': buildings are stabilised but not restored

𝟑𝟑. Legend says anything taken from Bodie brings bad luck, and visitors mail stolen items back to the park

𝟑𝟒. Rhyolite, Nevada, boomed after a 1904 gold strike and was almost empty by 1920

𝟑𝟓. Rhyolite's Bottle House was built in 1906 from tens of thousands of glass bottles

𝟑𝟔. Beneath Centralia, Pennsylvania, a coal-mine fire has been burning since 1962

𝟑𝟕. Most of Centralia's residents were relocated in the 1980s, and the 2020 census counted just 5 people

𝟑𝟖. Centralia's ZIP code was discontinued in 2002

𝟑𝟗. Kennecott, Alaska, was a booming copper town until its mines closed in 1938

𝟒𝟎. Calico, California, a silver town of the 1880s, was rebuilt as an attraction by Walter Knott of Knott's Berry Farm

𝟒𝟏. Cahawba was Alabama's first state capital and is now an archaeological ghost town

𝟒𝟐. Monowi, Nebraska, has a single resident, Elsie Eiler, who runs the tavern and the library

𝟒𝟑. Buford, Wyoming, once billed as 'population 1', was sold at auction in 2012 for $900,000

🏝️ ISLAND GHOST TOWNS
𝟒𝟒. 🇯🇵 Hashima Island, off Nagasaki, is nicknamed 'Gunkanjima', meaning Battleship Island, for its shape

𝟒𝟓. Its undersea coal mine operated from 1887 to 1974

𝟒𝟔. In 1959 about 5,000 people lived on its roughly 6 hectares, one of the highest densities ever recorded

𝟒𝟕. Hashima's 1916 apartment block is considered Japan's first large reinforced-concrete residential building

𝟒𝟖. In 2015 it became part of a UNESCO World Heritage site on Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution

𝟒𝟗. Its ruins inspired the villain's island lair in the 2012 James Bond film 'Skyfall'

𝟓𝟎. 🇲🇸 Plymouth, the capital of Montserrat, was buried by the Soufrière Hills volcano from 1995 onwards

𝟓𝟏. Plymouth remains the island's official capital, making it a capital city nobody lives in

𝟓𝟐. 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 The last 36 residents of St Kilda, Scotland, were evacuated at their own request in August 1930

𝟓𝟑. 🇨🇳 Houtouwan, a fishing village on Shengshan Island, is now almost completely swallowed by green vines

𝟓𝟒. 🇬🇷 Spinalonga, off Crete, was a leper colony from 1903 to 1957 and inspired Victoria Hislop's novel 'The Island'

❄️ COLD & REMOTE OUTPOSTS
𝟓𝟓. 🇳🇴 Pyramiden on Svalbard was founded by Sweden in 1910 and sold to the Soviet Union in 1927

𝟓𝟔. The Soviet coal-mining town was abandoned in 1998, leaving its buildings almost untouched

𝟓𝟕. Pyramiden is said to have the world's northernmost monument to Lenin

𝟓𝟖. 🇷🇺 Kadykchan, in Russia's Magadan region, emptied out after a deadly mine explosion in 1996 closed its pit

𝟓𝟗. 🇬🇸 Grytviken on South Georgia was a whaling station from 1904 to 1966

𝟔𝟎. Polar explorer Ernest Shackleton is buried in Grytviken's cemetery

𝟔𝟏. 🇨🇱 The Humberstone and Santa Laura saltpetre works in Chile's Atacama Desert were abandoned around 1960

𝟔𝟐. They became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005

𝟔𝟑. 🇦🇺 Wittenoom, Western Australia, was a blue-asbestos mining town that was officially wiped off the map

𝟔𝟒. 🇧🇷 Fordlândia was Henry Ford's 1928 attempt to build a rubber-producing company town in the Amazon

𝟔𝟓. The project failed, and Ford sold the land back to Brazil in 1945

🕊️ SCARS OF WAR & HISTORY
𝟔𝟔. 🇫🇷 On 10 June 1944, a Waffen-SS unit killed about 640 people in Oradour-sur-Glane, France

𝟔𝟕. Charles de Gaulle ordered the ruins preserved as a memorial, and a new village was built nearby

𝟔𝟖. Burnt-out cars and sewing machines still sit where they were left in 1944

𝟔𝟗. 🇪🇸 Belchite, Spain, was ruined in a 1937 Spanish Civil War battle and its old town left standing as ruins

𝟕𝟎. 🇨🇾 Varosha, a resort district of Famagusta, Cyprus, was fenced off and abandoned in 1974

𝟕𝟏. In its heyday Varosha was one of the Mediterranean's most fashionable resorts

𝟕𝟐. Part of Varosha reopened to visitors in 2020 after more than 45 years

𝟕𝟑. 🇹🇷 Kayaköy, near Fethiye, holds hundreds of empty stone houses, abandoned after the 1923 population exchange

𝟕𝟒. Kayaköy inspired the village in Louis de Bernières' novel 'Birds Without Wings'

𝟕𝟓. 🇬🇧 Tyneham, in Dorset, was evacuated for army training in December 1943, and its people never returned

𝟕𝟔. Departing villagers pinned a note to the church door asking soldiers to treat their homes with care

𝟕𝟕. Imber, on Salisbury Plain, was also emptied in 1943 and is opened to the public only a few days a year

🌊 DROWNED & DISASTER TOWNS
𝟕𝟖. 🇦🇷 The spa town of Villa Epecuén, Argentina, was flooded by a salt lake in 1985

𝟕𝟗. At its worst, the water reportedly rose about 10 metres over the streets

𝟖𝟎. As the lake receded, from around 2009, its ruins re-emerged, bleached white by salt

𝟖𝟏. Pablo Novak lived among Epecuén's ruins for years as its lone resident

𝟖𝟐. 🇮🇹 In Lake Reschen, South Tyrol, the church tower of the drowned village of Curon sticks out of the water

𝟖𝟑. Curon was flooded in 1950 when a dam raised the lake level

𝟖𝟒. 🇺🇸 St. Thomas, Nevada, was swallowed by Lake Mead in 1938 and reappears when water levels drop

𝟖𝟓. 🇵🇹 Vilarinho da Furna, Portugal, was submerged by a reservoir in 1972 and resurfaces in droughts

𝟖𝟔. 🇮🇳 Dhanushkodi, India, was destroyed by a cyclone in 1964 that also swept away a passenger train

𝟖𝟕. 🇮🇹 Craco, in Basilicata, was abandoned after a landslide in 1963

𝟖𝟖. Craco appeared in films such as 'The Passion of the Christ' and 'Quantum of Solace'

𝟖𝟗. 🇧🇪 Doel, Belgium, mostly emptied by port expansion plans, became famous for its giant graffiti murals

👻 LEGENDS & ODD FACTS
𝟗𝟎. 🇮🇳 Kuldhara, Rajasthan, was abandoned in the 19th century, and legend says its villagers cursed it as they left

𝟗𝟏. Bhangarh Fort, also in Rajasthan, is often called India's most haunted place, and entry after dark is not allowed

𝟗𝟐. 🇹🇼 Taiwan's San Zhi 'UFO houses', futuristic pod homes that were never occupied, were demolished around 2008-2010

𝟗𝟑. 🇯🇵 In Nagoro, Japan, artist Tsukimi Ayano made hundreds of life-size dolls that outnumber the residents

𝟗𝟒. Japan had about 9 million empty homes, or 'akiya', in a 2023 government survey

𝟗𝟓. 🇮🇹 Civita di Bagnoregio, nicknamed 'the dying town', has only about a dozen permanent residents

𝟗𝟔. Several shrinking Italian towns have offered empty houses for as little as €1

𝟗𝟕. Most ghost towns die because a mine runs out, a railway bypasses them, a disaster strikes or a dam floods them

𝟗𝟖. Many former boomtowns now earn more from tourists than they ever did from gold, silver or diamonds

𝟗𝟗. Ghost towns are popular with photographers, urban explorers and filmmakers around the world

𝟏𝟎𝟎. From Pripyat to Kolmanskop, they show how quickly nature reclaims what people leave behind

text:
The perfect gift for cats doesn't exist.

Every person who has ever loved one knows this in their bones. You stand in the pet aisle holding a feather wand, a catnip banana, a tunnel, a laser, a tiny fake mouse that cost more than your lunch. You bring it home. The cat inspects it for four seconds, delivers a verdict, and walks directly into the cardboard box it came in.

The box wins. The box always wins.

Cats are the toughest audience on earth, and they don't even have to say anything to prove it. A dog will pretend to love your gift. A dog will love your gift out of pure loyalty, even if it's a sock. A cat has no such courtesy. A cat will look you in the eye, look at the thing you spent money on, and slowly, deliberately, turn away.

That's the problem this post is about. And it's about the one object in a very long time that made me stop and ask whether the problem was ever the cat.

Because here's what I realized somewhere between the fifth abandoned toy and the sixth: we've been shopping for the wrong thing.

We shop for entertainment. Cats mostly ask for something else.

Stay with me for a minute. This gets stranger, and a lot more tender, than a gift guide has any right to be.

Start with the money, because the money tells the truth.

Americans spend well north of 140 billion dollars a year on their pets. Not in a decade. Every year. A big slice of that goes to toys, treats, beds, gadgets, fountains, scratching towers, cameras that let you watch your cat ignore the other things you bought. The industry has a shelf for every guilty feeling a person can have while leaving the house in the morning.

And yet ask any cat owner what their cat actually uses, and the answers come back almost embarrassingly small. The sunny spot on the floor. The one blanket that smells like them. The lap, if the lap is available and the cat has decided it is.

Warmth. A familiar smell. Someone close by.

That's it. That's the whole wishlist.

The billion-dollar aisle is built on the assumption that a bored cat needs stimulation. Sometimes that's true. But a lot of what looks like boredom in a cat is something quieter: a small animal in a large, silent room, waiting for the part of the day that has company in it.

So the real question for a gift-giver isn't "what will keep my cat busy?"

It's "what would make the empty hours feel less empty?"

And that question has a stranger answer than a toy.

Go back to the beginning of any cat's life, before the personality, before the opinions, before the knocking of glasses off tables.

A newborn kitten arrives with its eyes sealed shut. They stay that way for roughly the first week to ten days. Hearing is still switching on. The kitten's whole world, in those first days, is built out of three things it can feel without seeing: warmth, vibration, and rhythm.

Warmth from a mother's body and from siblings pressed against each other in a pile. Vibration from the purr, which a mother cat can produce while nursing. And rhythm, the steady pulse of a living body that is right there, every second, for as long as the kitten needs it.

That's the first environment. Not a room. Not a toy. A pile of bodies with a heartbeat in it.

Then something happens that every cat owner has seen and few have thought hard about. A fully grown cat, sleek and independent and entirely too proud to admit it needs anything, climbs onto a soft blanket and starts to knead. Slow, rhythmic, paws pressing in and out. Eyes half closed. Sometimes a faint purr.

The popular explanation, and a sensible one, is that kneading is a leftover from nursing, when kittens press on the mother to bring the milk down. The adult cat isn't hungry. The adult cat is remembering how safe felt.

Which raises a question I can't stop turning over.

If a cat's earliest memory of safety has a pulse in it, what happens when an adult cat is alone in a quiet house for nine hours?

We like to say cats are fine on their own. Many are. Cats are crepuscular, they sleep somewhere between twelve and sixteen hours a day, and a well-adjusted cat can pass a quiet afternoon with the calm of a monk.

But "fine" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

Plenty of cats, especially indoor ones, live in a world that is almost entirely silent for a large part of the day. The refrigerator hums. The radiator ticks. A car passes. And then, around the time the key turns in the lock, the whole apartment comes alive again.

Humans are very good at reading the way dogs feel about being left. The whining, the pacing, the shredded cushions. Cats are far better at hiding it. A cat that is struggling with solitude rarely does anything dramatic. It sleeps in odd places. It overgrooms. It waits at the door a little too long. It becomes very, very attached to the one warm thing in the house that doesn't leave.

If you've ever had a cat that follows you from room to room, that sleeps pressed against your ribs, that settles only when it can feel you breathing, you already know what I'm describing.

They aren't looking for a toy.

They're looking for a pulse.

And that is the idea that someone, somewhere, decided to build a product around.

Let's talk about what a heartbeat actually is to a mammal, because it's more interesting than it sounds.

A heartbeat is the first sound most mammals ever experience. Before light, before language, before any voice, there is a rhythm. In humans, a developing baby spends months inside a body that is thumping away at a steady pace, and the old folk wisdom that newborns settle when held against a chest is almost universal. Parents have known it for as long as there have been parents.

Animal keepers know a version of it too. For generations, people raising a lonely puppy or kitten have tucked a ticking clock or a warm bottle into the bedding on the first night home. Some swear by it. Others roll their eyes. The honest truth is that the scientific evidence for the ticking-clock trick is thin, and anyone who tells you it is a proven cure for a homesick animal is selling something.

But the intuition behind it is hard to dismiss. A slow, steady rhythm, paired with warmth and a soft body, is the closest thing a young animal gets to a signal that says: you are not alone.

Now add one more fact. A cat's own heart is not like ours. A resting adult cat's heart typically beats somewhere around 140 to 220 times a minute, depending on the cat, the moment, and how relaxed it is. Ours sits at roughly 60 to 100. A cat's whole life runs on a faster clock.

That means a convincing heartbeat for a cat is not a human heartbeat. It's a different tempo, a different weight, a different feel.

Which makes the idea at the center of this post either very clever or completely absurd.

And the only creature qualified to judge is the one with the whiskers.

Here is what nobody tells you about cats and fakes.

A cat is a precision instrument. Its nose can pick up scent information we cannot imagine. Its whiskers read air movement and tiny changes in space. Its hearing reaches far above the range of human ears, high enough to catch the squeak of a mouse a room away. Its eyes are built for dim light. This is an animal engineered over millions of years to detect the difference between something alive and something that only looks alive.

Which is why most "realistic" cat toys fail so fast. The fur is right. The shape is right. And the cat knows in about a second and a half that nothing inside is moving.

Cats have been living near humans for something like ten thousand years. Archaeologists found a cat buried alongside a person on Cyprus roughly 9,500 years ago, which tells us the bond is ancient. But even after all that time sharing hearths and barns and sofas, cats never lost their instinct for spotting a bluff.

That's what makes any object that claims to comfort a cat such a risky claim. You cannot persuade a cat with a label. You cannot reason with it. You cannot post a five-star review that it will read.

The cat decides in its own time, on its own terms, with its own body.

It will either walk past, or it will do something else.

I won't tell you which. That part belongs to the cat.

There's a reason this kind of object lands so hard with people, and it has nothing to do with plush.

Gifts for pets are never really for pets. They're for the part of us that feels guilty at 7:40 in the morning when the door closes and a small face watches us leave. They're for the version of us that wishes we could be two places at once. They're for the quiet apology that no cat will ever accept and no cat will ever need.

That's not cynical. That's love, working with the tools it has.

And the strangest thing about caring for an animal is how much of the work is guesswork. The cat can't tell you what it needs. It can't say "I'm lonely" or "I'm anxious about the new furniture" or "that vacuum cleaner is a personal enemy." You get signals. A slow blink. A tail held high. Ears turned flat. A cat that curls up in the exact spot where your jumper was.

Researchers at the University of Sussex reported in 2020 that cats were more likely to approach a person who slow-blinked at them, which suggests even the smallest gestures, well timed, carry meaning in the cat's world.

Small gestures. Large effects.

That might be the single most useful thing a cat owner can learn. You don't need a grand gesture. You need the right small one, delivered at the right moment, in the language the animal actually speaks.

Warmth is a language. Rhythm is a language. Closeness is a language.

The only question is whether a person can learn to speak it through an object.

Now the season matters, and I'm not going to pretend it doesn't.

Winter changes a household. The nights come early. The heating goes on. People stay in, and then they don't. They go away for the holidays, or they fill the house with guests, or they drag a tree through the front door and cover it in lights. To a cat, a living room that was a predictable kingdom in October becomes a place where the furniture moves, strangers appear, and strange smells arrive in bags.

Many cats handle all of it beautifully. Some hide under the bed until January.

Most owners I know have a version of the same Christmas story. The cat who ignored every wrapped present and fell asleep inside the wrapping paper. The cat who treated the tree as a personal jungle gym. The cat who, after the guests had gone, went straight to the one soft thing in the room and refused to move.

That last cat is the one I think about.

Because after the noise ends, what does a cat reach for? Not the toys. Not the treats. It reaches for whatever feels like the end of the day. Something warm. Something that holds still. Something that, to a very small and very sensitive animal, feels like it is breathing.

A gift that understands that is a different category of gift.

It isn't there to entertain. It's there to stay.

I should be straight with you, because trust is the only currency that matters when a post gets this long.

A plush with a mechanism inside it is not a cure. It's not a vet. It's not a substitute for your time, your attention, or a proper bed and a proper diet and a house a cat feels safe in. If a cat is truly distressed when left alone, if it stops eating, cries for hours, overgrooms to the point of bald patches, soils outside the litter tray, that deserves a conversation with a veterinarian, not a shopping cart.

And the claim in the video, that the heartbeat calms and comforts, is exactly that: a claim. A promise made by a caption. Cats are individuals. Some fall in love with a thing in a day. Some never notice it. Some sniff it once, file it under "unimportant," and go back to staring at a wall.

That's not a flaw in the idea. It's the honest nature of cats.

But here's why I keep coming back to it anyway.

Almost every cat product on the market is designed to make a human feel something. This one is built around a question the cat might actually care about. Not "what will she find fun?" but "what does she find safe?"

That's a better question. Even if the answer turns out to be different for every cat in your life.

And there's only one way to see how a cat answers it.

Maybe the deeper issue is that we've misread cats for centuries.

The stereotype is that cats are aloof. Independent. Barely interested in us beyond the can opener. It's a flattering story for people who prefer their pets low-maintenance, and it has quietly shaped how the whole pet industry treats them.

Then researchers started testing it.

In 2019, a team led by Kristyn Vitale at Oregon State University published a study in Current Biology adapting a classic attachment test, the kind used on human infants and dogs, for cats. Roughly two-thirds of the cats showed a secure attachment to their owners, a share in the same range as infants. The cats took comfort from their person's return and used them as a base from which to explore.

Read that against the stereotype. The aloof cat is, for most cats, a story we told ourselves.

What looks like indifference is often a quieter dialect. Cats don't stand at the window howling. They don't throw their whole bodies at you in the doorway. They sit nearby. They check. They keep you in their peripheral awareness the way a tide keeps the shore.

If that's true, then a lot of cat behavior reads differently. The cat that appears at the bathroom door. The cat that sleeps on your side of the bed the moment you leave it. The cat that chooses to be in the room, but not on you, close enough to hear you breathe.

That's attachment. It simply doesn't make a lot of noise.

And attachment, unlike entertainment, is something you can feel at three in the morning.

Which brings us, finally, to the box.

In 2014, researchers at Utrecht University in the Netherlands studied newly arrived cats in an animal shelter. Some were given a simple cardboard hiding box. Others were not. The cats with boxes settled in faster and showed lower stress scores in the first days.

So the box doesn't win because cats are unreasonable. The box wins because it solves a real problem: it makes a small animal feel contained, hidden, and held.

Read that again. Contained. Hidden. Held.

Cats don't look for novelty when they're uneasy. They look for enclosure. They squeeze into drawers, shopping bags, laundry baskets, the gap behind the sofa, a sink you were about to use. They find the tightest, warmest, quietest space in the house and make it theirs.

And now you can see why the pet aisle keeps failing. It sells things to look at. The cat is looking for something to lean on.

Every cat owner has watched this happen in miniature. The cat who ignores the expensive bed and sleeps in the laundry you just folded. The cat who chooses the lap of the one person in the room who dislikes cats. The cat who ends up pressed into the warm hollow you left in the duvet.

Comfort, for a cat, is not decoration. It's contact.

So any object that wants to earn a place in a cat's life has to pass a very old test. Not "is it interesting?"

Is it safe enough to sleep against?

There's one more piece of cat biology that quietly rewires how you think about all this.

Purring.

Most people assume a purr means a cat is happy, and often it does. But cats also purr when they're hurt, when they're frightened, when they're giving birth, and when they're being examined at the vet. Researchers have long noted that the purr falls into a low-frequency range, commonly cited as somewhere between about 25 and 150 hertz, and some scientists have speculated that it may help a cat soothe itself. That part is still debated, and you should be wary of anyone who treats it as settled.

What isn't debated is the pattern. A purr is a rhythm. A low, steady, repeating vibration, produced by the cat, felt through its own body, shared with whatever is pressed against it.

A cat that purrs against you is broadcasting something. A cat that purrs alone is talking to itself.

Think about what that implies. A cat's most reliable comfort signal is rhythmic, bodily, and close. It's a sound you feel as much as hear.

So the idea that a cat might respond to a steady pulse, low and warm, held right against its chest, isn't an absurd leap. It's an extension of the way the animal already soothes itself.

Whether it works for your cat is a separate question. But the question is a good one.

And good questions are what make people hit play.

I've watched a lot of animal content. Rescues, reunions, strange friendships, birds adopting kittens, dogs guarding sleeping babies. After a while you develop a feel for what actually works on the human nervous system, and it's rarely the thing the creator thinks it is.

It isn't the spectacle. It's the decision.

A person can watch a thousand clips of cats doing cat things and feel nothing. But put a cat in front of something unfamiliar and let it decide, and a room full of strangers leans in. Because the cat's reaction can't be faked, can't be directed, can't be hurried. It happens in the animal's own timing.

There's a small, old thrill in watching a creature choose.

We live in a world of curated reactions. Influencers perform surprise. Brands rehearse authenticity. A cat will do none of it. A cat will not act pleased for the camera. If it hates the thing, you will know in one second. If it loves the thing, you will know that too, and it will feel earned, because you watched the cat make up its mind.

That's why fifteen seconds is plenty.

Fifteen seconds is enough time for a cat to walk across a room, make a judgment, and change the way you think about a very small object.

I'm not going to tell you what the cat decides.

I'll just say that I've seen a lot of reactions in my time, and I did not see this one coming.

Let me ask you something that has nothing to do with a plush.

Who in your life is waiting for a pulse?

Not literally. I mean the cat who sleeps at the door at 4 p.m. and doesn't know why. The older cat who moves more slowly this year and has started choosing the radiator over the windowsill. The shy rescue who has lived with you for months and still keeps one eye open while sleeping. The new arrival who cried the first three nights in a strange house. The one who wakes at 3 a.m. and walks the length of the hallway, looking for something she can't name.

Every cat has a version of that. Most of us call it personality.

Sometimes it's personality. Sometimes it's an animal doing the best it can with a nervous system built for a much busier, more crowded, more physically close world than the one we've given it.

The idea behind this particular gift is almost embarrassingly simple. It doesn't try to entertain. It doesn't promise to fix. It offers a soft body, a steady rhythm, and a place to put a chin.

And honestly, that may be the most cat-aware thing a person can give a cat.

Not a thing to chase.

A thing to rest against.

The best gifts you've ever received probably weren't expensive.

They were accurate.

Somebody noticed something about you that you hadn't said out loud. The book that arrived a week after the bad week. The scarf in exactly your color. The tiny, odd thing that proved they had been listening when you thought nobody was.

That's what accuracy feels like. It's the opposite of generic.

A cat can't write a wishlist, so the burden of accuracy falls entirely on the person. You have to watch. You have to learn which corner of the house she keeps returning to, which fabric she kneads, what time of day she gets restless, how she behaves when the front door closes behind you. You have to interpret a creature who speaks in posture and silence.

Which means the real gift, the one underneath all the other gifts, is attention.

An object can only be as good as the attention that chose it. A plush chosen because it was cute is a plush. A plush chosen because you noticed your cat gravitates toward warm, soft, steady things is an answer to a question you asked by paying attention.

That difference never shows up on a product page. But it shows up in the house. In whether the thing gets used or gets ignored. In whether the cat treats it as furniture or as company.

So if there's a lesson hiding in a fifteen-second clip about a stuffed animal, maybe it's this.

Don't shop for the cat you imagine.

Shop for the cat who actually lives with you.

I know exactly what the comment section is going to say, because I've read this comment section before.

"My cat would destroy it in four minutes."

Fair. Some cats are hunters first and snugglers second. A cat that wrestles everything it meets might treat a soft toy as prey, and that's worth knowing before you buy anything. Watch how your cat treats stuffed objects. If she kicks, bites, and disembowels them, a heartbeat won't change her personality.

"My cat doesn't care about toys."

Also fair. Some cats genuinely don't. Some will sniff an object once and walk off for good. Cats are not an audience you can win by volume.

"This is a gimmick."

Maybe. Plenty of pet products are. A healthy amount of skepticism is exactly right, especially when a caption makes a promise about calming an animal. If you do look into one, treat it like any pet purchase. Read independent reviews, check that anything with a battery or electronics is securely enclosed, make sure no small parts can come loose, and keep an eye on how your cat uses it, particularly in the first days. If she chews it open, it goes away.

None of that makes the question less interesting.

It makes it more honest. The people who will love this idea are not the people who believe in magic. They're the people who have watched a cat curl against a warm laundry basket and thought, there must be something more deliberate than that.

And the people who are skeptical?

Good. You're the audience this was made for. Cats are skeptics too.

If you take only one practical thing from this post, let it be this.

A cat's sense of safety is built from many small ingredients, and an object is only one of them. Before anything arrives in a box, it's worth asking whether the basics are in place.

Does she have somewhere to hide that no one will disturb? Cats like options at different heights, so a shelf, a cat tree, or the top of a bookcase can matter as much as a bed. Is there a predictable routine? Cats read time through habit, and meals, play, and quiet hours that arrive at the same moments tell an animal that the world is stable. Does the house have enough of her scent in it? A blanket she sleeps on, unwashed for a few days, can do more than a new purchase. Is there a calm place away from the loud parts of the household when guests arrive?

And is there play, real play, with you, for a few minutes each day? A cat that gets to stalk, pounce, and catch sleeps differently afterward.

Get those right, and a soft companion becomes an extra, not a crutch. Get them wrong, and no object, no matter how clever, will rescue a cat who feels unsafe in her own house.

That's the part that gets forgotten when something goes viral. The thing that gets shared is the object. The thing that works is the home.

I say this because I want you to leave with something better than a product.

I want you to leave looking at your cat differently.

Watch her for ten minutes tonight. See where she sleeps. See what she leans against. See what she chooses when nobody is choosing for her.

That is the real shopping list.

One last thought before the cat gets the final word.

We spend so much energy trying to make animals fit our idea of a good life. Bigger towers. Smarter feeders. Louder toys. Meanwhile the animal on the rug is asking for something so old it predates every product ever sold: to be near something warm that is quietly alive.

If an object can honor that, even a little, even for one cat, it deserves a look. Not because it is magic, but because it listens to what the cat has been saying all along, in the only language she has, and that's closeness.

So here is where I'll leave it.

A white cat. A soft object. A very old rhythm. And a caption that dares to claim the perfect gift for cats does exist after all.

I don't know if it's true for every cat. I'd be lying if I said I did. What I know is that I've spent years watching people try to buy affection from animals that can't be bought, and I've never seen a fifteen-second clip make me rethink the entire approach so quickly.

Because it flips the question. It stops asking what a cat might find amusing and starts asking what a cat might find like home.

That's a different kind of gift. A quieter one.

And it has a way of making you wonder who else in your house, or in your life, has been waiting for something steady to rest against, and never found a way to ask.

Watch the video. Look at the cat, not the object. Notice the moment her attention changes. Then ask yourself the question I couldn't stop asking.

Who needs one?

 13-Day Small Group Journey from Tokyo to Kyoto

Experience the rich heritage, timeless traditions, and modern wonders of Japan on this immersive small-group adventure. From the dazzling energy of Tokyo to the breathtaking landscapes of Hokkaido and the cultural treasures of Kyoto, this carefully crafted journey reveals the many faces of Japan through authentic encounters and unforgettable experiences.

Begin in Tokyo, where ancient traditions thrive alongside futuristic innovation. Navigate the city's world-famous subway system as you explore iconic landmarks including the serene Meiji Shrine, the historic Asakusa Kannon Temple, and the vibrant Nakamise shopping arcade. Discover the hidden rhythms of daily Japanese life while immersing yourself in one of the world's most fascinating cities.

Fly north to Sapporo, the capital of Hokkaido, known for its broad boulevards, open spaces, and distinctive local culture. Here, gain a deeper understanding of Japan's Indigenous heritage during a moving visit to Upopoy National Ainu Museum and Park, where traditional performances and exhibits celebrate the history and customs of the Ainu people.

Continue to the charming mountain town of Tendo, where Japan's cherished traditions come to life. Sample locally crafted sake at a traditional brewery, master the art of making hand-cut soba noodles during an interactive cooking experience, and enjoy an elegant performance by a maiko, an apprentice geisha, showcasing centuries-old cultural traditions.

Travel in true Japanese style aboard the famous Shinkansen bullet train to Kanazawa, a city renowned for its artistry and refined beauty. Stroll through the celebrated Kenroku-en Garden, considered one of Japan's finest landscape gardens, and participate in a hands-on gold leaf craft experience to create your own decorative bento box.

Venture into the picturesque village of Inami, famed throughout Japan for its exceptional woodcarving traditions. Walk along historic woodcarving streets, meet master artisans, and learn the techniques behind this centuries-old craft during a hands-on workshop.

Your journey concludes in Kyoto, Japan's cultural and spiritual heart. Explore magnificent landmarks including the shimmering Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion) and the remarkable Sanjusangendo Temple, home to hundreds of awe-inspiring Buddhist statues. Here, surrounded by centuries of history and tranquility, you'll experience the enduring beauty and profound traditions that define Japan.

Included intra-Japan flights as outlined in the itinerary

text:
It will soon be a year since I made a pivot in my life and started building Hyperion...
Right now, I'm at the other end of the country and had a moment to step onto the tennis courts. I still haven't played a single time since then, and for now, I don't want to. Not even "for fun", because that sport was never just fun for me. However, looking back now, I definitely don't regret a thing.

It's hard for me to believe that exactly a year ago at this time, I was still at the academy in Italy... 😅

Before my first self-tests in my room and reading literature at nights. 
Even before the project of a stationary biological renewal clinic and later before the clash with my own medical university, which didn't even want to talk or consult... 
Before asking AI to find the top 10 physiology professors in the country and call with Prof. Paweł Chmura. Before the PhD offer and later the official acceptance of my doctoral dissertation, whose direct subject is my system...
Before meeting Justyna Krzywdziak with experience at Samsung, who also joined and now says herself that "she's hyped about this project", or Radek and Ina – young Polish tech talents 😉
Before the first versions, the first partnerships, the first real athletes and clubs who also trusted me and are now building this with me ❤️
Before meeting many people from the business world – those who helped me, dedicated their time and knowledge, as well as those for whom I am still too early and who didn't understand me – because all of them gave important lessons that I tried to accept (even though they weren't always easy)

Today, I happen to be at the other end of Poland and dropped by the court just for a moment along the way. I came to Wrocław to talk with the professor about our first publication, which I want to aim even higher with right away, and we're making quite a pivot in it 😅 I also had to discuss matters related to the company itself and the fact that we soon need to formally register the business and how I see his role in all of this. Plus, present the stage of our work with the tech team on the v2 version or the upcoming special event for the karate club that collaborates with us. On top of that, matters related to the bioethics committee and applying next year for a Fulbright scholarship to do some of-site research in a lab at Stanford or another American university...

I still don't want to play for now, and I don't know if I ever will. But it's cool to come to the court and gain some perspective. That's when I see even more clearly how crazy all of this is 😅

And the best part is that this isn't the end, but just the beginning, and my project isn't even a year old yet 😉

Life is brutal.
But it definitely writes the best stories 😊

Me: Humankind: A Hopeful History

Ai: Humankind: A Hopeful History is an engaging and thought-provoking book that challenges one of society's most deeply rooted assumptions: that human beings are naturally selfish, aggressive, and driven primarily by their own interests. Written by Dutch historian Rutger Bregman, the book presents an alternative perspective on human nature, arguing that people are fundamentally more cooperative, compassionate, and decent than conventional history, psychology, and popular culture often suggest.
Bregman examines historical events, psychological experiments, scientific research, and real-life stories to question widely accepted beliefs about human behavior. He revisits famous studies, including the Stanford Prison Experiment, and explores events such as wartime cooperation, survival situations, and communities that have demonstrated extraordinary kindness under difficult circumstances.
One of the book's central arguments is that cooperation, trust, and mutual assistance have played a much greater role in human survival and civilization than competition and violence. Bregman suggests that when people are treated with trust and given opportunities to cooperate, they often rise to the occasion rather than exploit one another.
The book also challenges the way institutions, governments, businesses, and societies are organized around the assumption that people cannot be trusted. It encourages readers to reconsider leadership, education, politics, criminal justice, and workplace culture through a more optimistic understanding of human behavior.
At its core, Humankind is a powerful exploration of human nature and the possibility of building a better society by starting with a more positive view of one another. It invites readers to replace cynicism with curiosity, suspicion with trust, and pessimism with a renewed belief in humanity.

Key themes:
Human nature and human behavior.
Kindness, empathy, and cooperation.
Trust and the importance of community.
The psychology of power and authority.
Historical misconceptions about humanity.
Building better institutions and societies.

Who should read it: Anyone interested in psychology, sociology, philosophy, history, leadership, human behavior, and understanding why people act the way they do.

Overall: Humankind offers an inspiring alternative to the belief that people are inherently bad. It encourages readers to see humanity through a more hopeful lens and consider how trust, compassion, and cooperation can transform the world.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On the morning of November 18, 1863, Abraham Lincoln rose in the White House with more than the usual weight on his shoulders. His son Tad was ill with fever. Mary Todd Lincoln, already the mother of two lost boys, was nearly frantic at the thought of her husband leaving. Lincoln himself was quietly fighting the early stages of a mild case of smallpox, feeling weak and worn. Yet the invitation from Gettysburg could not be set aside. The cemetery for the Union dead of the great battle fought four months earlier was to be dedicated the following day, and he had been asked to say a few words. He intended to go.

A special train of four cars stood waiting. It pulled out of Washington around noon, carrying the President and a small company that included Secretaries Seward, Blair, and Usher, along with his secretaries John Nicolay and John Hay. The journey north was slow and deliberate. In Baltimore the cars had to be drawn by horses from one station to another. At Hanover Junction, Pennsylvania’s governor climbed aboard. When the train halted at Hanover, crowds pressed close. Lincoln stepped onto the rear platform, spoke briefly of loyalty and the Union, and stood still long enough for Mathew Brady to make a photograph. He was in better spirits than the circumstances might have suggested, though the short speech he had been working on still rested unfinished in his pocket.

They reached Gettysburg at dusk, the light already fading over the low hills and the fields where so many had fallen. David Wills, the local lawyer who had organized the ceremony, and Edward Everett, the renowned orator who would speak the next day, met the train at the station. A telegram waited for Lincoln: Tad was improving. That evening, in the Wills house on the town square, there was dinner, then a serenade by the Fifth New York Artillery Band. Later, alone in his room, Lincoln returned to the few pages he had brought with him, refining the words he would offer the following afternoon—words meant to say what the sacrifice at Gettysburg had meant, and what remained to be done if the nation was to endure.

The next day would bring the long oration by Everett and then Lincoln’s brief remarks. On the eighteenth, though, there was only the journey itself: a president traveling by rail through a still-divided country, carrying with him the unfinished draft of a speech, the private burdens of family and illness, and the quiet determination to stand among the graves and speak for the living and the dead.

Let me offer you a few pieces of serious advice.

Before attempting to dictate the future of Berbera or interfere in Somaliland’s affairs, first regain full control over Mogadishu’s seaport and international airport, where Turkish companies exercise extensive operational control.

These are two of the most important strategic facilities in your own capital, yet their management raises serious questions about sovereignty, accountability, and national authority. Allegations of mistreatment involving Somali citizens at these facilities also deserve answers.

How can you lecture Somaliland about sovereignty when your own government struggles to exercise effective authority over its most important national infrastructure?

Now, let us turn to Middle Shabelle, your own home region and the political heartland of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud.

For nearly two decades, Al-Shabaab has terrorized communities across this region, controlling or threatening significant areas while ordinary citizens continue to suffer insecurity, displacement, poverty, and the absence of effective government services.

Even areas under government authority have depended heavily on African Union peacekeeping forces, including Ugandan and Burundian troops, for military and security support.

Ali Omar, before claiming authority over Berbera, explain why the people of your own home region are still waiting for freedom from terrorism, lasting security, functioning institutions, and meaningful economic development.

You speak loudly about Somaliland’s territory while your government continues to struggle with the fundamental responsibility of protecting its own citizens.

The people of Middle Shabelle deserve security, dignity, economic opportunity, and a government capable of protecting them without indefinite dependence on foreign military forces.

Berbera does not need your permission, your political lectures, or your interference.

Instead of dreaming about governing Somaliland, focus on the security failures in Middle Shabelle, the governance challenges in Mogadishu, and the responsibilities your government has yet to fulfill.

text:
Dismantling the Victimhood Ledger: No Absolution, No Castigation

DIOGENES REIPUBLICAE AMERICAE

History is neither a confession booth nor a criminal courtroom. Yet much of contemporary commentary treats the transatlantic slave trade as an active indictment requiring modern spectators to either absolve one group or castigate another. That framing is not merely poor scholarship; it is a psychological trap. There is nothing to absolve and nothing to castigate, because the events in question belong to the settled past. Yes, the ramifications of history echo into the present, as the consequences of every war, migration, and empire always do. But human beings do not possess a time machine, and if we did, reaching backward to rewrite the seventeenth century would only manufacture new paradoxes. A nation and a people can only move forward with the ground beneath their feet and the value system they carry today.

This is precisely why articles like Debay Tadesse's "Africans Sold Africans: Myth or Reality?" in the Fresno Alliance are so corrosive. On the surface, Tadesse purports to correct simplistic social media slogans about African participation in the slave trade. In practice, the essay replaces one shallow caricature with a set of glaring historical distortions, all in service of a modern ideological agenda that demands permanent grievance and external atonement.
To take the historical record seriously, the factual errors in Tadesse's narrative must be dismantled first.
First, Tadesse claims that sixteenth century European powers, Portugal, Spain, Britain, France, and the Netherlands, relied on Arab merchants' coastal trading posts along West Africa and that African leaders sold captives primarily under pressure from Arabs already on the ground. 

That assertion is geographically and historically false. Arab and Berber merchants dominated the trans Saharan caravan routes across the interior and the Indian Ocean trade along East Africa, not the Atlantic littoral of West Africa.  European powers built their own fortified stone castles and trading factories directly along the Gulf of Guinea, beginning with the Portuguese at Sao Jorge da Mina (Elmina) in 1482, and negotiated face to face with coastal African sovereigns.

Second, Tadesse portrays West African rulers almost exclusively as cornered, helpless victims coerced into selling captives merely to survive European gunfire. That narrative strips major African polities of their genuine military, diplomatic, and economic power. Far from conquering the African interior in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, 

Europeans were pinned to narrow coastal enclaves by tropical disease and formidable African armies. Powerful centralized states, such as the Kingdom of Dahomey, the Asante Empire, and Oyo, controlled the trade routes, taxed European factors, dictated terms of exchange, and waged deliberate wars of expansion to capture prisoners for the export market. Recognizing that West African states exercised real agency does not excuse European buyers; it simply restores historical reality instead of reducing entire civilizations to passive props.

Third, Tadesse flattens eight centuries of distinct regional history into a single seamless blur, linking the eleventh century Almoravid invasion of the Sahelian Ghana Empire directly to the nineteenth century Sokoto Caliphate, which was founded in 1804, just three years before Britain and the United States abolished the transatlantic slave trade. Treating medieval Sahelian conflicts, nineteenth century Islamic jihads, and sixteenth century Atlantic commerce as a single undifferentiated wave of external coercion is polemic, not history.

Yet the deeper danger of Tadesse's essay lies not in its factual sloppiness, but in its conclusion. The author insists that flattening the history of external exploitation prevents society from confronting modern racial and social inequalities, the familiar prelude to demands for institutional penance and financial reparations.

Here is the hard truth that modern grievance merchants refuse to confront: demanding money from people alive today accomplishes nothing, and browbeating strangers into feeling accountable for the eighteenth century accomplishes even less. Worse than being futile, that posture is actively destructive to the very people it claims to champion. 

When you tell a people that their ancestors were purely powerless victims and that their future depends on extracting checks or moral confessions from the outside world, you are not empowering them; you are robbing them of their humanity their toughness, and their self command. Saying "do not worry, we will force society to fix everything for you" breeds dependency where discipline and fortitude are required.

As the great Satchel Paige warned, never look backward, because something might be gaining on you. Alexis de Tocqueville saw the same forward driving engine in the American character nearly two centuries ago when he observed that the greatness of the United States lies not in being more enlightened than other nations, but in its perpetual capacity to repair its faults. America had slavery in both the North and the South, and America ended slavery.

The enslaved men and women who survived the Middle Passage and built lives on North American soil did not endure centuries of hardship so their descendants could beg for pity or financial handouts. Their endurance was an active triumph, not a permanent wound. To honor them properly requires facing history without flinching, rejecting self serving myths regardless of who writes them, and walking forward with the toughness and dignity they bequeathed us.

The distortions in Debay Tadesse's Fresno Alliance essay are not an isolated lapse in scholarship; they belong to a wider cultural habit of rewriting and altering history to flatter modern sensibilities. Whenever writers or filmmakers decide that real history is too uncomfortable, they either sanitize the villains or turn real human beings into comic book superheroes. Both impulses destroy historical truth.

Consider how the exact same distortion plays out in popular cinema. In 2022, Hollywood released The Woman King, a film portraying the Kingdom of Dahomey and its female Agojie warriors as noble freedom fighters battling to end the transatlantic slave trade. In reality, King Ghezo and the Dahomean state were among the fiercest defenders of the slave trade on the West African coast, fighting wars to capture neighbors for export and resisting British naval efforts to shut down the commerce. Just as Tadesse's article erases West African state agency to cast coastal rulers as helpless victims, The Woman King erases Dahomey's slave trading empire to manufacture a modern liberation fantasy. Neither version respects the truth.

That same flight from reality explains why so many people today cling to fictional mythologies like "Wakanda Forever." Black Panther was an entertaining motion picture with fine acting, and there is nothing wrong with enjoying a well crafted story. 
Yet watching grown adults adopt a comic book salute as a substitute for historical identity is embarrassing, especially when real Black American history is filled with men and women who accomplished extraordinary things without fictional superpowers.

Why would anyone trade real American titans for a comic book character like T'Challa when history offers General Daniel "Chappie" James Jr.? Born in Pensacola, Florida, in 1920, James trained with the Tuskegee Airmen during World War II, flew over a hundred combat missions in Korea, led fighter wings in Vietnam, and rose to become the first Black four star general in the United States Air Force.

Similarly, turning enslaved ancestors into mythical superheroes misses the entire point of their greatness. They were not superheroes; they were human beings who endured unimaginable hardship through grit, faith, and intelligence. Mythologizing them into cartoon characters diminishes what they actually survived. Questions have to be asked. Why would they want the populace to be more enamored of a comic book character than real historical characters? Because they want you to be recalcitrant to your natural claim as Americans they resent it 

True scholarship requires the discipline to tell the truth even when it complicates your own side, and even when an ideological adversary happens to get a fact right. One may encounter online commentators who traffic in racial pseudoscience and bad faith generalizations, yet engagement is necessary. You don’t have to like someone just respect civil discourse. 

Nowhere is that need for clear eyed honesty more obvious than in the modern debate over Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) and the affirmative action policies that preceded it. Critics and defenders alike routinely treat those programs as if they were built exclusively to rescue Black Americans. 

Yet look at the empirical record: from the 1970s onward, the single largest demographic beneficiary of affirmative action and corporate DEI mandates in higher education, management, and federal contracting has been white women. Those policies dramatically reshaped opportunities for women across America, even as Black Americans were left holding the political blame for programs whose primary material gains flowed elsewhere.

You cannot build a serious future on fairy tales, whether those fairy tales come from a partisan article in the Fresno Alliance, a Hollywood script about Dahomey, a comic book salute, or selective corporate slogans. Real respect comes from facing the ledger honestly, honoring real heroes like Chappie James over fictional ones, and refusing to flinch from the truth.
Historical amnesia is rarely an accident. 

When writers, activists, and institutions strip away the true record of Black American endurance and sacrifice, replacing it with cartoonish tales of helpless victims or comic book fantasies, they do so by design. If a people learn their real history, they might become genuinely patriotic. They might realize that their forefathers bled for this republic from its inception, and that realization shatters the political dependency required to keep them marching in lockstep.

To understand why the American story unfolds the way it does, one must first understand the ideological architecture of the English speaking world. Unlike the absolutist empires of Spain, Portugal, or pre revolutionary France, where royal decree and rigid hierarchy needed no philosophical apology, England and its American colonies were built upon common law, parliamentary representation, and the natural rights tradition of John Locke. Precisely because the Anglo American framework was crafted in liberty, enslaving human beings created an unbearable moral contradiction. To avoid appearing as hypocrites to their own creed, colonial lawmakers engineered permanent, racialized chattel statutes, such as Virginia's 1662 partus sequitur ventrem law, defining the enslaved outside the political community of freeborn subjects.

Demographic reality further separated mainland North America from the rest of the Western Hemisphere. On the sugar plantations of Jamaica, Saint Domingue, and Brazil, enslaved workers were treated as expendable fuel in a lethal industrial machine; mortality outpaced birth rates, forcing planters to import millions of fresh captives just to maintain their workforce. Mainland North America absorbed less than four percent of the transatlantic trade, yet climate conditions, staple crops, and material subsistence allowed the enslaved population to grow naturally from roughly 388,000 arrivals to nearly four million by 1860.

That natural growth forged a true ethnogenesis on American soil. Diverse West and Central African peoples, Wolof, Fulani, Mandinka, Igbo, Akan, and Bakongo, merged with one another and experienced European genetic admixture over centuries, giving birth to a distinct, native born American people whose culture is inseparable from the soul of the United States. 

Even the laws designed to keep them down confessed their full humanity: Southern legislatures did not ban enslaved people from learning to read because they thought them incapable of forming the neural pathways; they passed anti literacy laws precisely because they knew enslaved people possessed full intellect, agency, and grace, and that literacy would unlock coordinated resistance.

Across every subsequent generation, those men and women, and their sons and grandsons, paid the price of citizenship in full. They fought in the American Revolution, the Civil War, the Spanish American War, and two World Wars, often serving in segregated ranks and returning home only to be denied the G.I. Bill benefits they had rightfully earned.

A serious historian can recite that ledger chapter and verse, backed by indisputable receipts. Yet here lies the trap that ensnares so many people today: winning an intellectual argument over past injustices while remaining stagnant in the present is a classic Pyrrhic victory. It is like winning a modern electric appliance as a prize in eighteenth century colonial America before electricity existed; you can polish it, admire it, and prove to every neighbor that you won it fair and square, yet you still cannot plug it in or put it to work.

Ask yourself why a movie as Black Panther is being made but not a movie about Daniel Chappie James or Henry Johnston of the Harlem Hellfighters. I was glad to see a Vietnam era film a couple weeks ago called Soul Patrol about a black LRRP unit in Vietnam . My Dad served in Vietnam as an LRRP for two years. I’m glad  these movies are being made so that people can reach out and touch. They can these guys were there . instead of looking at fiction.

You can remain angry that your grandfather was cheated out of the G.I. Bill after World War II, or spend your life demanding a check for what your great great great grandfather endured in bondage, but neither posture builds a single brick of real world power today. Your forefathers did not sacrifice so that their descendants could sit at the edge of the table begging for pity or retroactive compensation. They endured and fought to earn you a permanent seat at the American table. The only question that matters now is what you intend to do with it.

Dismantling the Victimhood Ledger: No Absolution, No Castigation

DIOGENES REIPUBLICAE AMERICAE

History is neither a confession booth nor a criminal courtroom. Yet much of contemporary commentary treats the transatlantic slave trade as an active indictment requiring modern spectators to either absolve one group or castigate another. That framing is not merely poor scholarship; it is a psychological trap. There is nothing to absolve and nothing to castigate, because the events in question belong to the settled past. Yes, the ramifications of history echo into the present, as the consequences of every war, migration, and empire always do. But human beings do not possess a time machine, and if we did, reaching backward to rewrite the seventeenth century would only manufacture new paradoxes. A nation and a people can only move forward with the ground beneath their feet and the value system they carry today.

This is precisely why articles like Debay Tadesse's "Africans Sold Africans: Myth or Reality?" in the Fresno Alliance are so corrosive. On the surface, Tadesse purports to correct simplistic social media slogans about African participation in the slave trade. In practice, the essay replaces one shallow caricature with a set of glaring historical distortions, all in service of a modern ideological agenda that demands permanent grievance and external atonement.
To take the historical record seriously, the factual errors in Tadesse's narrative must be dismantled first.
First, Tadesse claims that sixteenth century European powers, Portugal, Spain, Britain, France, and the Netherlands, relied on Arab merchants' coastal trading posts along West Africa and that African leaders sold captives primarily under pressure from Arabs already on the ground. 

That assertion is geographically and historically false. Arab and Berber merchants dominated the trans Saharan caravan routes across the interior and the Indian Ocean trade along East Africa, not the Atlantic littoral of West Africa.  European powers built their own fortified stone castles and trading factories directly along the Gulf of Guinea, beginning with the Portuguese at Sao Jorge da Mina (Elmina) in 1482, and negotiated face to face with coastal African sovereigns.

Second, Tadesse portrays West African rulers almost exclusively as cornered, helpless victims coerced into selling captives merely to survive European gunfire. That narrative strips major African polities of their genuine military, diplomatic, and economic power. Far from conquering the African interior in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, 

Europeans were pinned to narrow coastal enclaves by tropical disease and formidable African armies. Powerful centralized states, such as the Kingdom of Dahomey, the Asante Empire, and Oyo, controlled the trade routes, taxed European factors, dictated terms of exchange, and waged deliberate wars of expansion to capture prisoners for the export market. Recognizing that West African states exercised real agency does not excuse European buyers; it simply restores historical reality instead of reducing entire civilizations to passive props.

Third, Tadesse flattens eight centuries of distinct regional history into a single seamless blur, linking the eleventh century Almoravid invasion of the Sahelian Ghana Empire directly to the nineteenth century Sokoto Caliphate, which was founded in 1804, just three years before Britain and the United States abolished the transatlantic slave trade. Treating medieval Sahelian conflicts, nineteenth century Islamic jihads, and sixteenth century Atlantic commerce as a single undifferentiated wave of external coercion is polemic, not history.

The author insists that flattening the history of external exploitation prevents society from confronting modern racial and social inequalities, the familiar prelude to demands for institutional penance and financial reparations.

Here is the hard truth that modern grievance merchants refuse to confront: demanding money from people alive today accomplishes nothing, and browbeating strangers into feeling accountable for the eighteenth century accomplishes even less. Worse than being futile, that posture is actively destructive to the very people it claims to champion. 

When you tell a people that their ancestors were purely powerless victims and that their future depends on extracting checks or moral confessions from the outside world, you are not empowering them; you are robbing them of their humanity their toughness, and their self command. Saying "do not worry, we will force society to fix everything for you" breeds dependency where discipline and fortitude are required.

As the great Satchel Paige warned, never look backward, because something might be gaining on you. Alexis de Tocqueville saw the same forward driving engine in the American character nearly two centuries ago when he observed that the greatness of the United States lies not in being more enlightened than other nations, but in its perpetual capacity to repair its faults. America had slavery in both the North and the South, and America ended slavery.

1,700 years ago in what's now Turkey there was a young guy named Platon.

A smart educated man who could talk circles around anyone.
 He went city to city telling people about Christ.

The Roman Empire arrested him because that’s what they did.

You are lucky to live when you do, but understand as we see with leftists, this can happen again.
 They the pagans dragged him into the temple of Zeus in front of the governor.

The governor didn't start with torture. 
He started with offers.
First flattery. "You're so smart you could rank with the philosopher Plato." Platon said Plato's wisdom was great but it passes. The Gospel's doesn't.

Then a woman. The governor offered him his own beautiful niece as a wife.

Then his life. All he had to do was say one sentence. "Great is the god Apollo."

He wouldn't say it.
So they beat him.
 Boiling cauldrons then red hot irons, followed by hooks.
 18 days in prison with no bread and no water.

Platonas still wouldn't say it.

They cut off his head.
Today is his feast day.

Here's the lesson whether you believe or not.

Most people don't sell their soul in one big betrayal.
 They sell it one small sentence at a time. This especially holds true in today’s age of social media and the world’s town hall on X.
 Saying what's convenient, or saying what they tell you, for shekels,  a promotion or approval and comfort.

Platon was offered fame, a wife and his life for one sentence he didn't believe.

He wouldn't say it.
Know what you won't say. At any price. ❤️ 🙏 ☦️

text:
#TheCholas: Stories of a South Indian Dynasty and a Changing World by Jennifer Clare

Across South India, the Cholas are remembered for their military might, their staggering wealth and their generous support of art and architecture, including the temples that still cover the South Indian landscape. 

At the height of their 400-year reign, the reach of their empire extended throughout the South Indian peninsula and across the Indian Ocean. How did this local ruling family rise from obscure origins to emerge as kings on a global stage? What were the forces that shaped their world-conquering ambitions and led to their eventual decline? How do we make sense of this larger-than-life dynasty, who transformed politics, religion, art, language, agriculture and global trade in South India and beyond?

 Drawing on Tamil and Sanskrit inscriptions, art and architecture, poetry and legend, Jennifer Clare revisits the history of the Cholas as a set of interconnected stories: of kings and conquests, of land and water, of beauty and devotion, of knowledge, labour and power. We encounter emperors like Rajaraja I and Rajendra I alongside farmers, priests, artisans and merchants whose lives were bound together by temples, irrigation systems and a vast economy of gifts, taxes and trade. At once local and global, the Cholas emerge as master engineers of river landscapes, builders of some of the world’s most awe-inspiring temples, patrons of bronze sculpture and poetry, and key players in a pre-modern world stretching from Egypt to Southeast Asia. 

Written with narrative appeal and critical insight, The Cholas probes the contradictions of empire. It shows how beauty and bloodshed could coexist in royal power and how key developments under the Cholas – consolidation of castes, burgeoning temple wealth and global trade – fuelled prosperity even as they sowed the seeds of political fragmentation and decline. It offers readers a bold reimagining of South Indian history and a compelling portrait of a dynasty whose legacy continues to shape the modern India.

text:
Hey, I took a look at your graphic and there are a couple of problems with it. The first is that the citations are made up.
D&C 132:15 is about marriages not done by God's authority. There's nothing in it about a curse on anyone's "seed."
D&C 107:41 describes the priesthood passing down from Adam. Cain isn't in it.
D&C 93:24 defines truth as "knowledge of things as they are, and as they were, and as they are to come." "Line upon line" is from 2 Nephi 28:30 and D&C 98:12.
The 1978 quote you used isn't in Official Declaration 2. It's one page, so you can check it in about a minute.

That's four fake citations on one graphic. I'm not saying you made them up, but whoever did never opened the books they were quoting.

The history is off too. Black men held the priesthood while Joseph Smith was alive. Elijah Able was ordained an elder and a seventy in the 1830s and took part in the Kirtland temple ordinances. Walker Lewis was ordained in the 1840s, and Brigham Young later called him one of the best elders in the Church. The restriction started in 1852, eight years after Joseph died. Native Americans were never restricted at all. And the "less valiant" idea came along in the 20th century, not the 1830s.

Your whole argument also hangs on the headline, that the ban was once "eternal truth." So which canonized revelation established it?

I don't mean a sermon, a letter, or an apostle's book. I mean a revelation that was presented to the Church and sustained as scripture, the way every book in our canon was. If the ban was eternal truth, you should be able to point to it.

You won't find one, because it doesn't exist. Here's what did happen. A policy started in 1852, leaders and members offered explanations for it over the years, and in 2013 the Church said plainly that none of those explanations is accepted as doctrine. That isn't doctrine evolving. It's leaders being fallible, and our own scriptures say they would be. In D&C 1:24-28 the Lord says He gave revelation to His servants "in their weakness" so that "inasmuch as they erred it might be made known."

Polygamy works the same way. Jacob 2:30 teaches that God commands plural marriage at certain times and forbids it at others. So when He stops commanding it, that isn't a contradiction. The Book of Mormon told you it would work that way.
As for calling us "ever-changing," we believe God "will yet reveal many great and important things" (Article of Faith 9). When a church that claims continuing revelation changes course through revelation, it's doing exactly what it said it would do. For your point to land, you'd need to show me a church that promised it would never change and then did.

So I'll ask again, and I mean it as a real question. Can you show me the canonized revelation that made the ban eternal truth? If you can't, then the headline is just an opinion, and the citations under it aren't real

text:
#LUREOFLANKA DIARIES DAY 4 – 🏹 RAMAYANA AND 🌱 TEA

On Day 4 of our first-ever #LureOfLanka tour, we drove from Kandy to Nuwara Eliya, high into Sri Lanka’s hill country, where Ramayana legends meet British-era tea estates.

We began at the hilltop Sri Bhakta Hanuman Temple at Ramboda, with sweeping views over the tea gardens, and stopped at the nearby Ramboda Falls.

Further up the road was Sita Eliya. The Sita Amman Temple there is said to stand where Ravana held Sita captive in the Ashok Vatika, and is believed to be the only temple in Sri Lanka dedicated to Sita alone. Beside it, hollows in the rocks of the stream are said to be Hanuman’s footprints.

Nearby were the Hakgala Botanical Gardens, among Sri Lanka’s oldest, founded in 1861 to grow cinchona, the source of the anti-malaria medicine quinine. Some of the island’s earliest tea trials took place here. In the Ramayana tradition, Hakgala Rock is a piece of the mountain Hanuman carried back with the Sanjeevani herb.

We then explored Nuwara Eliya, known as “Little England” for its colonial charm. We saw its red-brick post office, walked through Victoria Park, named in 1897 for Queen Victoria’s Diamond Jubilee, and stopped at Gregory Lake, created in 1873 from what was once a marsh.

After lunch, we headed back towards Kandy, touring a tea factory on the way, where we saw how fresh leaves become the tea in our cups, and of course had a cup ourselves.

On Day 5, we leave the hills for the coast at Beruwala and Bentota.

A Bengaluru-based Lightspeed India executive tested the voice-detection technology behind Deepinder Goyal's Rs 85,000 Temple wearable and recreated it on a laptop. 

Krishna Veera Vanamali Y, Lightspeed India's VP of content, shared on LinkedIn how he used his laptop's built-in accelerometer to detect speech vibrations without a microphone.

Vanamali clarified that he did not own Temple and that his experiment required slowed-down audio played through the laptop's speakers.

‘Talking at the laptop did nothing. I shouted, I hummed, I even talked while resting my chin on it. The sensor picked up nothing useful. It all comes down to frequency’, Vanamali said.

Goyal responded, "Nicely done," and offered him a one-day trial of Temple.

He explained that the device uses two accelerometers and increases its sampling frequency to 16 kHz when activated by a double tap to conserve battery.

The experiment also drew appreciation from users, who praised Vanamali's innovative approach to recreating the technology using a laptop. 

‘Great observation! I really appreciate your curiosity and hands-on drive to verify things for yourself’, a user wrote.

‘This is brilliant’, another wrote.
