text:
🗞️18 November 2026 | Daily Edition: Pre-Market

Nvidia Lifted Futures, Bitcoin Stopped Short of the Weekly Close

Nvidia's beat lifted stock futures and pulled Bitcoin to $65,199 after the bell, but IBIT's selling came back, the Binance hackers moved another $142 million of Ether and Europe sold the morning back toward $64,100, with the Fed minutes due at 2:00 PM EST.

Prepared around 5:50 AM EST on Wednesday 18 November. This edition picks up from Tuesday's US Close, prepared at 4:10 PM EST, and only adds what happened since: Nvidia's results, the evening session, Asia and the first hours of Europe. Crypto prices are live prints as of about 5:45 AM EST, and futures, oil, Treasury, dollar and gold figures are live overnight prints.

1⃣ Bitcoin broke Tuesday's ceiling after the bell, then handed most of it back

Bitcoin was near $63,930 at last night's edition. It made its evening low of about $63,870 in the 4:00 PM EST bar, then cleared the $64,050 ceiling that had capped it four times on Tuesday afternoon and reached about $64,600 in the 4:30 PM EST bar. When stock futures reopened at 6:00 PM EST on Nvidia's results, it jumped to $65,199, about $115 short of the $65,315 weekly close. Tuesday's daily candle closed near $64,875 at 7:00 PM EST, just above Monday's $64,815 close. The fade started at 8:00 PM EST and found a floor at about $64,035 to $64,070 in the 9:00 PM EST hour, right on the old ceiling. Asia's best was about $64,890 at 2:45 AM EST. Europe sold from about $64,580 at 5:05 AM EST to a low of about $64,095 at 5:35 AM EST, and Bitcoin trades near $64,250, about 0.5% above last night's edition and roughly flat over 24 hours.

🖊️ Market significance: The breakout through $64,050 held as support twice overnight, but the rally stalled below the weekly close for a fourth time in three days.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Turning yesterday's ceiling into a floor is real progress. Still, the best risk news of the week only bought about 2% from last night's low, and that tells me sellers are still waiting above $65,000.

2⃣ Ether was turned back under $1,835 again, XRP touched $1

Ether rose from about $1,801 at last night's edition to $1,834 in the 6:00 PM EST bar, just under the $1,835 to $1,842 band that has capped it since the weekly close. It held about $1,795 in the 9:00 PM EST hour, reached about $1,818 in Asia at 2:45 AM EST and slipped to about $1,796 at 5:35 AM EST. It trades near $1,802, flat against last night's edition and about 0.5% higher over 24 hours. XRP was the overnight leader: it briefly traded above $1.00 at about 3:15 AM EST and is near $0.997, up about 4% over 24 hours. Solana peaked at $75.70 at 6:00 PM EST and is near $74.65, up about 3% over 24 hours, as its London conference wrapped up. Zcash is near $936 to $939 and HYPE near $68.25 to $68.50.

🖊️ Market significance: Ether has now been turned back at or just under the same band four times since Sunday night, while XRP and Solana carried the relative strength.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Rotation into XRP and Solana while Ether stalls is not a market-wide bid. I need Ether to close above $1,842 before I treat it as anything more than a range.

3⃣ On-chain traders added Bitcoin longs while offshore funding turned negative

Bitcoin open interest on the largest on-chain perps venue rose about 3.1% since last night's edition to about 38,700 BTC, while on a large offshore exchange it was flat at about 31,170 BTC, with price up about 0.5%. Funding split: the on-chain venue pays longs about +0.01% per eight hours, while the offshore exchange is slightly negative at about -0.002%. In Ether, the pattern flipped: open interest fell about 1.5% on the on-chain venue to about 608,300 ETH but rose about 3.4% offshore to about 687,800 ETH, with offshore funding slightly negative. Solana and XRP funding on the on-chain venue is negative despite their gains.

🖊️ Market significance: Overnight positioning was a two-way trade, with on-chain longs chasing the Nvidia bounce while offshore traders kept a small short bias.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Negative funding on Solana and XRP while they rally is the cleanest squeeze setup on the board. In Bitcoin, if the new on-chain longs were added on the jump toward $65,000, they are now under water, and that is fuel for the downside if $64,000 breaks.

4⃣ IBIT's one-day pause ended, Goldman showed a large Ether fund book

Tuesday's spot Bitcoin ETFs lost about $239.9 million, with BlackRock's IBIT down about $209.5 million, Grayscale's GBTC down $17.7 million and ARK's ARKB down $13.1 million, against small inflows into Morgan Stanley's fund and Grayscale's mini trust. Monday's final count had shown IBIT taking in about $76.5 million, its first inflow in more than a week. Spot Ether ETFs lost about $29.1 million, almost all from BlackRock's ETHA, their sixth outflow in seven sessions. Separately, Goldman Sachs' third-quarter 13F shows about $1.22 billion across seven spot Ether ETFs at 30 September, up from about $211.6 million in June, led by about 29.96 million ETHA shares worth about $602.9 million.

🖊️ Market significance: Monday's IBIT inflow did not start a streak. The biggest Bitcoin fund was back to being the main source of selling within a day.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Goldman's Ether book is a 30 September snapshot, taken before Ether's slide into the $1,800s. Today's flows matter more to me: one inflow day followed by a $210 million outflow is still a distribution pattern.

5⃣ DBS opened 24/7 USDC minting for Asian institutions, Tether funded a payments network

Singapore's DBS, Southeast Asia's largest bank, said eligible institutional clients in Asia can now mint and redeem USDC directly through the bank, with dollar and stablecoin settlement around the clock, building on its work with Circle in the Monetary Authority of Singapore's Project BLOOM. Separately, Tether's investment arm took a strategic stake in Stables, which connects local banking systems to USDT settlement across more than 160 markets and handles more than $2 billion of annual USDT volume. Early this morning, about 250 million USDC was minted at the issuer's treasury. USDT supply is about $175.2 billion to $175.3 billion and USDC about $68.9 billion to $69.2 billion.

🖊️ Market significance: The region's biggest bank becoming a direct USDC on-ramp removes a reliance on exchange liquidity for institutions that want stablecoins outside banking hours.

🗨️ My viewpoint: After the World Bank news on Tuesday, this is the second large institutional USDC channel in two days. Supply has not turned up yet, but a fresh 250 million mint is the kind of sign I watch for.

6⃣ Tokenized Anthropic exposure sold out at $500 million, Maple wants to lend against tokenized stocks

A Binance Wallet campaign selling tokenized exposure to Anthropic's IPO filled its 500 million USDC cap on Wednesday, inside an eight-hour window that opened at 1:00 AM EST. The tokens, called ANTx and issued by Backed through xStocks, were offered at an indicative 70 to 78 USDC each with a 5% fee. They track the price only, carry no voting or dividend rights, and can be backed by cash rather than shares. Separately, Maple Finance chief executive Sidney Powell said he targets $10 billion to $15 billion in assets by the end of 2027, from $4.7 billion at the end of the third quarter, and expects tokenized stocks to grow five to tenfold next year, allowing Maple to lend against tokenized shares. Maple is also in talks with banks about funding its Bitcoin-backed loans.

🖊️ Market significance: Half a billion dollars of stablecoins went into synthetic pre-IPO exposure in hours, while Bitcoin ETFs lost $240 million.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is the competition for crypto's marginal dollar in one number. Stablecoin holders are not leaving crypto rails, they are buying AI exposure on them, and that keeps the bid away from Bitcoin.

7⃣ The Binance hackers moved another 78,415 ETH

Wallets tied to the 29 October Binance theft moved about 78,415 ETH, roughly $142 million, overnight, split across six new addresses of 12,000 ETH each and one of 6,415 ETH, and continued swapping the Ether into Bitcoin through THORChain, according to on-chain trackers. Five of the 12,000 ETH transfers landed within about four minutes, from 2:48 AM EST. Together with Tuesday morning's 74,880 ETH, that is more than 153,000 ETH, about $280 million, moved in about a day, from a pile of more than 600,000 ETH held before Tuesday.

🖊️ Market significance: A second batch of about $140 million followed the first within a day, so the laundering is now steady rather than occasional.

🗨️ My viewpoint: These swaps go through cross-chain routers, not exchange order books, so the direct price impact is limited. But every batch adds Ether supply into thin overnight hours, and the 2:48 AM EST batch landed just after Ether's Asia high.

8⃣ Ledger implants reached Dubai, Etherscan flagged an access attempt

Two Ledger owners reported losing about $604,000 in total from hardware wallets they said were bought at Virgin Megastore in Dubai, a Ledger-authorised retailer: about 1,300 SOL from a Ledger Flex, which an independent implant registry confirmed as containing a hidden hardware implant, and 507,000 USDT from a Ledger Stax, where an implant is suspected. Separately, Etherscan said it detected unauthorized attempts to access its customer support ticketing system, has put preventive measures in place, has not confirmed any data exposure and warned users about impersonators.

🖊️ Market significance: Supply-chain attacks on hardware wallets have now spread beyond resellers in Asia and Europe to an authorised retailer in the Gulf.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Self-custody depends on trusting the device, and that trust now depends on where it was bought. For anyone holding size, I would treat any device bought through a reseller as suspect until it is checked.

9⃣ Coinbase's AI agent stopped a deepfake scam, a Scattered Spider hacker got six years

Coinbase said its AI scam defences stopped about $4.7 million from leaving customer accounts during a fake Tesla crypto giveaway that used a deepfake of Elon Musk, blocking about 91% of the attempted transfers with no human in the loop. More than 500,000 people watched the fake livestream. Separately, Scottish hacker Tyler Buchanan, linked by prosecutors to the Scattered Spider group, was sentenced in California to six years in federal prison over a phishing and SIM-swap scheme that stole at least $11.6 million in crypto. He is the last of five defendants sentenced.

🖊️ Market significance: AI is now on both sides of crypto fraud, used to fake the pitch and to stop the transfer.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The detail that matters is that nobody was hacked: hundreds of customers chose to send money. Platforms that can stop authorised scam transfers at that rate will have an edge with regulators and with banks.

1⃣0⃣ Bitwise filed for a Zcash ETF on the Texas Stock Exchange

Bitwise filed an S-1 for a spot Zcash ETF late on Tuesday, with shares expected to list on the Texas Stock Exchange under the ticker ZEC, Coinbase Custody as custodian and the fee still left blank. It would compete with Grayscale's Zcash fund, which already trades on NYSE Arca. Zcash is up about 1.5% to 2% over 24 hours.

🖊️ Market significance: This is a second major issuer betting on a privacy coin ETF, and a new exchange competing for crypto listings.

🗨️ My viewpoint: An S-1 is a filing, not an approval, and the existing Zcash fund reported no flows on Tuesday. The listing choice matters more to me than the coin: Texas is positioning itself as a home for crypto products.

1⃣1⃣ MEXC's card goes dark today, Hong Kong wants AI agents watching wallets

MEXC said its Global Card will stop working at 10:30 AM EST today, a week after its Asia-Pacific card was discontinued. The exchange blames changes by an unnamed third-party issuer, and it comes after a US Treasury order cutting MEXC off from US financial institutions, which takes effect on 10 December. In Hong Kong, Monetary Authority executive director Raymond Chan said the regulator is exploring AI agents that combine blockchain analytics, customer data and wallet freezing to detect crypto money laundering, citing more than $150 billion received by illicit addresses in 2025, 84% of it in stablecoins.

🖊️ Market significance: Offshore exchanges are losing payment partners ahead of the US order, while Asian regulators move toward automated on-chain monitoring.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Card networks and issuers act before the legal deadline, which is how US financial sanctions really bite. I watch whether other offshore venues lose banking partners before 10 December.

1⃣2⃣ MARA kept moving Bitcoin out after its results

On-chain trackers show MARA moved out about 1,713.9 BTC, about $121 million, in the eight days after its 10 November results, including 366 BTC on Tuesday afternoon, transfers they read as sales, although the receiving wallets are not confirmed as exchanges. MARA's own disclosures show it sold 13,597 BTC between 1 October and 10 November and 40,581 BTC so far in 2026, at an average of about $74,446.

🖊️ Market significance: The largest listed miner has gone from a long-term holder to a steady seller.

🗨️ My viewpoint: About $15 million a day of miner supply is easy to absorb in a normal market. In a week with ETF outflows and laundered Ether, it is one more seller the bid has to take out.

1⃣3⃣ The biggest Ether dip buyers look finished, an XRP whale moved to storage

Wallets linked to Erik Voorhees have now bought 92,052 ETH, about $165.6 million, over the past week at an average of about $1,921, and sit on about $11 million of unrealized losses. A separate tracker says November's largest on-chain dip buyer has spent all of its stablecoins after buying 95,020 ETH in six days at an average of about $1,906, taking its holdings to about 649,650 ETH. In XRP, a holder whose wallets trace back to a 2020 exchange withdrawal moved 281 million XRP, about $270 million, into two wallets over three weeks, the latest batch on Tuesday morning. Both wallets were set up a month earlier with test transfers, a pattern that points to custody rather than a sale.

🖊️ Market significance: The two largest dip buyers in Ether appear to be done buying, so the support they provided below $1,900 is fading.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Both buyers are under water at $1,802. If they stay patient, the supply is locked away. If $1,749 breaks, their losses become a story the market will trade.

1⃣4⃣ Analysts see a bid wall near $60,000 as demand keeps shrinking

An on-chain analytics firm said Bitcoin has returned to a bearish phase, with its analyst sentiment index at its most bearish since November 2025 and total demand growth contracting at its fastest pace since 1 July. It sees support between $62,000 and $65,000 but no confirmed bottom. A second firm's order-book analysis shows resting bids within 5% of price outweighing asks by about 2.3 times on two of the largest spot venues, with the biggest single bid level near $60,000 the largest on one venue since August, and said most forced liquidations have already happened. It also said realized losses have reached levels seen only near the 2018, 2020, 2022 and early 2023 lows.

🖊️ Market significance: Demand data and order books disagree. Flows are weak, but there is a large wall of resting bids below the market.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Resting bids can be pulled, so I treat the $60,000 wall as a magnet as much as a floor. Capitulation-level losses are what bottoms look like, but they do not tell me the timing.

1⃣5⃣ Nvidia beat and raised, Nasdaq futures rose about 1.1%

Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, against about $109 billion expected, with adjusted earnings of $2.68 a share against about $2.47 to $2.48. It guided fourth-quarter revenue to $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, above the roughly $125.1 billion expected, raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to about 75% from 70% and included no China data center compute revenue. The board said it will not reinstate Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares are up about 3% to 4% in premarket trading from Tuesday's $155.46 close. S&P 500 futures are up about 0.6% near 7,401, Nasdaq 100 futures about 1.1% near 27,365 and Dow futures about 0.3% near 50,946. In Asia, Korea's KOSPI rose about 2.0% to 5,067, the Nikkei about 0.3% and the Hang Seng fell about 0.9%. Europe's Stoxx 50 and the DAX are each up about 0.2%.

🖊️ Market significance: The AI trade got the confirmation it needed after Tuesday's 850-point Dow drop, and futures held most of their after-hours gain.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Futures peaked at the 6:00 PM EST reopen, faded into midnight and then recovered, the same path Bitcoin took, except Bitcoin has not recovered. That gap is the clearest sign this week that crypto is not trading the risk-on signal.

1⃣6⃣ Oil fell on a stock build, gold dropped below $3,800, the dollar firmed

Brent crude is near $92, down about 1.2%, and WTI is near $83.20, down about 1.7%, after industry data showed US crude stocks rose by about 5.3 million barrels last week against an expected draw. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5.09% to 5.10%, about 1 basis point lower. The dollar index is up about 0.25% near 103.75, and gold futures are down about 2.4% near $3,772.

🖊️ Market significance: Gold's slide alongside a firmer dollar shows rate-hike expectations, not fear, driving the macro tape this morning.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Gold falling more than 2% on a calm morning tells me higher real rates are pulling money out of non-yielding assets. Bitcoin has not been trading with tech this week, so it gets little help from the Nvidia rally, while the rate pressure hitting gold applies to it as well.

1⃣7⃣ Housing data at 8:30 AM EST, the Fed minutes at 2:00 PM EST

October housing starts and building permits are due at 8:30 AM EST, the weekly government crude inventory report at 10:30 AM EST, a 20-year Treasury bond auction at 1:00 PM EST and remarks from Fed Governor Michael Barr at 1:35 PM EST. The main event is the minutes of the 27 to 28 October Fed meeting at 2:00 PM EST. In crypto, MEXC's card shuts at 10:30 AM EST, and pricing for Anthropic's IPO, which sets the final terms for the tokenized campaign, is expected.

🖊️ Market significance: With the 10-year above 5% and Fed officials split between several hikes and no dramatic action, the minutes are the day's real test.

🗨️ My viewpoint: A 20-year auction an hour before the minutes makes the early afternoon the riskiest window of the day. A weak auction plus hawkish minutes is the combination that could push Bitcoin back through $64,000.

🗨️ My Overall Viewpoint:
The night gave me a better structure but not a better trend. Bitcoin broke through the $64,050 ceiling that capped it all Tuesday afternoon, used Nvidia's beat to reach $65,199, and then defended the old ceiling twice, at about $64,035 in the 9:00 PM EST hour and $64,095 this morning. That is a real improvement. But the rally stopped below the $65,315 weekly close for a fourth time, IBIT went back to selling $210 million a day, the two biggest Ether dip buyers appear to be done, the Binance hackers moved a second $140 million batch of Ether and MARA is still moving coins out. Under the price, the build-out kept going: DBS made USDC a 24/7 bank product in Asia, Tether funded a payments network, Bitwise filed for a Zcash ETF and a $500 million tokenized Anthropic campaign filled in hours, which also shows where speculative money wants to be.

For the US session, my Bitcoin support is $64,035 to $64,095, the overnight lows on Tuesday's old ceiling, then $63,870, last night's post-close low, $63,770, then $63,377 to $63,257, Tuesday's retest and low, and $61,950, Saturday night's low, with the long cluster between $59,500 and $62,200 and the bid wall near $60,000 below it. Resistance is $64,890, the Asia high, then $65,199, the overnight high, and $65,315 to $65,383, the weekly close and Tuesday's high. A daily close above $65,383 would end the run of rejections, while losing $64,000 would put the afternoon lows back in play. For Ether, support is $1,795, the overnight lows, then $1,790, $1,765 and $1,749, Tuesday's low. Resistance is $1,818, the Asia high, then $1,834, the overnight high, and the $1,835 to $1,842 band. I stay defensive but less so than last night. I watch the 8:30 AM EST housing data, the 1:00 PM EST bond auction, the 2:00 PM EST Fed minutes and Wednesday's ETF flows tonight. These are my analytical levels, not forecasts, and nothing here is financial advice.

DSA candidate challenging Fetterman calls to abolish ICE, doesn’t deny he’s pro-Hamas | Ari Hoffman, The Post Millennial

Ahmed Moor, a Democratic Socialists of America member challenging Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman in the 2028 Democratic primary, called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and replacing congressional Democratic leaders, while declining to deny being pro-Hamas.

During an interview with Fox News anchor Martha MacCallum, Moor dodged when asked whether Fetterman was correct to describe him as “very pro-Hamas,” but falsely accused Israel of being an apartheid state.

Moor then called for comprehensive sanctions against Israel modeled on the 1986 legislation targeting apartheid South Africa. When MacCallum continued pressing him during the interview, he dismissed the question as being asked in bad faith.

Fetterman, one of the Democratic Party’s most outspoken supporters of Israel, offered a blunt assessment of his challenger in comments to the outlet.

“I know he seems to really love Hamas,” Fetterman said.

Moor, 42, was born in Gaza and immigrated to Philadelphia as a child. A graduate of the University of Pennsylvania and Harvard, he is the first officially declared candidate challenging Fetterman in the 2028 Democratic primary. Fetterman has not announced whether he will seek another term.

In a separate Fox interview, Moor said he entered the race because he believes the United States faces a “constitutional crisis.” He criticized the treatment of campus demonstrators during the Biden administration and accused President Donald Trump of escalating an assault on constitutional rights.

“ICE is a lawless organization. ICE is a paramilitary militia. ICE is not law enforcement,” Moor said. “Let’s abolish ICE.”

Moor also urged local prosecutors to pursue immigration enforcement personnel, accusing them of killing Americans, kidnapping people and violating local laws. He did not identify specific cases in the supplied interview excerpt.

“That's a criminal matter today in America. I hope local prosecutors run with it,” he said.

His criticism extended to Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries.

“Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries don’t have what it takes to meet the moment. They need to be replaced,” Moor said, pledging to maintain pressure on both men if they survived their leadership contests.

Moor’s candidacy has also drawn scrutiny over his past commentary on terrorist organizations.

A November 9 Washington Free Beacon investigation highlighted an October 2023 Guardian discussion in which Moor described his reaction to footage of a bulldozer breaching Gaza’s border barrier during the October 7 massacre.

“The natives have broken free—good for them,” Moor said, while also describing mixed emotions and a sense of foreboding.

The investigation also identified writings in which Moor defended Hezbollah’s political legitimacy and characterized Hamas’s armed campaign as asserting Palestinian self-defense. It reported that he serves on the advisory board of the US Campaign for Palestinian Rights.

Moor’s domestic platform includes universal access to health care, childcare, and affordable housing. He told Fox that he supports enforcing immigration laws despite his demand to abolish ICE.

text:
Is another US-Iran war looming?
Washington has deployed a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as peace talks stall and hostilities with Tehran intensify
Published 18 Nov, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/9EiLjGtOad
The US has deployed a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as tensions with Iran flare again, raising fears of another round of large-scale fighting.
Nearly nine months after the US-Israeli bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic began, international efforts to end the conflict remain stalled. President Donald Trump has threatened further strikes while insisting that the war is effectively over.
How big is the US military buildup?
US Central Command announced on Monday that the USS Theodore Roosevelt had arrived in the Middle East after departing San Diego in September, bringing thousands of additional personnel to the region.
The Roosevelt and its accompanying strike group join the USS George H.W. Bush, which arrived in April, and the USS George Washington, deployed in August. The Pentagon last had three carrier strike groups in the region simultaneously in April, for the first time since 2003.
According to the US Navy, the American fleet in the Arabian Sea also includes 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship, with two additional destroyers stationed in the Red Sea. An accompanying amphibious group carrying around 2,000 Marines aboard three ships has yet to arrive.
The Roosevelt was initially expected to relieve the George Washington, although it remains unclear how long all three carriers will operate in the region simultaneously.
What’s behind the latest escalation?
The IRGC has launched several drone attacks against American facilities, accusing Washington of hostile military operations and violations of Iranian airspace.
US military installations in Bahrain came under attack three times in five days, most recently on Tuesday, when Iranian drones targeted a radar installation at Sheikh Isa Air Base.
Washington responded hours later with what it described as a “self-defense” strike against an IRGC missile launch site on Iran’s Qeshm Island, near the entrance to the Persian Gulf.
What happened to the ceasefire?
The US-Israeli strikes on Iran, launched on February 28, prompted retaliatory attacks by Tehran against American military bases and other US- and Israeli-linked targets across the Middle East. Iran effectively closed the vital Strait of Hormuz, while Washington imposed its own blockade of Iranian ports.
The two sides agreed to a ceasefire in April, but subsequent negotiations failed to produce a lasting settlement. A memorandum of understanding signed in June temporarily eased shipping restrictions and allowed 60 days for further talks before mutual accusations of violations derailed the agreement.
Washington reinforced its naval blockade in July and has since announced plans to disrupt land-based supply routes to Iran. Limited exchanges of strikes have continued, fueling fears of a major escalation following the US midterm elections earlier this month.
Is Iran plotting a ‘dirty bomb’ attack?
A CNN report on Monday, citing anonymous sources, claimed that Iranian officials had considered a possible chemical or radioactive “dirty bomb” attack in Washington. No officials went on record to confirm a new or credible threat.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the allegations as “rubbish” and accused pro-Israeli media of spreading “Iraq War-style propaganda” about nonexistent weapons of mass destruction to justify renewed hostilities.
Trump said Washington was taking the report seriously and threatened unprecedented consequences. He also warned that American forces were “locked and loaded” and threatened further action over Tehran’s nuclear activities, including at the underground Pickaxe Mountain facility.
Who controls the Strait of Hormuz?
The vital shipping route remains a major flashpoint, with Washington and Tehran both claiming control and issuing conflicting demands to commercial vessels.
Washington says it has cleared the waterway of mines and offers escorts to some ships. However, it continues to intercept and disable vessels traveling to or from Iranian ports, while heavily penalizing shipping companies that pay Tehran’s transit fees.
Iran requires commercial vessels to register with its Persian Gulf Strait Authority, pay transit fees and follow northern routes near Iranian waters. The IRGC has warned ships against using what it calls “unsafe” American-backed routes.
At least six commercial tankers have been struck and damaged by unidentified projectiles this month alone. Iranian officials have attributed such incidents to “disobedient” vessels hitting sea mines after entering restricted waters without permission.
Before the war, roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil passed through the strait. Traffic has since fallen to less than a third of prewar levels, according to maritime intelligence firm Lloyd’s List.
What’s blocking a peace deal?
Washington and Tehran remain divided over the conditions for ending hostilities.
Iran has proposed reopening Hormuz in exchange for the lifting of American sanctions, the release of frozen assets and an end to the blockade. It has also demanded an end to fighting on all fronts, including Israeli operations in Gaza and southern Lebanon.
Washington insists that any agreement must address Iran’s nuclear program. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed Tehran’s conditions as “absurd,” while Trump recently declared that the US no longer needs a deal.
“The ball is now in the American court,” Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said last week.
Qatar has led efforts to revive negotiations, supported by Oman and other regional mediators. Although the latest proposals have failed to produce a breakthrough, diplomatic contacts continue.
Has the war hurt Trump politically?
The prolonged conflict has become a political liability for Trump following heavy Republican losses in the November 3 midterms, which cost the party control of both chambers of Congress.
Opposition to the war and its economic consequences, particularly higher fuel and living costs, contributed to voter dissatisfaction, according to exit polls.
Vice President J.D. Vance initially blamed the election setback directly on the Iran war but subsequently rejected suggestions of a split with Trump, insisting that the campaign would not become an open-ended military commitment.
“We’re not going to stay there forever,” he told Fox News on Monday.
Will Trump strike Iran again?
Despite the growing American military presence and sporadic exchanges of fire, Washington appears to favor continued economic and military pressure over another major bombing campaign, according to media reports.
Rubio has argued that mounting “economic pain” will eventually force Tehran to make concessions, as “eventually you have to eat.” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei has accused Washington of committing war crimes through its blockade and sanctions, which deprive civilians of essential supplies.
Gulf countries have urged the White House to avoid renewed strikes, warning of Iranian retaliation against regional energy infrastructure. Former US diplomat Alan Eyre, who worked on nuclear negotiations with Iran, told Reuters that prolonged restrictions on Iranian oil exports could eventually force Tehran to escalate.
Meanwhile, Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pressed Washington to resume military strikes against Iran, reportedly engaging in a heated “shouting match” with Trump during a recent phone call.

text:
Lavrov mocks European negotiators with dysfunctional orchestra fable
There aren’t any reasonable interlocutors among the EU and UK leadership, the Russian foreign minister has said
Published 18 Nov, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/dJFDfZJOcB
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has ridiculed Europe’s proposed negotiating team on Ukraine. He invoked a famous fable about four animals who try and fail to perform as a musical quartet.
After being unable for months to agree on a single candidate to join the trilateral discussions between Moscow, Kiev and Washington, the Europeans announced last week that they expect to send a whole team, consisting of representatives of EU institutions and five countries – Britain, France, Germany, Italy, and Poland – to the next round of peace talks.
In an interview with TASS published on Tuesday, Lavrov questioned the prospects of the European negotiating team, saying, “I’m not sure which of the current leaders could even be considered a rational interlocutor.”
“[Russian fabulist] Ivan Krylov once wrote a fable about a quartet. We’ll see,” he said.
Lavrov was referring to Krylov’s famous 1811 story ‘The Quartet,’ in which a monkey, a donkey, a goat and a bear attempt to perform music together. Despite repeatedly changing seats in an effort to improve their performance, the animals fail again and again because none of them actually knows how to play their instruments.
The moral of the fable is that rearranging an incompetent group does nothing to improve its abilities. Its best-known line translates roughly as: “And you, my friends, however you arrange yourselves, will never be musicians!”
Lavrov’s remarks come as European governments seek a greater role in negotiations on the Ukraine conflict after refusing any dialogue with Russia since the escalation between Moscow and Kiev in February 2022.
The Russian foreign minister accused the EU and UK of repeatedly undermining diplomatic efforts to settle the conflict, citing the failure of the 2015 Minsk agreements and the collapse of peace negotiations in Istanbul in 2022. “They have quite a fine track record,” he said sarcastically.
He also claimed that European leaders had sabotaged an understanding reached between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump at their August 2025 summit in Anchorage, Alaska.
According to Lavrov, Putin had accepted an American peace proposal, which required certain concessions from Moscow as “any agreement (provided it is a robust one) inevitably relies, to some extent, on compromises.” But the Europeans swiftly intervened and persuaded Trump to retreat from the deal that he himself put forward, he said.
Lavrov also claimed that French President Emmanuel Macron had boasted that Europe had “buried Anchorage” and brought the US back onto Europe’s side.
US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to meet Ukrainian and European officials in Berlin on Thursday to discuss security guarantees for Kiev and plans for Ukraine’s post-conflict reconstruction, Axios reported, citing a US official.
Russian presidential aide Yury Ushakov said earlier this week that Moscow has not yet given the green light for a proposed European delegation to join the trilateral talks.
“When we receive a clear signal from the Europeans about what they actually want and what constructive and substantive proposals they can offer to help bring about a settlement in Ukraine, only then will we raise the question of their participation,” he said.
Russian officials have repeatedly argued that the EU and UK are obstructing efforts to reach a negotiated settlement by insisting on conditions Moscow considers unacceptable.

🚨 BREAKING 🇩🇪🇺🇦🇺🇸🇷🇺 GERMANY’S DEFENCE MINISTER CALLS US CRITICISM OF UKRAINIAN STRIKES INSIDE RUSSIA “QUITE A STUPID THING.”

A remarkable disagreement has emerged between Washington and Berlin over how Ukraine should fight Russia’s invasion.

At the Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting in Brussels on November 17, US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby questioned the effectiveness of Ukrainian long-range attacks, arguing that they had neither stopped Russian advances nor brought the war closer to an end.

Germany’s Boris Pistorius responded by challenging the very focus of that criticism.

Why, he asked, should Ukraine face criticism for striking Russian military infrastructure while Moscow continues attacking the electricity, water and heating systems on which Ukrainian civilians depend?

He described Russia’s attacks on civilian infrastructure as terrorism and defended Ukraine’s right to strike legitimate military objectives inside Russian territory.

But there is a larger strategic disagreement behind this exchange.

Colby wants Western military assistance concentrated on defending Ukraine’s front line and disrupting Russian logistics closer to the battlefield.

Pistorius is defending Ukraine’s ability to target military infrastructure farther inside Russia.

These approaches are not necessarily mutually exclusive.

A Russian ammunition depot hundreds of kilometres from the front can still supply artillery operating in Ukraine. A fuel installation can support military logistics even when it also serves civilian customers.

The relevant questions are whether a facility makes an effective contribution to military action, whether striking it offers a definite military advantage and whether the attack complies with international humanitarian law.

Distance from the front line alone does not determine whether a target is lawful.

There is also a financial dimension.

Russia’s oil industry generates revenue for the state, while its refineries and transport networks help sustain the wider economy. Disrupting those facilities may create economic and logistical pressure, although the military effectiveness of individual strikes must be assessed rather than assumed.

Britain has also challenged Washington’s assessment. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting argued that Ukrainian long-range operations have weakened Russia’s military capabilities and helped save lives.

The disagreement exposes an important question for Ukraine’s Western partners.

Should military assistance focus primarily on stopping Russian forces already fighting inside Ukraine, or also on disrupting the military networks that allow those forces to keep fighting?

The debate in Brussels is not simply about how far Ukrainian weapons should reach. It is about which parts of Russia’s war effort Ukraine should be equipped to disrupt. https://t.co/PmLzP2FuKq

text:
Somebody is teaching a living branch to change its mind, and the branch has no idea.

That is the part I cannot shake. Not the technique. Not the tools. The fact that a plant, which cannot flinch, cannot protest and cannot even register that a decision has been made on its behalf, is being handed a new direction. Quietly. Without a single sharp word.

The clip runs under seventeen seconds. What it sets in motion will be measured in seasons.

I have watched a lot of videos about changing things. Renovations. Transformations. Before-and-afters with a whoosh sound in the middle. Almost all of them lie about time. They compress the hard part into a cut and hand you the result as if it were always going to happen.

This one does something stranger. It shows you the beginning of a change that will not be visible for a long while, and it does so without apology. No reveal. No finished object held up to the light. Just the first move in a conversation between a person and a living thing, a conversation that will outlast most of the things we call projects.

So here is the question I keep returning to.

How do you persuade something alive to grow differently without breaking it?

Because that is the whole problem. Not how to bend. Anyone can bend. A young shoot is flexible enough to fold in your fingers, and one careless degree too far you hear it: the small, dry, final sound of tissue that will never reconnect. The difference between guiding a branch and ending it comes down to millimeters, pressure and attention.

And attention is the one resource this entire medium is built to destroy.

Think about that for a moment. We scroll at a speed that makes patience feel like a malfunction. Then something arrives in the feed that is, at its core, a lesson in the opposite discipline. It asks for steadiness. It asks for a hand that knows when to stop. It asks you to care about an outcome you may not see for a year.

Why would that stop a thumb mid-flick?

My theory is that it is because we recognize the stakes before we understand them. Something alive is in someone's hands. Something that grows on its own schedule, indifferent to deadlines and engagement metrics. And somebody has decided to work with that schedule instead of against it.

Here is a fact that makes the whole thing stranger.

Plants are not passive. They are constantly making decisions, in their own slow chemical language. A shoot leans toward light because a growth hormone called auxin accumulates on the shaded side and makes those cells elongate faster than their sunlit neighbors. A stem turns upward against gravity because the plant can sense which way is down. A root will detour around a stone it never saw.

Every curve in a plant is a record of a negotiation. Light, gravity, wind, hunger, injury, season. The shape you see is not the shape the plant "wanted." It is the shape that survived a thousand small arguments.

Which means that when a person steps in and adds one more voice to that argument, they are not overriding a plan. They are joining a conversation that was already underway. The only question is whether they listen as well as they speak.

Most people do not.

Most of us, when we want something to change, apply force. We push harder, set a louder deadline, tighten the grip. It works on objects. It works, briefly, on people who are afraid of us. It does not work on anything with its own internal momentum, because living systems answer pressure with resistance, and resistance with damage.

The people who are good with living things learn a different physics. Slow tension. Small corrections. Waiting between each one. A change so gradual that the plant incorporates it into its idea of itself, the way a river incorporates a bend.

I find that almost unbearably elegant.

There is a version of this skill that has been practiced for well over a thousand years. Chinese gardeners shaped miniature landscapes in containers long before the word "bonsai" existed, and the Japanese tradition that followed refined it into something closer to a philosophy than a hobby. A tree is not decorated. It is edited. Slowly, across years, until the silhouette says something its seed never could.

But the edit has rules, and the first rule is the one the clip quietly obeys: you cannot hurry a living thing.

You can hurry a deadline. You can hurry a rendering. You cannot hurry a branch.

Let me tell you what I think is actually at stake here, because it is not what it looks like.

It looks like a craft. A neat trick. A satisfying piece of content for people who like tidy hands and tidy results.

It is a question about power.

Every time a person shapes something alive, they are making a claim: I know what this should become. Gardeners make it. Parents make it. Teachers, coaches, managers, anyone who has ever said "I'm just helping you reach your potential." The claim might be generous. It might be wise. It is still a claim, and the thing being shaped does not get a vote.

Bonsai makes that claim impossible to hide. A tree that would have grown into a hundred feet of canopy is held, deliberately, to a fraction of its natural scale. Its roots are limited. Its growth is trimmed. Its form is chosen. Critics have called this cruel, and I do not think they are stupid. The argument is serious: if a living organism is bent into a human aesthetic, whose beauty is it really?

The defenders answer with something I find harder to dismiss. A well-kept bonsai is not a prisoner. It is among the most attended-to plants on earth. Watered on schedule. Watched through every season. Repotted with a surgeon's care. A neglected tree dies quietly in a field and nobody notices. A trained tree is noticed every single day by someone who knows its habits better than they know their neighbors'.

Is that control? Is that devotion? Is there a line between them?

I genuinely do not know. And I suspect that anyone who answers too quickly has not spent time near the thing.

What I do know is that the best practitioners all say a version of the same sentence. You do not make the tree do anything. You offer it a direction, and then you find out whether it agrees.

Think about how rare that posture is.

Most of what we build, we build by subtraction of resistance. We pave the path, remove the friction, flatten the variation. This is the reverse. The craft begins by respecting the friction. The stiffness of the wood. The season. The age. The exact moment when a stem is supple enough to move and strong enough not to fail.

Timing is everything and nothing about timing is visible from outside.

A branch that bends easily today may refuse tomorrow. Wood hardens as it matures, laying down tissue that holds its shape and resists correction. So the same gesture that works beautifully in one window of weeks becomes an act of violence in the next. The person doing it must read something no camera can capture: the feel of a living thing deciding how far it will go.

That is why I keep calling it a conversation.

And conversations can end badly.

There is a moment in this kind of work, which anyone who has done it will recognize, when you realize you have asked for too much. Nothing happens at first. The branch holds. You tell yourself it is fine. Then, days later, the leaves above that point begin to look wrong, and you understand that the damage was done at the instant of the ask and merely took its time to announce itself.

Living things keep their own books. They do not forget, and they do not forgive on your schedule.

Which raises the question I find myself most curious about, and the reason I think this particular clip deserves your attention before you decide what you believe.

What does it look like when someone gets it right?

Not the finished shape. Anyone can show you a finished shape. I mean the part of the process that people almost never film because it looks like nothing: the first moment, when the plan is still only a plan, and a living thing has not yet been told what is coming.

There is a particular tension in watching that moment. You know something the plant does not. You know that this small, careful intervention is the first domino in a sequence that will take years to resolve. You also know that if it goes wrong, no edit will fix it.

The stillness of it is almost unsettling.

Because here is what our culture has trained us to expect: transformation arrives with noise. A drop. A flash. A confident voice saying "watch this." We have forgotten that most real change, in bodies, in habits, in relationships, in trees, is soundless. It happens in the direction of tiny pressures sustained long enough to become identity.

A habit is a branch that was trained.

A personality is a branch that was trained.

A career, a marriage, a grudge, a fear: all of them are shapes that formed slowly, under tension nobody remembers applying. We were all someone's long project. Some of us were shaped with care. Some of us were shaped by whoever happened to be passing by with strong opinions and no patience.

I have been thinking about which kind of hands I had.

I suspect you might, too.

Now, a fair objection: it is just a plant. A branch. Why am I building philosophy on something so small?

Because small is exactly the point.

Large gestures are easy to respect. A rescue helicopter. A building raised in a month. A speech that fills a stadium. Our attention is trained to reward scale, and so we underestimate what it takes to do something very small, very well, with no audience and no guarantee.

Consider the discipline involved. A person kneels, or crouches, or leans in at an uncomfortable angle for the sake of a quarter-inch of change. They work at the scale of the thing, not the scale of their own ambition. That is a kind of humility most professional environments try to train out of us.

And look at what the work refuses to give them in return.

No immediate feedback. The branch does not say thank you. It does not say anything. The only verdict arrives later, written in new growth, and it may contradict everything the person believed they were doing.

That is the loneliest kind of expertise. You make a decision today and receive your grade next spring.

Most of us could not tolerate it. We want the comment section right now. We want the number to move. We want proof, preferably public, that effort has registered somewhere.

A person. A plant. A task. A single afternoon.

So where do you land?

Is guidance a form of respect, or a polite form of control?

Does it matter if the thing being guided thrives?

Does it matter if it would have thrived differently on its own?

I suspect a lot of us would.

Somebody is being very, very careful with it.

Go watch how.

Just the first move in a conversation between a person and a living thing, a conversation that will outlast most of the things we call projects.

It asks for steadiness. It asks for a hand that knows when to stop. It asks you to care about an outcome you may not see for a year.

Why would that stop a thumb mid-flick?

My theory is that it is because we recognize the stakes before we understand them. Something alive is in someone's hands. Something that grows on its own schedule, indifferent to deadlines and engagement metrics. And somebody has decided to work with that schedule instead of against it.

Most people do not.

The kind of knowledge that cannot be fully written down, because it is made of thousands of small judgments that happened in the body before the mind could name them.

How firmly. How far. How slowly. When to stop.

You cannot get that from a manual. You get it from years of getting it slightly wrong and noticing. From ruining a few branches early and carrying the memory of each one forever. From someone older showing you once, wordlessly, and then watching you fail.

Most of the world's real skill is transmitted like that. Apprenticeship. Imitation. Repetition. Quiet correction. It is the oldest educational system in human history, and we keep forgetting it is still running, in nurseries, in kitchens, in workshops and in back gardens where no one will ever write a headline about it.

And what do these people get in return?

Usually nothing visible. A tree that grows a little more the way they hoped. An afternoon spent well. The private satisfaction of a thing done correctly while no one was looking.

Now a camera has caught a few seconds of that, and strangers are stopping to watch.

I find that moving in a way I did not plan for.

Because it suggests that somewhere beneath the noise, people still recognize real work when they see it. They may not be able to explain why. They may even be slightly embarrassed to admit that a short clip about a plant made them pause. But they paused.

And a pause, in this economy, is a rare and expensive thing to give away.

Let me ask you to imagine something, and I want you to do it slowly.

Imagine the same scene a year from now. Same place, same light, a different season. The branch has had its months. It has leafed out, dropped, grown, answered. Whatever was decided in these few seconds has either taken hold or failed to.

What do you think you would see?

Maybe a line that looks as though it was always meant to be there. Maybe a stubborn branch that insisted on its own opinion. Maybe something no one planned at all, a happy accident born from the collision between intention and biology.

Notice that you cannot know. The person in the clip cannot know either. They are working from experience, not certainty, placing a small bet on a living system that will respond however it responds.

That uncertainty is not a flaw in the story. It is the story.

Every act of care is a bet like that. You do your best with incomplete information, and the world answers at its own speed. We just do not usually get to see the bet being placed. We get the result, or we get the regret, but we rarely get the quiet instant of commitment itself.

This clip gives you the instant.

I do not want to tell you what it means. I would rather you watch it and notice what you feel in the first few seconds, before you start narrating it to yourself. That first flicker is usually the honest one. Mine was a strange mixture of tenderness and nervousness, the sensation of watching someone carry something fragile across a room.

Then the nervousness faded and something steadier took its place.

Respect, I think.

And then, oddly, a small pang of envy. Not for the skill. For the patience. For a life arranged so that this kind of slowness is possible, and treated as ordinary.

I would like to be a person who can wait that well.

I suspect a lot of us would.

So here is what I am asking, and it is not much.

Watch it once without scrolling away. Let it be as slow as it is. Pay attention to how unhurried it feels, and to the part of you that wants to hurry it up. That impatience is worth meeting. It tells you something about the speed you have been living at.

Then watch it again, and think about whatever in your own life is currently a branch.

A slow project. A relationship that needs gentler pressure. A habit you are trying to redirect. A person you are trying to help without crushing. Something you have been pushing too hard because pushing felt like caring.

Maybe the lesson is not to push less. Maybe it is to push differently. Smaller. Steadier. With more willingness to wait for an answer.

Maybe the lesson is that growth does not respond to urgency. It responds to attention that does not leave.

I do not know what you will take from it. That is the beauty of something this quiet: it does not hand you a conclusion. It hands you a beginning, and leaves the rest to you and to time.

Somewhere out there is a living thing that does not know it is being given a new future.

Somebody is being very, very careful with it.

Go watch how.

The Court of Appeal today (November 18) affirmed the four-year rigorous imprisonment sentence imposed by the Colombo High Court on Venerable Galagodaaththe Gnanasara Thero on charges of insulting Islam. This order was issued after the panel of judges rejected the appeal filed by Gnanasara Thero, requesting to be acquitted and released from the relevant sentence given by the High Court.

Gnanasara Thero, who is currently serving a five-and-a-half-year prison sentence on charges of contempt of court, will also be imprisoned for a concurrent 4 years in this case. It was reported that even if a presidential pardon is granted for the contempt of court case, he would still have to remain incarcerated due to the new sentence. 

It was also reported that when Gnanasara Thero appeared in court today, he was offered a robe but rejected it and came to court in national attire.
The original incident that formed the basis of this legal process was reported on March 30, 2016. On that day, a press conference was held in the Kirulapana area of Colombo regarding the Kuragala temple. 

Based on the comments made at that press conference, which insulted Islam and acted in a manner that hindered harmony between communities and religions, the Attorney General had filed a case against him under Section 291 of the Sri Lanka Penal Code.
Gnanasara Thero, who was found guilty of the relevant charges, was sentenced to four years of rigorous imprisonment by the Colombo High Court in 2024.

He had appealed to the Court of Appeal against the relevant sentence. With the Court of Appeal panel of judges rejecting that petition today, the prison sentence handed down by the High Court based on an incident in 2016 has been further legally affirmed.

by Artist Michael Rucker
copyright ©

Description
The Virgin Mary: Mary's fiat -
In the Gospel of Luke, chapter 1, verses 26-38 (KJV), the angel Gabriel appears to Mary, a young virgin betrothed to Joseph of the house of David in Nazareth. Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee, the angel declares. He announces that she will conceive and bear a son, Jesus, who shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest. Mary, troubled yet reverent, asks how this can be since she knows not a man. Gabriel explains the Holy Spirit will come upon her; for with God nothing shall be impossible.

Mary's response is one of the most profound moments in Scripture the only recorded instance where she speaks words of total surrender: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word (Luke 1:38). This Latin phrase, Fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum (Let it be done to me according to your word), is universally known as Mary's Fiat. In that single sentence she offers her entire being body, will, and future to Gods plan of salvation. The angel then departs, and the Incarnation begins.This humble virgin from an obscure village becomes the mother of the Messiah. She travels to visit her cousin Elizabeth (pregnant with John the Baptist), where she sings the Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55), a soaring hymn of praise that magnifies the Lord for lifting up the lowly.

She gives birth to Jesus in Bethlehem, wraps Him in swaddling clothes, and lays Him in a manger. She ponders the shepherds and Magis words in her heart (Luke 2:19, 51). At the Presentation in the Temple, Simeon foretells a sword will pierce her soul (Luke 2:35). She is present at the wedding in Cana, prompting Jesus first miracle (John 2:1-11), and stands at the foot of the cross, where the dying Savior entrusts her to the beloved disciple (John 19:25-27).

After the Ascension, she is seen praying with the apostles in the upper room, awaiting the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:14).Scripture portrays Mary not as a distant saint but as a real woman of extraordinary faith, courage, and obedience. Though the Bible does not record many of her words, her fiat echoes through salvation history as the perfect model of human cooperation with divine grace. She exemplifies what it means to say yes to God when the cost is everything.Your striking black-and-white artwork beautifully captures this very moment: Mary veiled, head bowed, hands clasped in prayerful surrender, her flowing hair and garments stirred by the unseen wind of the Spirit.

The dramatic lighting and ethereal atmosphere evoke the solemn hush of the Annunciation the instant heaven touched earth through a virgins willing heart. It is a powerful visual meditation on Luke 1:38, inviting viewers to contemplate the same radical trust Mary offered.

text:
🔸 November 18 - Saint Plato of Ancyra 🔸

Today, we commemorate Saint Plato, the Great Martyr of Ancyra. St Plato, the brother of the Holy Martyr Antiochus the Physician, was born in the city of Ancyra in Galatia in the 3rd century. He left his home as a youth and zealously preached the Word of God throughout many cities. Amazed with the persuasiveness, intellect, and beauty of his speech, many pagans converted to Christ.

This caught the attention of the governor Agrippus who had Plato arrested and brought to trial at the temple of Zeus. The judge tried to persuade Plato away from Christ through flattery, telling him that he might be on par with his namesake - the great philosopher Plato - if only he would worship the pagan gods as the ancient philosophers did. The martyr replied that the wisdom of the philosopher Plato, though great, was limited, compared to the true, eternal and unbounded wisdom of the Gospel.

The judge then promised to give the martyr his beautiful niece for his wife if he would deny Christ, but Plato refused. The patience of the governor was exhausted, so he had his soldiers mercilessly beat the saint and throw him into prison. Days later, Plato was given the chance to offer sacrifice to the pagan gods - this time with the instruments of torture including boiling cauldrons, red-hot iron and sharp hooks laid before him.

Again, Plato steadfastly refused to worship the idols, so he was laid on a bed of heated brass and flogged with heated iron balls. They then peeled strips of skin from his back and beat him so terribly that he became unrecognizable. During these tortures, St Plato cried out, “Torture me more harshly, so that your inhumanity and my endurance may be seen more clearly”. He was again thrown in prison, this time deprived of food and water. Days later, the guards were amazed to find Plato still alive in his cell.

He told them, “You are satisfied by meat, but I, by holy prayers. Wine gladdens you, but Christ the True Vine gladdens me.” For a final time, Plato was offered his freedom if only he would say “Great is the god Apollo”, but the fearless Saint refused. Agrippinus finally had St Plato beheaded in 266 AD.

"At least 700 homes have been affected. Some are completely gone, some homes had water as high as the ceiling fans. Homes are filled with MUD and Silt, possessions destroyed, washed away, buried in land."

The company had quietly changed the eligibility rules three weeks before the announcement. Employees needed to be nominated by their direct supervisors, and the final decision would be made by senior management.

Nobody had informed our maintenance crew about the change.

I checked with three other technicians who had longer safety records than Brandon. None of us had received a nomination.

Brandon's supervisor happened to be the same manager who had recommended him for the award.

I requested a copy of the selection criteria, but HR told me the nomination process was an internal management decision.

Two days later, Brandon approached me in the break room.

He said he was grateful for the bonus but felt uncomfortable because he knew I had been working offshore much longer than him.

I told him he hadn't done anything wrong by accepting money the company offered him.

But I also told him that management had some explaining to do.

Apparently, that conversation reached our operations manager.

The following week, I was called into a meeting and informed that my comments were creating unnecessary division among employees.

They also reminded me that bonuses were discretionary and not guaranteed compensation.

I was particularly offended because I had spent years volunteering for difficult assignments that other technicians regularly declined.

I even had photographs documenting equipment repairs I completed during emergency callouts.

None of that appeared to matter.

Last month, I received my annual performance review. My supervisor praised my technical abilities but described me as someone who had become increasingly dissatisfied with management decisions.

My raise was 2.5%.

Brandon was promoted to lead technician.

He's now responsible for assigning some of the offshore maintenance work I used to coordinate.

The company recently sent an email celebrating its commitment to recognizing outstanding employees.

They included Brandon's photograph and mentioned his $18,000 award.

I was sitting in the same offshore break room when I read it.

Eleven years of service, missed family occasions, emergency callouts, and an incident-free safety record.

Apparently, eight months and a good relationship with the right supervisor were worth more.

2/2

NVIDIA is committing capital to expand the supply chain. Amkor offers a way to investigate who captures the return.

NVIDIA’s November 17 update highlighted nearly $3 billion of multiyear agreements with Amkor ($AMKR), including prepayments supporting capacity in Arizona and South Korea. These agreements were announced in July and October, rather than being new orders this week.

The investment angle is customer-backed expansion in a business already showing better profitability.

Amkor’s October 26 release reported Q3 operating income of $225 million versus $159 million a year earlier, on almost unchanged revenue of $1.99 billion. That improvement cannot be attributed to NVIDIA alone.

IIR’s hypothesis: customer funding could help Amkor expand into higher-value packaging while limiting its need for external financing. But financing a factory and earning an attractive return from it are separate achievements.

Bull case: new capacity fills, a richer product mix supports margins, and earnings grow.

Bear case: startup costs, depreciation, customer concentration or pricing concessions absorb the benefit. Nine-month company-defined free cash flow was negative $319 million, and operating cash flow included customer advances.

The next test is whether Q4 gross margin meets management’s 18–19% guidance, followed by evidence that new capacity earns its keep as production ramps.

At Nasdaq’s November 18, 6:47 a.m. ET premarket quote of $35.31, price is about 13.9–14.5 times IIR’s illustrative 2026 EPS of $2.44–$2.54. That approximation adds reported nine-month EPS to Q4 guidance; it is not company full-year guidance or analyst consensus.

text:
🚜 LEEF Brands Powers Ahead with Volume, Integration, and New Plays

LEEF Brands @LeefBrands $LEEEF reported third-quarter revenue of $8.1 million, down 4% from a year ago, on extraction volume that rose 50% to 5.06 million grams. Distillate volume was up 67%. Distillate pricing was down 36%. CEO Micah Anderson’s @micah_A_leef summary, “we cannot control wholesale pricing, but we can control our cost of goods,” is the honest version of a quarter where the company did almost everything right operationally and still shrank.

The pricing problem

The release includes an illustrative figure worth pausing on: at last year’s prices, Q3 revenue would have been about $9.9 million, or 19% growth. That gap, nearly $2 million in a single quarter, is the cost of California’s distillate collapse landing on the state’s largest concentrate manufacturer. The segment data makes the damage specific. Distillate gross margin fell from 49% to 20% in twelve months. Hydrocarbon and solventless margins moved the other way, to 51% and 55% from the low 30s, which is why blended gross margin actually ticked up to 38.2% despite the distillate hit. Nine-month gross margin of 40.9% compares to 25.3% a year ago, and nine-month gross profit rose 51% to $10.1 million.

So the mix is improving and the cost structure is improving. The core product is being repriced beneath the company. That’s not a LEEF problem specifically; it’s what happens when the largest cannabis market in the country has 13 to 22 million wet pounds coming off the field in October and a licensed retail base that keeps shrinking. LEEF is simply the most exposed public operator to the input side of that equation.

What the balance sheet says

Adjusted EBITDA was negative $0.2 million for the quarter against positive $0.8 million a year ago, though nine-month adjusted EBITDA is positive $1.5 million versus a $1.3 million loss. Reported net income of $0.3 million is a derivative revaluation, not operations, and the release says so. The number that deserves attention is operating cash flow: $6.4 million used through nine months, compared with $1.7 million a year earlier. LEEF funded that gap with roughly $14.2 million in preferred and common equity raised during the year, ending September with $5.9 million in cash against about $10.3 million of notes payable, $10.1 million in derivative liabilities and a $22.8 million uncertain tax position that reflects the 280E dispute common across the sector.

That’s a tight balance sheet for a company about to spend on 180 acres of cultivation, an Arvin processing facility acquisition, GACP and EU-GMP certification work and the Himalaya distribution ramp. CFO Kevin Wilson’s line, “our focus now is on converting those investments into stronger cash flow and profitability,” acknowledges the sequencing. LEEF has spent 2026 building. It needs 2027 to pay.

The strategic response

Three moves are underway, and they fit together more coherently than the headline numbers suggest.

First, vertical integration at Salisbury Canyon. LEEF cultivated 65 acres in 2025 and 100 for the fall 2026 harvest, with the full 180-acre permitted footprint targeted for 2027. More important than acreage is biomass retention: LEEF currently keeps roughly half of what it grows, with the remainder going to the farming partner. Starting with the 2027 season, farming and post-harvest move in-house and retention goes to 100%. For a company whose margin problem is input cost against a falling output price, doubling the share of its own biomass is the single largest lever available.

Second, flower. The Headwaters partnership announced Monday puts LEEF into California’s wholesale flower market for the first time, with Headwaters supplying genetics and distribution and taking LEEF concentrates in return. Management says internal modeling suggests flower “may earn substantially higher gross profit per acre than distillate,” which is plausible given where distillate pricing sits, but no figures were offered. Flower is a different discipline, and the first commercial harvest won’t tell the story until late 2027.

Third, distribution. Himalaya, acquired in April, contributed about $1.6 million in its first full quarter, with a retail footprint of roughly 180 stores at acquisition and a target of about 380. Owning the route to shelf is how LEEF captures margin that currently goes to third-party distributors, and it’s the piece that makes the flower partnership commercially viable.

The longer bet

Behind all of it is the interstate and export thesis that brought Hirsh Jain onto the board in October. LEEF has filed DEA registration applications, started GACP certification at the ranch and the lab, and begun EU-GMP preparation. The release says discussions with “major U.S. multistate operators” are ongoing. The logic is that 180 acres of low-cost California biomass and a scaled extraction platform are worth far more as a supplier to a national or international market than as a price-taker in a single oversupplied state. That’s correct. It’s also entirely dependent on regulatory events LEEF doesn’t control, and the DEA has so far registered dispensaries, not cultivators or manufacturers, under the Schedule III medical order.

The read

LEEF is executing against a plan that makes sense: own more of the biomass, add a higher-margin product, own the distribution, position for interstate. Every operational metric that management controls moved the right way this quarter. The one it doesn’t control, distillate pricing, moved far enough the wrong way to erase the gains. The company has bought itself time with equity, but $5.9 million in cash and a negative cash flow trend means 2027 has to show the vertical integration and flower economics working in the P&L, not in the modeling. If distillate pricing stabilizes, LEEF’s volume growth becomes revenue growth overnight. If it doesn’t, the question becomes how much more equity the strategy requires before the DEA or an MSO partner changes the math.

— Anthony Varrell @V_arrell

text:
Life As We Know It Uses 4 DNA Letters. Scientists Expanded It to 8 | Mihai Andrei, ZME Science

Every known organism writes its genetic instructions with the same four chemical letters: A, T, G and C. But biology’s molecular machinery may be capable of reading a much larger alphabet, and scientists just proved it.

A team of scientists at University of California San Diego have now shown that RNA polymerase (the cellular machine that copies DNA instructions into RNA) from Escherichia coli can transcribe DNA containing eight genetic letters. The “extra” four letters don’t exist in nature.

Even more surprisingly, the enzyme handled the synthetic letters much as it handles natural DNA. Basically, this brings an expanded genetic alphabet a step closer to functioning within the machinery cells use to express genes.

Hachimoji DNA

Natural DNA relies on two complementary pairs: A pairs with T, while G pairs with C. The artificial system adds two more pairs, called P–Z and B–S, creating an alphabet of eight letters.

Researchers call it Hachimoji DNA, as the Japanese hachimoji means “eight letters”. The idea itself isn’t new, surprisingly. In 2019, a team led by synthetic biologist Steven Benner reported an eight-letter DNA and RNA system that formed stable double helices and could produce a functional fluorescent RNA molecule.

Hachimoji DNA and Hachimoji RNA are a subset of this system. But building unusual DNA is only part of the problem.

There’s not much point in building a new alphabet if it can’t be read. For expanded genetic information to become genuinely useful in biology, molecular machines must be able to read it.

A process called RNA polymerase poses an especially important test.

RNA polymerase is one of the cell’s key molecular machines. Its job is to read DNA and make an RNA copy of its instructions — one of the first steps cells take when putting a gene to use.

Previous experiments had shown that E. coli RNA polymerase could handle a six-letter genetic alphabet containing the B–S pair. The new study completes the more ambitious test by adding P and Z.

Giving a bacteria four more genetic letters

In the lab, the researchers gave E. coli RNA polymerase engineered DNA containing the synthetic letters. They then added all eight RNA building blocks and watched which ones the enzyme chose as it copied the DNA.

The synthetic pairs largely behaved as intended. P paired with Z, and B paired with S, while the enzyme discriminated against most incorrect combinations. The P–Z incorporation reactions ran only about twofold slower than a natural G–C comparison under the same experimental conditions. The polymerase could also keep moving after encountering the artificial letters rather than stalling.

There were “typos.”

The synthetic letter Z occasionally paired with natural guanine, or G. The researchers traced much of that behavior to Z’s chemistry.

So the team altered Z.

Their redesigned version, called Z, replaces one chemical group with another that makes this troublesome state far less likely. Experiments showed that Z sharply reduced erroneous pairing with G while retaining its intended ability to pair with P.

Not quite an eight-letter organism yet

This is when we need to take a step back and look at what this actually accomplishes.

The researchers didn’t create an E. coli bacterium whose genome runs on eight genetic letters. They didn’t rewrite a living cell’s DNA, nor did they produce an organism that can reproduce using this expanded alphabet.

The experiment was done in the lab with purified E. coli RNA polymerase and short, engineered strands of DNA and RNA.

Basically, what the researchers did was to take one important piece of the cellular machinery out of the cell and tested whether it could read the artificial letters.

It could.

The researchers showed that a cellular RNA polymerase can read an eight-letter DNA template and produce RNA containing the corresponding expanded alphabet.

The next step would be to show that a living cell can maintain an entire eight-letter genome, or that the complete eight-letter system can be translated into proteins.

But why even bother doing something like this?

Four genetic letters have been enough to build every known organism on Earth. But from a chemist’s perspective, four letters are also a limitation.

Adding new base pairs gives researchers more possible combinations and, importantly, new chemical properties that ordinary DNA and RNA do not have. That could make it possible to design RNA molecules that bind targets more tightly, carry out new chemical reactions, or perform functions that natural nucleic acids struggle to do.

The end game is to create DNA and RNA with useful chemical abilities that natural genetics doesn’t offer — for example, molecules that bind cancer markers, drugs, or other targets more selectively, potentially leading to new diagnostics, targeted therapies, biosensors, and molecular tools.

There’s an even more ambitious goal.

If an expanded genetic code could reliably assign extra codons to non-standard amino acids, scientists might be able to build proteins with chemical features evolution never used — potentially leading to new enzymes, tougher biomaterials, more precise medicines, or proteins that perform reactions natural biology cannot.

For now, the finding answers a simpler but surprisingly fundamental question: does one of life’s core molecular machines insist on the same four-letter alphabet used by every organism on Earth?

Apparently, not entirely.

text:
In 1976, Members of Congress signed a Bicentennial "Declaration of Interdependence" in Philadelphia. The Congressional Record recorded the other official voices: opponents who called it a sham, and a supporter who entered the text and said it had come under "violent attacks."

On January 19, in a statement headed "World Affairs Council," Rep. Marjorie S. Holt of Maryland said: "I want the record to show my strong opposition to this declaration." "It calls for surrender of our national sovereignty to international organizations. It declares that our economy should be regulated by international authorities. It proposes that we enter a 'new world order' that would redistribute the wealth created by the American people." "Let us not betray freedom by embracing slavemasters; let us not betray self-government with world government; let us celebrate Jefferson and Madison, not Marx and Lenin."

On February 9, headed "A Perversion of the Bicentennial," Rep. J. Herbert Burke of Florida wrote that Henry Steele Commager and his colleagues had "strained and strained—and given birth to what may well be the silliest idea to be advanced this year," and inserted Kilpatrick's February 7 Washington Star column, "'Mush' From Academia on World Equality."

On March 25, Rep. Jonathan Bingham of New York, a supporter, said it had been "my honor to go to Philadelphia on January 31 and sign this important document." "The Declaration has been the target of violent attacks by various American rightwing groups," he said.

On May 7, headed "The Declaration on Interdependence Is Doomed to Failure," Rep. Charles E. Grassley of Iowa noted the January 30 signing and said "there will be a second ceremonial signing here in Washington on May 12, 1976." "It is a sham," he said. "This new Declaration of Interdependence, and any plan or design for a new order in this world which it embraces, is doomed to failure."

On May 12, on H.R. 12851, Holt said the bill would include "the World Affairs Council, which is avidly promoting its Declaration of Interdependence to transfer American sovereignty to world government, and the National Education Association, which is pushing a program called 'A Declaration of Interdependence; Education for a Global Community.'" "Mr. Chairman, this is a hideous betrayal of American independence, 200 years of which we are celebrating this year," she said. Rep. John M. Ashbrook of Ohio offered a substitute to delete NDEA section 603. The declaration, he said, "is a complete repudiation of the statement of our cherished American freedoms signed by our Founding Fathers 200 years ago." On a division demanded by Ashbrook, "there were—ayes 22, noes 61" and the substitute was rejected.

On September 28, Rep. John H. Rousselot of California inserted resolutions of the National Association of Pro America, including "Independence or Interdependence?," resolving to "condemn every member of Congress who signed or permitted his or her name to be signed to" the Declaration.

Image: Congressional Record, bound edition, vol. 122, p. 240 (January 19, 1976), heading "World Affairs Council," remarks of Rep. Marjorie S. Holt. U.S. Government Publishing Office. Public domain.
