text:
Clarence Thomas calls foul on California ruling he says could turn citizens into government mouthpieces | Robert Schmad, Fox News

Justice Clarence Thomas warned Monday that the Supreme Court is leaving the door open for states to compel speech from private citizens by not taking up a challenge to a California law.

On Monday, the Supreme Court declined a petition to hear a case from a California physician who argued that the state government was forcing her to make statements she disagreed with while teaching a mandatory course for doctors. Thomas was joined by Justice Samuel Alito in dissenting from the decision, arguing that allowing the law to stand could have implications reaching far beyond the medical field.

The case stems from California’s requirement that all its licensed physicians complete 50 hours of state-approved continuing education courses every two years. California requires continuing medical education courses to include instruction on implicit bias, either through examples of how it affects physicians’ treatment decisions and health outcomes or strategies for addressing how those biases may contribute to health care disparities.

Advertisement “When, as here, the government does not issue its own messages but instead requires private speakers to communicate the government’s viewpoint, the First Amendment applies,” Thomas wrote. “A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny. We should not permit the government-speech doctrine to be wielded as ‘a cover for censorship’ or a cloak for compelled speech.”

Dr. Azadeh Khatibi, who teaches a continuing education course in California, sued the state alongside the right-of-center nonprofit Do No Harm, arguing, as Thomas did, that it compels private instructors to convey a government-favored message in violation of the First Amendment.

Advertisement “She does not want to include discussion of implicit bias in her courses. It is not relevant to her topics, and it would eat away at the limited time she could use to discuss topics that are relevant,” her legal team wrote. “Dr. Khatibi also disagrees that implicit bias is the primary factor driving disparities in health care.”

California countered that while instructors must include discussion of implicit bias in their courses, they are not required to personally endorse the theory and may openly disagree with it.

“Under the second option, instructors who do not believe that implicit bias exists are free to say so,” California wrote in the brief defending its law. “Petitioners are also free to inform CME attendees that any discussion of implicit bias is included solely to comply with state requirements.”

California further argued that states must be given broad authority to determine what doctors must do to retain their licenses.

The Ninth Circuit ruled last year that continuing medical education courses constitute government speech because of California’s extensive regulation of the medical profession, meaning the state’s requirements are not subject to First Amendment free-speech scrutiny.

Thomas, however, disputed California’s characterization of whether it was compelling instructors to take certain positions.

“California’s implicit-bias-training requirement leaves petitioners no choice but to discuss the topic in a way that affirms the State’s view that implicit bias causes ‘disparities in health outcomes,'” he wrote.

The justice went on to argue that allowing California’s law to go unchallenged could have implications for Americans working in many fields beyond medicine.

“What of other professions whose members California licenses and regulates? At the next statewide legal conference at which lectures are offered for continuing legal education, could California require a keynote speaker to oppose racial preferences in law firm hiring?” Thomas wrote. “Applying the Ninth Circuit’s logic, enough government regulation of the field would convert the private speaker’s message in each of these hypotheticals into government speech unprotected by the First Amendment. That result does not follow from this Court’s precedents, and it certainly does not follow from the Constitution.”

Justice Neil Gorsuch also dissented from the court’s decision not to hear the case, though he did not sign on to Alito and Thomas’ argument. His rationale for wanting to grant certiorari is not publicly known.

The Supreme Court’s decision leaves the Ninth Circuit’s ruling intact but does not settle whether California’s requirement violates the First Amendment.

“Medical professionals should not be compelled by the government to participate in evidence-free implicit bias trainings. It is disappointing the Supreme Court declined to take up our case, but we remain encouraged that some Justices acknowledged the importance of the First Amendment issues at stake in our case, issues that will undoubtedly continue to surface in courts across the country. We will keep fighting for constitutionally-protected free speech to ensure that health care providers are never conscripted to deliver the government’s message,” a spokesperson for Do No Harm told Fox News Digital after publication.

A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics | University of California - San Diego, ScienceDaily

Scientists have spotted hints of a mysterious rotation in the universe’s oldest light that could reveal new physics and shed light on dark matter and dark energy. A new technique developed at UC San Diego could help rule out misleading telescope errors, bringing researchers closer to determining whether the strange signal is real.

---

A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover. But before researchers can determine whether this subtle signal reveals something extraordinary about the cosmos, they must answer a crucial question: Is the effect actually coming from the universe, or could it be an illusion created by the telescopes observing it?

The mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang. This ancient light provides a remarkable snapshot of the "baby universe" as it existed nearly 13.8 billion years ago, allowing scientists to investigate conditions from the earliest stages of cosmic history.

When the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space. As radiation scattered off free electrons during this transition, it acquired a small amount of linear polarization. Polarization describes the direction in which light's electric field oscillates, and a similar effect occurs when sunlight scatters through Earth's atmosphere.

Now, observations suggest that the polarization of this ancient radiation may have shifted slightly as the light traveled across the universe. This possible rotation, called cosmic birefringence, is especially intriguing because it could point to physical processes not explained by the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions. Confirming the effect might even provide new insights into dark matter and dark energy (see Sidebar).

A Mysterious Cosmic Signal or a Telescope Error?

There is a major obstacle to interpreting this potential discovery. An extremely small error in how a telescope's polarization detectors are aligned can produce a signal that looks almost identical to cosmic birefringence.

To help address this problem, physicists at the University of California San Diego developed a new technique for checking how accurately different groups of detectors measure polarization angles. They tested their approach using existing observations collected by the European Space Agency's Planck satellite, which mapped the universe's ancient radiation in extraordinary detail.

The research was led by Postdoctoral Fellow Anto I. Lonappan, Chancellor's Distinguished Professor of Physics Brian Keating, and Associate Professor of Physics Kam Arnold. Their findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Separating Real Cosmic Effects From Instrument Errors

Previous studies have suggested that the polarization of the CMB may have rotated by just a fraction of a degree over its nearly 14 billion years of travel. Although that sounds insignificant, such a tiny change could have enormous implications for fundamental physics.

Unfortunately, a telescope whose polarization detectors are misaligned by a similarly small angle could produce precisely the same apparent rotation. If every detector shares the same alignment error, the resulting measurements cannot distinguish that error from a genuine rotation of the cosmic signal.

The UC San Diego researchers found a way to investigate the problem from another angle. Rather than relying on a single combined measurement, they compared separate polarization maps generated by different groups of detectors.

If cosmic birefringence is real, its effect should appear consistently across all these maps. By comparing the maps with one another, the researchers can effectively eliminate any rotation shared by all of them. What remains reveals differences in the calibration of the individual detector groups, making it possible to identify inconsistencies that might otherwise complicate the search for new physics.

"The signal we are looking for is incredibly small, so we have to be certain that we are seeing the universe and not our instrument," said Lonappan. "Our method gives us a complementary way to check that distinction. Before interpreting a tiny rotation as new physics, we want to know that the calibration itself can be trusted."

Testing the Mystery With Planck Satellite Data

To evaluate their technique, the researchers analyzed eight polarization maps produced using Planck observations. They then compared their findings with results from an established approach called the Minami-Komatsu analysis, which is used to distinguish instrumental rotation from possible cosmic birefringence.

Although the two methods rely on different assumptions, they produced consistent results. This agreement provides an important independent check on how relative detector calibration errors are being assessed.

The new approach also has a deliberate limitation. Because it removes any rotation common to all the maps, it cannot independently measure the overall polarization angle or determine how much the universe itself may have rotated the light. Establishing that absolute rotation still requires an independent reference for calibrating the overall angle.

To demonstrate how their findings fit with existing measurements, the researchers combined their reconstruction of relative calibration differences with the common calibration value inferred from the established analysis. This produced an estimated cosmic birefringence angle of 0.37 ± 0.12 degrees, matching the Minami-Komatsu result.

Importantly, this agreement does not independently confirm that the ancient light has actually rotated. Instead, it shows that the new method can reproduce results from the existing framework while providing a separate way to examine potential calibration problems.

Searching for Gravitational Waves From the Early Universe

The technique could also play an important role in another major pursuit in cosmology: the search for gravitational waves generated during the universe's earliest moments.

To understand why, scientists distinguish between two patterns of polarization in the cosmic microwave background, known as E modes and B modes.

E modes were first detected in 2002. They arise from density variations in the early universe and form symmetric polarization patterns. B modes have a different appearance, featuring patterns that resemble curls or swirls.

One known source of B modes is gravitational lensing, which occurs when the gravity of matter between Earth and the early universe bends and distorts the path of ancient light. Scientists have already observed B modes created through this process.

However, researchers are also searching for a different kind of B mode that could have been produced by primordial gravitational waves. These ripples in spacetime may have originated during an extremely early period of rapid cosmic expansion, known as inflation. The distinctive B mode signal associated with those primordial gravitational waves has not yet been detected.

Finding it would provide powerful evidence about gravitational waves in the early universe and could offer strong support for particular models of cosmic inflation, potentially transforming scientists' understanding of how the universe began.

Why Extremely Precise Measurements Matter

The challenge is that even a slight error in a telescope's polarization calibration can cause some of the much stronger E-mode signal to appear incorrectly as B modes. This contamination could make an instrumental artifact look like an exciting cosmological discovery.

The UC San Diego method could help prevent such mistakes by identifying differences in polarization angle calibration among detector groups. That makes it a potentially valuable tool for future experiments searching for the extremely faint signatures of primordial gravitational waves.

This kind of independent verification will become increasingly important as observatories develop the ability to measure cosmic polarization with greater precision. One example is the Simons Observatory, where Keating serves as principal investigator.

As these instruments become more sensitive, researchers will need equally rigorous methods for confirming that the faint signals they detect are genuine features of the universe rather than imperfections in their equipment.

"The detection of primordial B modes would transform our understanding of the early universe, so the measurement must survive rigorous calibration checks," said Keating. "Anto has developed a useful new framework for testing relative polarization-angle calibration. This is ultimately about knowing when we can trust a measurement."

Beyond the Standard Model: Dark Matter and Dark Energy

The possibility of cosmic birefringence is particularly fascinating because it could reveal physics that lies beyond the Standard Model.

Although this framework has been remarkably successful at describing fundamental particles and their interactions, it cannot explain everything in the universe. Among its most important unanswered questions are the identity of dark matter and the origin and observed magnitude of dark energy. Together, these mysterious components account for approximately 95% of the universe's total energy density.

One possible explanation for cosmic birefringence involves a hypothetical field associated with particles resembling axions. Such a field could interact with light and gradually alter its polarization as it crosses the universe. However, these particles have not been confirmed to exist, and they would not necessarily be responsible for dark matter.

Other theoretical explanations connect the possible rotation to fields associated with dark energy, the mysterious phenomenon linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe.

If cosmic birefringence is eventually confirmed, it could provide an entirely new way to investigate these cosmic mysteries and reveal evidence of physical laws beyond those currently understood.

For now, the first challenge is ensuring that the subtle signal can be trusted. By giving researchers another way to identify potential measurement errors, the new technique strengthens the foundation for future discoveries that could reshape our picture of the universe.

Waymo has paused its driverless rides on freeways in every US city where it offered them, after California banned its robotaxis from the state's freeways.

California's DMV, the state office that licenses self-driving cars, called Waymo's driverless freeway rides an "imminent hazard". It pointed to cars repeatedly driving into active construction zones, and one car near San Francisco that tried to get past a highway patrol "traffic break", where officers slow down every lane on purpose.

Waymo says the construction zone cases caused no injuries or crashes. Beyond California it has also stopped freeway rides in Phoenix, Austin and Miami, and keeps testing on freeways with a trained person behind the wheel.

Rides on normal city streets carry on as usual. The ban stays until Waymo shows the DMV it has fixed the problems. No date has been given.

Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth today at 5:16 a.m. EST, about 16 billion miles away, the first human-made object ever to get that far (NASA).

text:
One California order just led Waymo to pause freeway rides in every state where it runs them.

California's DMV barred Waymo's driverless cars from state freeways on Nov. 11, calling them an "imminent hazard to public safety." The order went public Tuesday, per TechCrunch.

The DMV cited three Waymos that entered an active construction closure on US-101 near Burlingame, plus a separate incident with Highway Patrol cars on Highway 280. Waymo says the Burlingame incident caused no injuries or collisions.

Waymo had offered freeway rides in 5 of its 13 operating areas: the Bay Area, Los Angeles County, Phoenix, Miami and Austin, per CNN.

Freeways are how Waymo gets riders to airports fast. Surface streets still carry over half a million trips a week, the company says.

The ban holds until Waymo shows "effective corrective actions," per the DMV.

Waymo's last freeway comeback, May to July, took about two months and a software update. The DMV's order names those May corrective actions as the ones that didn't stop the incursions.

text:
One stolen login. Four months of downloads. Millions of student files.

The state of California hires testing giant ETS to run its assessments. Someone with one compromised credential entered the file-exchange site ETS uses with the education department — and copied files quietly, several times, from May to September. ETS noticed on Sept 25. Yesterday the Sacramento Bee reported the state itself is being sued.

• The lawsuit: filed Nov 2 in Sacramento Superior Court by former student Dane Wilson — a proposed class action against the California Department of Education and ETS. October's federal suits targeted ETS alone; this one names the state. It alleges failures in monitoring and in acting quickly when the breach began, and cites the exposure of disability records — "information that can never be changed or retrieved."

• The haul: names, dates of birth, home addresses, gender, race, country of origin, disability records, program eligibility, English-proficiency data and assessment scores. Not included: Social Security numbers, passports, financial accounts. Millions of current and former students affected, per Reuters.

• The window: one compromised login on the file-transfer site; files accessed and copied several times between May and September; identified Sept 25. Roughly four months of quiet downloads before anyone noticed.

• The archive: everyone enrolled since 2023 — plus students who left a California school any time after 2006 without confirming a transfer. Records up to 20 years old were still sitting on a contractor server, one credential away.

• The remedy so far: two years of Experian monitoring, offered for minors through their parents. Disability status and home address don't expire in two years. That file is permanent.

One vector. Same root cause: the most sensitive archive in the state hung off a single contractor login — no step-up check, no bulk-download alarm, no expiry. The wall held. The file room didn't.

Why now: the suit makes "we hired a contractor" stop working as a defense — the department is a defendant now. And a child's record is near-perfect loot: clean, stable, verifiable for decades. A name, birthdate and address that never change are useful to an attacker long after Experian's two years are up.

What works now:

1. Kill shared logins on every file exchange. Each partner gets its own credential, phishing-resistant MFA, and step-up approval for bulk exports. One SFTP password should never reach a 20-year archive.
2. Alarm on volume, not just logins. "Several times" over four months means nobody watched download size. A bulk export from a records store should page a human.
3. Give the archive an expiry. Records from 2006 were downloadable in 2026. If there's no legal duty to keep a file, the safest copy is the one you deleted.
4. Parents: any call, email or text that knows your kid's school, grade or disability status is the follow-up attack — that's CDE's own warning. Verify through channels you own.

text:
Most days in her chambers, Judge Maritza Braswell, a federal magistrate judge in Colorado, sifts through stacks of documents written by people without a lawyer. Many of them can’t afford to hire a lawyer, and others have cases too weak or too small to interest one. She reads each one carefully, mindful of how daunting it is to walk into the courtroom alone. 

Lately, like many judges across the US, she has seen a noticeable uptick in such filings. According to a new study that examined 4.5 million federal civil cases from 2005 to 2026, the share of lawsuits brought by self-represented people increased from 11% in 2022 to 16.8% in 2025. Within those cases, the number of filings made more than doubled from pre-2023 levels. 

Judge Braswell puts that jump down to AI. 

“I do correlate that to AI in part because I see AI use,” she says. As a tech-savvy judge who uses AI to vet court documents, she’s learned to recognize how large language models write. She can tell from the prose and at times, hallucinated cases and fabricated quotes. 

“I’m also actually seeing better-drafted pleadings,” she says. 

But while AI appears to be expanding access to justice, it doesn’t seem to be improving people’s chances of winning. Judges are also starting to question what kinds of rights and responsibilities large language models should bear as they step into lawyers’ shoes. For example, they ask whether a chatbot has a duty to provide good advice, as a human lawyer does. And a growing number of lawmakers across the US are starting to grapple with who should pay the price when chatbots dish out bad legal advice. 


AI supercharges lawsuits

To test whether AI was driving the increase in lawsuits filed by people without a lawyer, the authors of the study, Anand Shah at MIT and Joshua Levy at the University of Southern California, ran 1,600 randomly sampled court documents through Pangram, a commercial AI-text detector. The share flagged as containing AI-generated writing rose from 1% in 2023 to 18% in 2026. 

To Judge Braswell, that’s not necessarily a cause for concern. While the surge of AI-assisted filings might be adding to their workloads, she and many other judges find the cases easier to rule on because AI is helping people without legal training better articulate their arguments. 

Court documents written by people without lawyers are notoriously hard to decipher. Some arrive as handwritten scrawls bordering on gibberish that judges take a while to decode. However cryptic, judges are required to read them charitably.

These days, Judge Braswell has been churning through motions drafted by AI faster than the ones written by the litigants. “I have to be really careful because some of them contain hallucinations and errors, but I can generally understand what they’re arguing better with AI assistance from them than without it,” she says.

The clearer filings let Judge Braswell hear them better. “If I understand an argument a little bit better, I’m probably going to be able to help a little bit more,” she says.

Online communities are springing up to trade self-help guides on using AI to sue. In December 2024, a viral Reddit post walked immigration applicants through suing the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services over delayed review of their applications: draft a writ of mandamus with Microsoft Copilot, pay a lawyer $150 to polish it, and file in the expedient District of Vermont. Cases filed by people without lawyers in Vermont rose from about 45 a year before 2022 to more than 1,100 in 2024. 

Even so, people without lawyers are far more likely to lose their case than people with lawyers, and that’s not changing even with the addition of AI, the study found. 

“It turns out that mounting a lawsuit is a complex, multifaceted task. Not all of it is just drafting text,” says Levy. 

Chatbot-client privilege

Judge William Garfinkel, a federal magistrate judge in Connecticut, has served on the bench for three decades, pondering all sorts of questions about lawyers’ relationship with their clients. Lately, he has been wondering whether people’s conversations with chatbots dispensing legal advice should be privileged, the way their conversations with lawyers are. 

“You can make a good argument that … conversations with large language models like Claude or ChatGPT or Grok should deserve some protection,” he says.

Courts are starting to grapple with this question. In February, a federal court in Michigan ruled that a self-represented person’s conversations with ChatGPT to prepare her case were work product—legal work that is shielded from the opposing side.

The decision came on the same day a federal court in New York held that documents a criminal defendant had generated using Claude were not privileged attorney-client conversations or work product. The court argued that Claude is not an attorney and that a user has no “reasonable expectation of confidentiality in his communication” with it because AI companies can disclose user data to third parties. 

In March, Judge Braswell ruled that a self-represented person’s use of a chatbot should stay off limits. “It is true that AI systems like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and others … collect user data for training and other purposes. But … that does not eliminate all expectations of privacy,” she wrote. Courts have since remained split on the issue.

Malpractice without a pulse

Some judges are also wondering whether a chatbot, like a lawyer, has a duty to provide good legal advice. Judge Allison Goddard, a federal magistrate judge in California, has noticed that people without lawyers often get the wrong advice from ChatGPT when trying to assess the value of their case during settlement negotiations. In one case, a plaintiff who slipped and fell in a store asked for $700,000 from the store, which was wildly more than the case was worth.

“Where are you getting the idea that you’re getting $700,000? Did you go to ChatGPT?” Judge Goddard asked. “Well …” the plaintiff mumbled. She then walked the person through the law to explain why ChatGPT was wrong and suggested a lower amount. “It’s like Dr. Google went to law school,” she says.

Then there’s the question of who’s liable when a chatbot makes such mistakes. In March, Nippon Life Insurance Company sued OpenAI alleging that ChatGPT practiced law without a license and helped a woman reopen a lawsuit that was already settled, flooding the court with frivolous filings. “ChatGPT is not an attorney,” the lawsuit said. 

In May, OpenAI asked the court to dismiss the case, arguing that ChatGPT does not practice law. “ChatGPT is not a person and neither has nor uses any degree of legal ​knowledge or skill,” OpenAI said in its filing. The case is still pending before the court.

States have started to weigh legislation that would hold AI companies liable when their chatbots offer bad legal advice. New York introduced a bill in March that would bar chatbots from impersonating lawyers, even if they notify ​users that they are interacting with chatbots. In Congress, a series of bills have been proposed to ban chatbots from posing as lawyers, doctors, and other licensed professionals. The bills have yet to gain traction.

For now, people will continue turning to AI to be their lawyer. For many of them, the rewards outweigh the risks. Not long ago, when Judge Braswell asked self-represented litigants why they wanted a particular piece of evidence, they mumbled timidly. Now, they answer her questions confidently, having rehearsed with a chatbot. 

“This is a really tough system to navigate. With AI, though, it gets a little less complex,” she says.

Now the first hundred, #2 to 101, become an 80 minute performance, commissioned by the Whitney for artport: A History of Internet Art. Runs Nov 19 to 22, with livestreams on Nov 21 and 22 at institutions including the V&A (@V_and_A) in London and NODE (@nodefnd) in Palo Alto.

Masquerade: a hooded man carrying a heavy pack covered in the masks Spratt made for his collectors. He writes that the offer came while he sat in a Manhattan ER with his infant daughter, after months of quiet research on Luci for Howard and his advisory team, and that Masquerade had already led to Infinite Images at the Toledo Museum of Art (@ToledoMuseum), an exhibition filled with works from Howard's collection.

03 · The forest, trained and painted. At Art Basel Miami Beach (@ArtBasel), Zero 10 booth Z6 brings back Winds of Yawanawa, the 2023 collaboration between Refik Anadol (@refikanadol) and the Yawanawa people of the Brazilian Amazon, Artnet (@artnet) reports. His studio trained a bespoke AI model on the community's 2023 works and paired it with readings from a weather station in the village, set to Yawanawa song. A dozen screens will run all 1,000 pieces, beside drawings and three new canvases by sisters Nawashahu and Mukashahu Yawanawa. Produced with HOFA Gallery (@hofagallery) and Instituto Nixiwaka, Dec 2 to 6.

04 · New on https://t.co/hIfCL7iz9M: satellite art against Big Brother. On New Year's Day 1984, Nam June Paik linked WNET in New York and the Centre Pompidou in Paris for Good Morning, Mr. Orwell, a live broadcast MoMA puts at 25 million viewers. John Cage played cactus needles with a feather, Charlotte Moorman played TV Cello, and Laurie Anderson and Peter Gabriel (@itspetergabriel) premiered Excellent Birds. The link kept failing and the two cities ended up watching different shows; Paik said the glitches only made it feel more live. A 38 minute version is in MoMA's collection.

05 · Copenhagen's future, prompted by the public. On Nov 24 the Royal Danish Academy opens AI Imaginaries at the Pioneer Centre for AI, using generative AI to picture how climate change and the green transition will reshape Danish landscapes, cities and coasts. The images draw on IPCC and CONCITO scenarios, and most were made by visitors who rewrote urban, rural and coastal views in their own words, more than 800 visual surveys so far.

text:
The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets | University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science, ScienceDaily

Establishing a permanent human presence on the Moon will require more than rockets, habitats, and life support systems. Engineers must also find ways to protect astronauts and equipment from extreme temperatures that can swing from hundreds of degrees below zero to boiling hot. Reliable insulation will be essential, but keeping heat under control is only part of the problem.

Materials used in lunar construction must also survive transportation, installation, accidental impacts, and years of handling. Many of the best insulators are surprisingly delicate, making them poorly suited to the demanding conditions of a working Moon base.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania may have found an answer in an unexpectedly familiar material: Mylar. This lightweight plastic is used in everyday products such as food wrap and, when coated with aluminum, the reflective emergency blankets that help marathon runners retain body heat. By arranging hundreds of extremely thin Mylar sheets into carefully designed stacks, the team has created insulation that remains effective even after being bent or subjected to intense pressure.

The research, published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, introduces a material known as hybrid layered insulating film stacks (HyLIFS). Its main advantage is the ability to combine two qualities that are difficult to achieve together: excellent thermal insulation and resistance to physical damage.

"These stacks of Mylar can bend, withstand substantial compression and maintain their insulating performance," says senior author Igor Bargatin, Associate Professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM), "potentially allowing them to be packed, transported and survive rough treatment over many years of use."

If engineers can eventually manufacture the material on a large scale, it could be used to protect lunar habitats, spacesuits, and other equipment designed to function for extended periods in the vacuum of space.

"The combination of thermal and mechanical robustness is critical for long-term use on the Moon," notes first author Danielle R. Levin, a recent Penn doctoral graduate in chemistry, who also received a master's in MEAM. "This material could open a pathway to inexpensive, durable and reusable lunar insulation."

Why Moon Bases Need Tougher Insulation

Designing insulation for the Moon involves a difficult balancing act. A material must slow the movement of heat through a vacuum while also remaining strong enough to withstand the stresses of everyday use.

Some existing materials are outstanding at preventing heat transfer but offer little protection against physical damage. Aerogels, for instance, consist mostly of empty space, which makes them extremely lightweight and effective at retaining heat. They have been used in applications ranging from industrial pipelines to NASA's Mars rovers. However, their delicate internal structure can make them vulnerable to impacts and compression.

Another widely used space technology, multilayer insulation, relies on reflective sheets separated by insulating spacers. It works particularly well at reducing heat transfer through radiation, but it is not intended to support substantial weight. Even routine contact can cause tearing or other damage.

Strengthening insulation often creates another problem: the changes that make it more durable can also allow more heat to pass through. For future lunar infrastructure, engineers need a material that can resist damage without sacrificing thermal performance.

"For lunar infrastructure, we would ideally like both," says Bargatin. "The ideal material is both resistant to damage and to the loss of heat."

How Ordinary Mylar Became Powerful Space Insulation

The Penn researchers focused on Mylar, a well-known plastic formally called biaxially oriented polyethylene terephthalate, or BoPET. Already used extensively in aerospace technology, the polymer is also found in the lightweight emergency blankets distributed after marathons. Adding a metallic coating such as aluminum allows Mylar to reflect infrared radiation, helping prevent heat from escaping.

Rather than relying on a single sheet, the researchers investigated what would happen if many thin layers were stacked together. They experimented with different film thicknesses and applied extremely thin coatings of aluminum oxide, also called alumina, to some samples to make the sheets stiffer.

Assembling the experimental stacks was surprisingly difficult. Each delicate film had to be positioned individually, requiring painstaking manual work.

"At the moment, the process is very time-consuming," says Levin. "We use two pairs of tweezers and small weights to handle and stack the delicate films. Even breathing near the stack can send the layers flying."

Despite the simplicity of the basic idea, testing revealed an impressive combination of properties. In a vacuum, the best stacks achieved thermal conductivity comparable to other advanced vacuum insulation materials while retaining their flexibility.

The researchers also tested the material under compression similar to what insulation could experience inside a lunar habitat, where the interior air pressure would push against walls exposed to the vacuum outside.

Additional mechanical testing showed that stacks coated with alumina could tolerate the greatest compressive stresses available with the laboratory equipment while maintaining their insulating performance. The results demonstrated that improving durability did not necessarily require giving up thermal protection.

Crushing Pressure Reveals Unexpected Durability

One of the most striking findings came when the team subjected the material to repeated compression. Even the researchers were surprised by how well the thin plastic layers held up.

The samples were compressed to approximately 20 megapascals, a pressure comparable to concentrating 200 pounds of force onto an area the size of a fingertip. Instead of testing the material only once, the researchers repeated the process 10 times.

"We were concerned about the material failing under such high compressive stress," recalls Levin. "But the stacks didn't survive just one high stress cycle -- they survived 10 in a row."

This resistance to damage could be especially valuable for lunar exploration. Every piece of equipment needed on the Moon must first endure the challenges of being packed, launched, transported, and installed. Insulation that can bend, withstand pressure, and potentially be reused would offer significant practical advantages.

Durability would remain important after construction is complete. Astronauts living and working inside a lunar habitat could accidentally strike or compress insulation during maintenance or ordinary activities.

"You could use these stacks to insulate a lunar habitation, but astronauts will inevitably have little accidents where they bump into them," notes Bargatin. "When we're talking about long-term habitation on the moon, it's really important to have tough materials that can last long enough."

Tiny Particles Reveal a Hidden Secret of Heat Transfer

Beyond demonstrating the material's durability, the experiments uncovered an important clue about how heat travels through layers of Mylar.

The discovery involved microscopic particles already present in commercially manufactured plastic films. Extremely thin sheets naturally tend to stick to one another and to nearby surfaces, which complicates manufacturing and handling. To prevent this, producers add tiny "antiblocking" particles that extend slightly above the plastic surface and keep neighboring sheets from clinging together.

Although manufacturers have long understood why these particles are useful, their influence on heat transfer in stacked Mylar films had received relatively little attention.

Traditional multilayer space insulation is primarily designed to control heat transferred by radiation. As a result, researchers have had less reason to investigate how small points of physical contact between films might affect heat conduction.

The Penn team examined this possibility by constructing mathematical models of heat transfer between individual layers and comparing the predictions with laboratory measurements.

The findings indicate that, in a vacuum, much of the heat moving from one Mylar sheet to the next passes through the tiny contact points created by the antiblocking particles.

That result could have important implications for future insulation design. Instead of accepting the particles as an incidental feature of commercial plastic, engineers might deliberately control their size, abundance, and placement to reduce unwanted heat transfer.

Why Thinner Plastic Does Not Always Insulate Better

The role of these microscopic particles also helped explain another unexpected result.

At first, the researchers assumed that thinner Mylar sheets would produce better insulation. Using thinner films would allow more layers to occupy the same amount of space, increasing the number of boundaries that heat must cross.

However, the experiments did not fully support that expectation. When coated with alumina, the thinnest films the team successfully characterized provided thermal performance similar to films of medium thickness.

The researchers suspect that the antiblocking particles help explain why. In thinner sheets, the particles can produce more contact between adjacent layers, creating additional routes for heat to move through the material. Those extra contact points can offset the expected advantages of adding more layers.

The finding suggests that making films thinner is not automatically the best approach. Engineers must also consider how the sheets bend and deform under pressure, along with the number and arrangement of microscopic contact points.

"As you compress the layers, the contact landscape changes," says Levin. "It's not just a matter of minimizing the film thickness or the number of particles; we must also account for how the contacts change and the films deform as pressure increases."

Ultimately, the ability of these stacks to limit heat transfer depends on several interacting factors, including the thickness and stiffness of the plastic and the distribution of particles within it.

From Tiny Laboratory Samples to Future Moon Bases

Although the early results are encouraging, the new insulation is still far from being ready for lunar construction.

The experimental HyLIFS samples currently measure only about one square centimeter, and producing them requires hours of careful cutting and manual stacking. That painstaking process would be impractical for manufacturing the large sheets needed to insulate an entire habitat.

To make the material useful on a larger scale, the researchers will need a more efficient production method. One possibility involves continuously applying coatings to large rolls of Mylar, using manufacturing techniques that could eventually produce sheets measured in meters rather than centimeters.

Such an approach might also allow engineers to adjust the thickness of the plastic, the protective coatings, and the distribution of antiblocking particles before assembling the material into larger stacks.

Important questions remain. The researchers still need to determine whether large versions of the material will retain the same insulating properties and mechanical strength seen in the laboratory. Further testing must also establish how well the stacks tolerate repeated bending, accidental impacts, scratches, and other wear associated with real-world use.

If those challenges can be overcome, the technology could provide lightweight, flexible, durable insulation for lunar habitats, rovers, electronic equipment, and other systems operating in space.

For Levin, the results also offer a broader lesson about materials engineering. Even familiar products can reveal unexpected capabilities when researchers examine how their structures behave under different conditions.

"The simplest configuration ended up being the best one," she says.

Me: Schliemann of Troy

Ai: Schliemann of Troy is a biographical account of Heinrich Schliemann (1822–1890), the German businessman and amateur archaeologist best known for his excavations at Hisarlik in present-day Turkey, where he helped uncover the archaeological remains associated with the legendary city of Troy.
The book explores Schliemann’s extraordinary transformation from a self-made businessman into one of the most famous and controversial archaeological figures of the nineteenth century. Fascinated by the ancient Greek epics of Homer, particularly The Iliad, Schliemann became convinced that the stories of the Trojan War were rooted in historical reality. Defying the skepticism of many scholars, he devoted his fortune and much of his life to locating the places described in the ancient texts.
It recounts his dramatic excavations, his discovery of ancient settlements buried beneath the earth, and his celebrated claim to have uncovered the treasures of King Priam. It also examines the controversies surrounding his archaeological methods, including his destructive excavation techniques, questionable interpretations, and the removal of valuable antiquities from Turkey.
Beyond the archaeological discoveries, the book presents a fascinating portrait of an ambitious, obsessive, and often controversial individual whose determination helped transform the study of ancient history.

At its heart, Schliemann of Troy is a story about ambition, adventure, archaeological discovery, and the complicated relationship between mythology and historical fact. It offers an engaging look at the man who helped turn the legendary city of Troy into one of archaeology's most enduring subjects.

On the 25th of every month, I switch the Zillow map from "For Sale" to "For Rent"

Any house sitting empty for 60+ days has a tired landlord who just paid two mortgages out of pocket and is 5 days away from paying a third

That tab is how I bought 5 rentals for $40,000+ under market value:

When a house sits on the "For Sale" tab, you're competing against 40 other buyers and two realtors taking 6%

When a house sits on the "For Rent" tab for 45+ days, the owner is bleeding cash out of their personal checking account on an empty house, getting stood up at showings, and mowing the lawn themselves every Saturday

Here is how I find them in 10 minutes from my laptop:

- Switch Zillow to "For Rent", filter for single-family houses, and scroll to the bottom for listings up 45+ days. Look for listings with cell phone photos and a recent $100 to $200 price cut on the rent

- Type the address into your free county auditor site. Check that the owner is an individual (not a giant property management company), bought the house 10+ years ago so they have plenty of equity room, and lives in another city or state

- Call the phone number on the Zillow rental listing on the 25th of the month, six days before their next empty mortgage payment is due, and say:

"I saw your rental on Oak Street. Instead of putting another tenant in it, would you take a cash offer as-is and close in 10 days with zero realtor fees?"

Last fall I called a landlord in Florida whose 3-bedroom house outside Columbus had been sitting on the Zillow rental tab for 58 days after his last tenant wrecked the carpet

Clean houses on that block sell for $195,000, but he was tired of paying two mortgages and didn't have $15,000 to remodel it from 900 miles away

He sold it to me off-market for $148,000 ($47,000 under market value) so he wouldn't have to make December's mortgage payment

He only took $148,000 because I could close in 10 days without a 45-day bank loan or an appraiser flagging the torn-up floors

We keep $100,000 to $250,000 in 0% introductory business credit sitting under our LLC before we make those calls.

Our $14,500 floor and paint remodel sat on that credit at 0% for 12 to 18 months with nothing reporting to our personal credit score, and refinancing the house paid that balance off

Most investors with a 700+ credit score apply for business funding on their own, put "Real Estate" on the application, and get capped at a single $10,000 card, because banks auto-flag real estate as high risk

Unlocking $100,000 to $250,000 at 0% in one round depends on how your LLC is set up and the order your applications go in

If you're a real estate investor or business owner with a 700+ credit score, book a call at the link in my bio and my team will build that $100k to $250k in 0% business credit for you, so you can lock up off-market rentals before they ever hit the "For Sale" tab

text:
#cozymystery #horses #dogs  
Why Florida Small Town Storytelling Feels Like Home

A Florida town can keep a secret longer than a pelican can keep its eye on a fish sandwich. Behind the pastel storefronts, porch swings, and sun-faded historic markers, everybody knows somebody - and somebody always notices when a familiar car is parked where it should not be. That is the particular pleasure of **Florida town storytelling**: a setting warm enough to invite readers in, with just enough local memory, personality, and gossip to make a mystery matter.

For cozy mystery readers, a small town is never merely a backdrop. It is a living collection of neighbors, old grudges, rescue pets, community events, and unofficial experts who have opinions about everything from zoning changes to who makes the best key lime pie. Add a clever dog with a sensitive nose, and even a quiet afternoon may turn up a clue.

## Florida Town Storytelling Starts With a Sense of Place

Florida is often reduced to beaches, theme parks, and postcards full of palm trees. Those things certainly belong here, but they are only part of the picture. A town near an inland lake has a different rhythm from a Gulf Coast fishing community. An old railroad town feels different from a neighborhood built around citrus groves, horse farms, or a historic downtown square.

The most memorable stories use those distinctions. Maybe the town library occupies a former train depot. Maybe a century-old hotel has survived hurricanes, changing ownership, and a few suspicious legends. Maybe the annual seafood festival brings in enough visitors to make a missing person difficult to spot - or a stolen antique easy to hide.

A good setting gives characters something to react to. Summer heat can make tempers shorter. A sudden thunderstorm can send witnesses scurrying indoors. Hurricane preparation may reveal which neighbors show up with bottled water and plywood, and which ones have something to conceal. These details should serve the plot, not crowd it, but they make the story feel rooted in a real place.

## The Best Small Towns Have Long Memories

In a large city, a person can disappear into the crowd. In a small Florida town, a new haircut may be noticed before lunch. That closeness brings comfort, but it also brings complications. People remember high school rivalries, old business disputes, family scandals, and the one unfortunate incident at the charity auction ten years ago.

That long memory is a gift to a mystery writer. A crime in the present can have its roots in an old land deal, a vanished family heirloom, or a friendship that broke apart years earlier. Historical tidbits are especially useful when they do more than decorate the scene. The date on a town monument, a closed-off room in an old building, or a name repeated in cemetery records can quietly point toward the truth.

Still, small-town life should not be treated as a collection of nosy stereotypes. The people who ask too many questions may also bring soup when someone is sick, look after a neighbor's cat, or organize a fundraiser without being asked. Their concern can be genuine even when their methods are a little enthusiastic. That mixture of kindness and curiosity is where cozy mysteries find much of their heart.

### Familiar Faces Make the Stakes Personal

When readers return to the same town book after book, they want more than a new suspect list. They want to check in on familiar faces. Has the bakery owner finally taken a vacation? Is the town council still arguing about the old theater? Did the veterinarian's assistant adopt that mischievous kitten?

Recurring characters create a sense that life continues between mysteries. They also make danger feel more personal. If the person in trouble is someone readers have shared pancakes, parades, and pet-adoption days with, the case is no longer just an interesting puzzle. It is a problem that needs solving before the town's sense of safety is damaged.

That is one reason a canine narrator can be such a joyful guide. Dogs do not care who is wealthy, well-connected, or trying to impress the mayor. They notice nervous voices, unfamiliar scents, altered routines, and who slipped out the back door. In the Doc and Daisy Mysteries, Daisy's warm snout and sharp observations bring a playful angle to the clues while keeping the people around her very human.

## Why Dogs Belong in Florida Town Mysteries

Dogs naturally connect a town. They meet people on sidewalks, at parks, in veterinary offices, and outside cafes where someone has thoughtfully placed a water bowl. A dog may recognize the scent of a visitor before the humans do. She may also understand that a person who says, “Nothing is wrong,” does not smell quite as calm as they sound.

Canine forensics works best when it honors both the limits and gifts of a dog's senses. A dog can detect a scent trail, alert to a hidden object, or react to a familiar smell in an unfamiliar place. But a dog cannot explain every clue in a neat paragraph, and that is part of the fun. The human sleuth must interpret what the dog has found, test assumptions, and avoid leaping to conclusions just because someone was carrying bacon.

A veterinarian's perspective adds another layer. Animals often notice changes before people do, and their care can bring all kinds of residents through one door. A lost pet, an injured bird, an anxious horse, or a suspiciously ill show dog can open a path into the community. It also creates a natural foundation of compassion. The mystery may be lighthearted, but the care for animals should feel sincere.

## The Cozy Balance: Sunshine, Shadows, and Smart Clues

A Florida setting can be bright and cheerful without making every story sweet as orange marmalade. The best cozy mysteries make room for real motives: jealousy, greed, grief, fear, and the mistakes people make when they believe nobody is watching. The difference is in the treatment. Readers come for the puzzle and the company, not for graphic violence or despair.

That balance depends on tone. A funny moment should not erase a character's loss. A dangerous discovery should have consequences, even if the sleuth finds it while wearing flip-flops and carrying a bag of dog treats. Humor works because it grows from character: the retired neighbor who has a theory for everything, the cat who chooses the worst possible moment to sit on an important document, or the dog who knows a snack opportunity when she sees one.

The clues need to be fair, too. Readers enjoy being surprised, but they also want the satisfaction of realizing the answer was in front of them. A seemingly ordinary conversation at the farmers market, a contradiction in a local-history tale, or a muddy paw print near a locked gate can all become meaningful later. Modern twists such as digital messages, security cameras, and online rumors can add complications, but they should not replace careful observation.

## What Readers Carry Away From a Florida Town Story

The lasting appeal is not only the solution to the crime. It is the feeling of having visited a place where people know the streets, care about the animals, and show up when trouble arrives. Florida offers plenty of color and contradiction for this kind of story: old and new, wild and carefully manicured, peaceful mornings and dramatic weather by late afternoon.

A fictional town does not need to be perfect to be welcoming. In fact, its quirks are what make it believable. Let the local diner run out of pie. Let the town sign have a misspelled word nobody has bothered to fix. Let one neighbor know every secret and another be determined to prove them wrong. Then give readers a sleuth with common sense, a good heart, and perhaps a canine partner who knows that every investigation goes better after a walk.

The next time you open a cozy mystery set in a Florida town, pay attention to the details that make you linger: the old stories, the friendly faces, the suspicious footprints, and the dog waiting patiently beside the clue. That is where a town begins to feel like somewhere worth returning to.

text:
‘I Have Seen the Enemy, and It Is Us’: Inside Team Trump’s Historic Collapse https://t.co/y6Tt5XhTrq

What is Downgrading Trump’s Presidency?

Was it the Iran war or overambitious tariffs that triggered inflation and damaged President Trump’s presidency? It was a combination of these and several other policy failures. 

Domestically, inflation and ICE excesses badly tarnished his image. If we look back his presidency, six years, Trump was not the politician we see him today. His defeat in 2020 pushed him closer to ultra-conservatives, whose influence reshaped his outlook. They surrounded him with incompetent but fiercely loyal advisers and cabinet members, all committed to advancing the MAGA agenda. What was supposed to deliver a stronger America has instead produced a political debacle.

Trump’s honeymoon is over. The midterm voters have rejected his policies, costing Republicans their majorities in both houses of Congress. 

His political troubles are far from over. The controversy surrounding Defence Secretary Hegseth and the threat of impeachment may have been temporarily stalled, but a heavily Democratic Congress is unlikely to let the matter rest. To limit further political damage, Trump may eventually have to replace him with a more competent figure.

Tariffs and Inflation: A Self-Inflicted Wound.

Tariffs and inflation became everyday concerns in American households. Trump promised that import duties would fill government coffers with billions of dollars while protecting American industry. 

The reality was quite different. Courts blocked much of his tariff programme, forcing him to use emergency powers to restore some duties. Meanwhile, foreign exporters raised prices to offset the tariffs, leaving American importers and consumers to bear much of the cost. The Treasury collected less than promised, while consumers faced higher prices. Trump had created an economic and political disaster for himself.

Iran War: The Biggest Strategic Miscalculation
Trump became overconfident after the relatively quick operation in Venezuela, where control over its oil resources appeared to offer a political victory. He seemingly believed Iran could be dealt with in much the same way. 

Under the pretext of stopping its nuclear ambitions, he launched a bombing campaign, overlooking the strategic consequences.

Iran survived the attacks and retaliated through the one weapon it could effectively deploy: disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The resulting surge in global oil prices hurt economies worldwide, including America’s. Whatever damage tariffs had not caused, the unfinished Iran war compounded. With no clear resolution in sight, the conflict became another major liability for Trump.

ICE Excesses: Losing Public Sympathy

The aggressive ICE crackdown also damaged his standing. Illegal immigrants working in low-paid jobs, often shunned by American workers, were rounded up, detained and deported. While many Americans have limited sympathy for illegal immigration, they strongly objected to the heavy-handed methods. The excesses in Minnesota became a particularly damaging example. Public resistance grew, adding another burden to an already unpopular presidency.

Trump now has two years left in office. The midterm verdict should be a wake-up call. Unless he changes his approach, replaces poor advisers and rethinks his policies, he risks turning the remainder of his presidency into a prolonged political decline.

Last of the mid-term election results has Mary Peltola beating Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska to give Democrats 56 Senate seats

Democrat Mary Peltola will be Alaska’s next senator after beating the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, with the result called two weeks on from midterm elections which saw Donald Trump’s party lose ground across the country.

Peltola, a former US House lawmaker, is the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate since 2008. Her victory comes just two years after Alaska voters unseated her while supporting Trump by a double-digit margin.

“From Juneau to Utqiagvik, the message from Alaskans is clear: the status quo in DC is not working for Alaska,” Peltola said in a statement on Tuesday.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” she said. “As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska’s working families.”

Alaska was the last Senate race remaining to be called, and with Peltola’s victory, Democrats will control 56 seats in the upper chamber, after winning campaigns in conservative states including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and Mississippi. 

The party gained nine Senate seats in the midterms, a sweeping victory that will put them decisively back in the majority beginning next year, when they are expected to embark on an aggressive campaign of both lawmaking and investigating.

Peltola, who is Yup’ik, will join Minnesota senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, a member of the White Earth band of Ojibwe, as the first two Native American women to serve in the US Senate.

Under Alaska’s voting system, the top four candidates from the non-partisan primary advance to the November general election. Voters then rank the candidates in order of preference. 

If no candidate receives more than 50% on the initial round of counting, the last-place finisher is eliminated and that candidate’s supporters will have their second-choice votes counted.

With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had secured 50.1% of the vote, according to Associated Press, while the incumbent senator received 45.8%.

The Democrats dare not rest on their laurels. They need to do what Trump promised to do but cheated voters by doing the opposite.

**Introducing Berkshire Hathaway Inc. (USD-BRK-B / BRK.B)**

Berkshire Hathaway Inc. is one of the world’s largest and most iconic conglomerates, headquartered in Omaha, Nebraska. Originally a textile manufacturer founded in 1839, it was transformed under Warren Buffett’s leadership starting in the 1960s into a diversified holding company with massive operations in insurance, railroads, energy, manufacturing, and retail.

Today the company is led by CEO Greg Abel (with Buffett as Chairman Emeritus). Its businesses include GEICO and other major insurance operations, BNSF Railway, Berkshire Hathaway Energy, and dozens of well-known brands such as Dairy Queen, See’s Candies, and Benjamin Moore. It also maintains a large portfolio of publicly traded stocks (notably Apple, American Express, and Coca-Cola).

**USD-BRK-B** refers to the company’s Class B common shares (ticker **BRK.B**), which trade on the New York Stock Exchange in U.S. dollars. These shares offer a more accessible way for individual investors to own a piece of Berkshire compared with the much higher-priced Class A shares. text:
Me: The Island of Lost Maps: A True Story of Cartographic Crime

Ai: The Island of Lost Maps is a fascinating work of investigative nonfiction that combines true crime, history, geography, and the unusual world of antique map collecting. Written by journalist Miles Harvey, the book investigates one of the most extraordinary cases of cultural theft in American history: the systematic stealing of rare, centuries-old maps from some of the most prestigious libraries and research institutions in the United States and Canada.
At the center of the story is Gilbert Joseph Bland Jr., an elusive antiques dealer from Florida who secretly removed valuable maps from rare books and archival collections, eventually becoming one of America's most prolific map thieves. His crimes went largely undetected for years, allowing him to steal and sell historically significant pieces of cartographic history.
Harvey reconstructs Bland's mysterious life, examining how he operated, how he managed to deceive librarians and researchers, and how the stolen maps entered the international marketplace. The investigation also explores the people who collect, trade, authenticate, and preserve antique maps, revealing a surprisingly secretive world driven by extraordinary wealth, historical fascination, and obsession.
Beyond the criminal investigation, the book offers an absorbing journey through the history of cartography. It explores the creation of early maps, the ambitions of explorers, the evolution of geographical knowledge, and the artistic craftsmanship involved in depicting a world that was once largely unknown. It also examines how maps have influenced exploration, commerce, warfare, politics, and humanity's understanding of the planet.

One of the book's most compelling themes is the relationship between knowledge and obsession. Harvey demonstrates that old maps are much more than geographical documents: they are historical artifacts that preserve the imagination, ambitions, mistakes, and discoveries of earlier civilizations.
At its heart, this is a book about theft, mystery, historical preservation, and the irresistible human desire to discover the unknown. It will particularly appeal to readers interested in true crime, rare books, antique collecting, exploration, cartography, and the hidden histories behind valuable cultural objects.
The book is especially interesting because it transforms an unusual case of library theft into a much larger exploration of history, art, geography, and human obsession.

San Francisco:

$95,000 − $36,000 rent − ~$4,750 state tax − $1,500 transit = ~$52,750

Houston:

$78,000 − $16,200 rent − $0 state tax − $9,500 car = ~$52,300

A difference of about $450 a year.
Yes, you read that right. In one city you earn $17,000 more, in the other your rent is half the price, and at the end of the year you end up basically in the same place.

(Before federal taxes, which are similar in both cases.)

The car is the expense nobody puts in the comparison. You pay it every month, it’s not in the job offer, and in Houston you don’t have a choice.

That said, some things money can’t measure: in San Francisco you can live without a car, and in Houston you can have a space where a whole life fits. No spreadsheet captures that.

Now imagine you get both offers today and have to decide by Friday.

🌉 San Francisco or 🤠 Houston?

And if you already live in one of them, tell me which expense surprised you the most when you moved.

🗣 I love this gritty, earthy, gutteral, pure rock & roll sound.  It is celebratory and electrifying.  I wish I found this album sooner.  It is wonderful. 

They took different routes, but both albums ended up in the same place in my heart.  Not sure why I'm not going to 9.  I certainly wouldn't say that's wrong.  8 is on the low side. 

Anyway, I'll go over the deluxe tracks now.

🤖 Big G, break it down🗯 
**The Southern Harmony and Musical Companion** is from 1992 (May 12 release on Def American). It was the follow-up to *Shake Your Money Maker* and the first album with Marc Ford on lead guitar (Jeff Cease was out) and Eddie Harsch on keyboards. They went into Southern Tracks in Atlanta in early 1992 with George Drakoulias again producing (alongside the band) and cut the bulk of it in about eight days—live tracks first, then overdubs. 

Chris has said they just wanted to get back in the studio after all the road time on the first record, and the new lineup gave them more tools and more confidence. The title comes from William Walker’s 1835 shape-note hymnal *The Southern Harmony*.

Nine of the ten songs are credited to the Robinson brothers. The closer, “Time Will Tell,” is a Bob Marley cover that they rearrange into something more New Orleans/gospel-tinged. “Remedy” was the big single and hit #1 on Mainstream Rock; so did “Sting Me,” “Thorn in My Pride,” and “Hotel Illness.” The album debuted at #1 on the Billboard 200 and went multi-platinum. 

A lot of listeners (and a fair number of critics) treat it as the point where the band fully arrived—looser, more gospel and percussion elements, stronger guitar interplay between Rich and Ford, and a denser, more lived-in sound than the debut. AllMusic and others called it bigger and more powerful than the first record, with the songs more incisive. Some reviews still noted the classic-rock debts, but most agreed the execution and songwriting carried it. Fan consensus often ranks it at or near the top of their catalog.

On the lyrics you flagged: for “Thorn in My Pride,” Chris has said the title is a play on “thorn in my side,” the lyrics are searching (“Who am I?”), and it came together quickly (he mentioned roughly 20 minutes at one point). Rich has called it a springboard for the rest of the record. It’s generally read as dealing with duality, ego, relationships that are both angel and devil, and the pressure of sudden success. 

For “Sometimes Salvation,” there isn’t as much direct commentary from the band in the usual interviews. The lyrics push back against “empty saviors,” vultures, and people who offer miracles without substance; the “lead a horse to water / faith is another matter” line and the “salvation in the eye of the storm” idea point toward rejecting false guidance while still looking for something real amid the mess. Listeners often tie it to toxic relationships or the cycles around addiction and recovery, but the band hasn’t spelled out a single definitive story for it the way they have for a few other songs.

It still gets played live a lot, and a deluxe/box set with remasters, outtakes, and a 1993 Houston show came out later. The gritty, earthy, gospel-tinged rock you like is exactly what a lot of people hear as their peak. “No Speak No Slave” and “My Morning Song” are frequent favorites for the guitar work and the lift between them.

[[[ I picked up the toxic relationship as a thread that goes through the entire set.]]]

Fair read. Toxic or at least dysfunctional relationships do run through a lot of these songs—Sting Me, Remedy, Thorn in My Pride, Bad Luck Blue Eyes Goodbye, Sometimes Salvation. The language keeps circling the same territory: people who are aloof or unreliable, empty saviors, pride getting in the way, bad luck blue eyes, the push-pull of wanting something that also hurts.
[continues➡️]

text:
My Friend: No, sir. I’ve already made arrangements to live close to my university in Houston.

Visa Officer: Does your cousin know you’re coming?

My Friend: Yes, sir. He knows about my admission.

Visa Officer: Has he offered you accommodation?

My Friend: He offered to accommodate me temporarily, but I intend to live near the university because of my academic schedule.

Visa Officer: Let me ask you something. If your brother is so successful, why doesn’t he send his own children to America instead of spending this money on you?

My Friend: His children already have their own educational arrangements, sir. He believes education is important, and he wants to help me achieve something meaningful with my life.

Visa Officer: What exactly do you intend to do after completing your Master’s degree?

My Friend: I intend to return home and establish a financial consulting firm. I also want to use my experience to help local businesses improve their financial management.

Visa Officer: What makes you think you will actually return?

My Friend: My career plans, professional experience, and family responsibilities are all back home, sir. This degree is part of my long-term plan, not an attempt to abandon everything I’ve built.

Visa Officer: You seem very confident about your plans. What if you receive a job offer in America after graduation?

My Friend: My immediate objective is to complete my programme and return home to pursue the business plans I’ve already discussed.

Visa Officer: Alright. One final question. You said your brother is sponsoring you because he believes in your potential. Has he ever sponsored anyone else in your family?

My Friend: Yes, sir. He sponsored our younger sister through university.

Visa Officer: And where is she now?

My Friend: She’s back home working as a pharmacist.

The officer stopped typing and looked at my friend for a few seconds.

Visa Officer: So your brother has already sponsored two siblings through higher education?

My Friend: Yes, sir.

Visa Officer: Interesting. What would you say if I told you that I have some concerns about your application?

My Friend: I would appreciate the opportunity to understand those concerns and clarify anything that isn’t clear, sir.

The officer looked through the documents again, picked up his keyboard, and typed something.

Visa Officer: Your academic history is good. Your financial documents are also here. However, I need you to understand that having a sponsor with money doesn’t automatically qualify you for a student visa.

My Friend: I understand, sir.

Visa Officer: Alright. Your passport will be retained for further processing. You’ll receive an update regarding your application.

My friend walked away from the counter without knowing whether he had passed or failed.

He had prepared for questions about his education, finances, and sponsor. But he wasn’t prepared for how thoroughly the officer would question his brother’s decision to sponsor him.

Now the question is: Was the visa officer simply doing his job, or were some of his questions unnecessarily personal?

text:
Visa Officer: Good morning. Why are you travelling to the United States?

My Friend: Good morning, sir. I’m travelling to pursue my Master’s degree in Business Administration at the University of Houston.

Visa Officer: Why did you choose the United States instead of studying in your home country?

My Friend: I researched several universities, sir, but the University of Houston offers a programme that aligns with my career goals. I also want international exposure and practical experience in business management.

Visa Officer: What did you study for your first degree?

My Friend: I studied Economics at the University of Lagos.

Visa Officer: What was your final CGPA?

My Friend: 4.21, sir.

Visa Officer: That’s a good result. When did you graduate?

My Friend: In 2023, sir.

Visa Officer: What have you been doing since graduation?

My Friend: I’ve been working as a financial analyst at a private investment company.

Visa Officer: How much do you earn monthly?

My Friend: Approximately $1,800.

Visa Officer: If you already have a good job, why are you leaving it to study in America?

My Friend: I don’t consider this a permanent departure from my career. I want to acquire advanced knowledge that will qualify me for more senior positions when I return.

Visa Officer: Who is paying for your education?

My Friend: My elder brother is sponsoring me, sir.

Visa Officer: What does your brother do?

My Friend: He’s a medical doctor and owns a private hospital.

Visa Officer: How long has he owned this hospital?

My Friend: Approximately seven years.

Visa Officer: Is he married?

My Friend: Yes, sir. He’s married with three children.

Visa Officer: So he has a wife, three children, a hospital to manage, and now he wants to spend over $50,000 educating his younger brother?

My Friend: Yes, sir. He offered to sponsor me because he believes in my potential. He’s always encouraged me to pursue further education.

Visa Officer: Why can’t your parents sponsor you?

My Friend: My parents are retired, sir. My brother is financially comfortable and volunteered to take responsibility for my education.

Visa Officer: How much does your brother earn monthly?

My Friend: His income varies, but he earns approximately $12,000 monthly from his medical practice and other business interests.

Visa Officer: Do you have evidence of his income?

My Friend: Yes, sir. I submitted his bank statements, hospital registration documents, and sponsorship letter.

Visa Officer: How much is your tuition?

My Friend: Approximately $35,000 per academic year.

Visa Officer: And how much have you budgeted for accommodation, feeding, transportation, and other expenses?

My Friend: Around $22,000 annually, sir.

Visa Officer: That’s approximately $57,000 every year. Are you telling me your brother is prepared to spend over $100,000 on your education?

My Friend: Yes, sir. He has made financial arrangements to cover my tuition and living expenses.

Visa Officer: What happens if he loses his business tomorrow?

My Friend: He has sufficient savings and other investments to support my education, sir.

Visa Officer: Have you ever travelled outside your country?

My Friend: Yes, sir. I’ve visited Ghana, South Africa, and the United Kingdom.

Visa Officer: Did you return from all those trips?

My Friend: Yes, sir. I returned before my permitted stay expired.

Visa Officer: Do you have relatives living in the United States?

My Friend: Yes, sir. I have a cousin who lives in Dallas.

Visa Officer: Is that where you intend to stay?
