By Susanne Delaney

Spare a thought for @RTE today, who have been forced to report on the ever-growing religious persecution of Christians by people who worship Mohammed. It must have damn near killed them, especially to specifically report that the European Union has been criticised for its handling of (ever-growing) Christian persecution across Europe—persecution that RTÉ does not provide details about.

Christian persecution (to a manipulated degree) is on their agenda today because churches will be lit up in red across Ireland this evening to highlight mass slaughter occurring in parts of the world (Red Wednesday).

The journalist appears to downplay the Islamic element by stating, "Some of it is religiously motivated."

Please, though, tell me: what other motivations could there possibly be?
She does not elaborate. Naturally.

She mentions nothing about a spate of recent attacks on Christian relics and places of worship in Ireland. The stabbing attack on chaplain Father Paul Murphy at an army barracks in Galway in 2024 is ignored also.

This article would be an apt opportunity to highlight warnings on the Department of Foreign Affairs website strongly advising Irish people that travelling to certain countries (like Somalia) is highly dangerous for Christians (because then the public might inquire as to why we are importing and housing so many from there).

To note, recent reports summarising county council figures indicate that Somali and Afghan (as well as Romanian and Polish) households combined account for nearly 13% of ALL social housing allocations.

The journalist in this report also does not mention priests being murdered and beautiful cathedrals and churches being set on fire in countries like France (by those who are new to the parish and those who are first-generation immigrants).

Terror attacks in Europe also do not feature. The reader is fed an "it is happening far away, not here" narrative.

To be unambiguous—for all the media propaganda about "Islamophobia," Christians remain the most persecuted of peoples.

Over 220 million face persecution daily. So, indeed, the future looks bright for us here in the EU, with its growing Islamic population, right?

RTÉ does mention aspects of the ACN (Aid to the Church in Need) report, which states, "Across Africa and Asia, Christians are part of a mass exodus from the lands where they have been present for centuries."

That part of the narrative is useful for state propagandists RTÉ—as it weaponises the reader's empathy around migrants coming into Ireland.

However, if you are a keen observer, you will note many of the migrants attempting to claim asylum here are Muslims, and of course, a portion are also falsely claiming to be Christians.

Despite this RTÉ article today, we aren't allowed to be legitimately concerned that this could one day happen to us without being labelled "racist" [note: Islam is not a race!], "far-right," or "Islamophobes."

That would be an affront to the people doing the murdering and, well, because "diversity is our strength."

Today, former EU Commissioner Mairead McGuinness will launch the ACN report in Dublin (another reason RTÉ cannot ignore this issue).

The report lists many geopgraphical areas of concern, such as northern Mozambique, where an Islamist insurgency has targeted communities in Cabo Delgado since 2017. Estimates put murders at around 1,000. Attacks involve beheadings and kidnappings.

RTÉ reports Islamist groups are controlling Burkina Faso and Mali, with "some Christian communities" (RTÉ does not want to specify females) being forced to abide by Islamic dress codes, while others have suffered killings.

As an Irish follower of Jesus Christ, I offer my thoughts and prayers to those affected, and use this opportunity to again warn Irish people of the dangers of allowing Islam to grow in our Christian society. It won't end well. You have been warned.

text:
Catholic Fun Fact: (for my new friends at @novafbclub ) Shelly Pennefather is a former All-American basketball star who left a lucrative professional career in 1991 to become a cloistered Catholic nun, now known as Sister Rose Marie of the Queen of Angels. Raised in a devout Catholic military family, her faith shaped every stage of her life and athletic career.
Pennefather attended Catholic high schools, winning three state titles at Bishop Machebeuf High School in Denver (70–0) and a fourth at Notre Dame High School in Utica, New York (26–0).
She chose to play for Villanova University, the oldest Catholic university in Pennsylvania, where she won the 1987 Wade Trophy as the top female college basketball player.
While playing professionally in Japan, where she was offered a $200,000 annual contract, she made a promise to God to volunteer at Mother Teresa's convent in Norristown, Pennsylvania, if her struggling team made the playoffs. After a buzzer-beater secured their spot, she fulfilled her promise and felt a deeper spiritual calling.
On June 8, 1991, at age 25, she walked away from basketball and joined the Order of Saint Clare (Poor Clares) at their monastery in Alexandria, Virginia. Taking her final solemn vows in 1997, Sister Rose Marie embraced strict enclosure, poverty, and silence. She sleeps on a straw mattress for roughly four hours a night, goes barefoot, fasts regularly, and never leaves the monastery except for medical emergencies. Under her order's rules, she communicates with the outside world primarily through letters and receives only two family visits a year behind a screen. She is permitted to physically embrace her family just once every 25 years, a milestone she celebrated during her silver jubilee in June 2019.
God bless Sister Rose Marie!

text:
PFAS are a group of more than 14,000 compounds that manufacturers began using in the 1940s. They’re designed to be strong and long-lasting thanks to their carbon-fluorine chemical bonds.

These chemicals were created with good intentions — to keep people safe, offer convenience, and toughen up products to resist heat, oil, stains, grease and water.

We interact with forever chemicals through a long list of everyday products, including:

Nonstick cookware
Waterproof clothing
Cosmetics and personal care products
Food packaging
Stain-resistant carpets, rugs and furniture

Collected data suggests that forever chemicals can bring harmful health effects. But how much these environmental toxins impact your health varies depending on:

-How much and how often you’re exposed
-Your age, sex, ethnicity, health and genetics

Nothing in medicine ever happens by itself. Exposure to these chemicals is probably not the only reason you develop a chronic disease, but it can contribute.

You may be exposed to forever chemicals when you:

-Use products that contain PFAS
-Eat food packaged in PFAS-treated material
-Drink contaminated water
-Eat fish from contaminated water
-Eat food grown near factories making or using PFAS
-Use cosmetics and healthcare products packaged in PFAS-treated containers

Repeated or high exposure to PFAS chemicals can cause them to build up in your blood. Today, nearly all people in the U.S. have a detectable level of PFAS in their blood. High levels may lead to health issues such as:

-Increased cancer risk
-Slowed development in children
-Reduced immune function
-Reproductive challenges
-Thyroid issues

text:
HSE Allows Minors Abortion Without Parental Knowledge

Should a Parent Be Informed and Have Input?

Official HSE guidance allows teenagers as young as 15, and in some cases younger, to be offered an abortion without their parents’ knowledge or consent. For 16 and 17-year-olds, a doctor may proceed if satisfied the young person understands the information and can give valid consent. 

For those aged 15 or under, the same is possible “if there are exceptional circumstances and an assessment has been completed.” Parents are merely “encouraged” to be involved, they are not required to be informed.

This policy has been public since 2019. It appears in HSE booklets on medical and surgical abortion and on the HSE website. Doctors must still report certain cases to Tusla, but these obligations do not require informing parents of the abortion itself. Ending a pregnancy is not a routine medical procedure. It is permanent, carries physical and psychological risks, and for a minor raises serious questions of maturity, coercion, and long-term consequences. 

In almost every other area of significant medical decision-making for children under 16, Irish law and HSE policy default to parental involvement. The statutory right of those over 16 to consent to treatment does not automatically justify treating abortion as uniquely exempt from ordinary safeguards for younger teenagers. “Exceptional circumstances” remains entirely undefined in public HSE materials. No clear criteria or transparent process exist, leaving wide discretion to individual doctors with little external accountability. 

Supporters argue that mandatory notification could endanger girls in abusive homes. Those risks are real. Child-protection law already exists for such cases: Tusla can intervene where there is evidence of abuse or risk. The difficulty is that the guidance does not limit non-notification to suspected abuse. It allows secrecy based on the minor’s preference and a doctor’s assessment of capacity, even in the absence of protective concerns.

Capacity is not a binary switch. Many 15 and 16-year-olds lack the life experience and future-oriented judgment to fully weigh a decision of this magnitude under the pressure of an unplanned pregnancy. Parents remain legally accountable for their children’s welfare. 
A system that systematically excludes them from a decision this consequential, while still holding them responsible afterwards, creates a clear inconsistency.The presumption should be that parents are informed and involved, with narrow, defined, and reviewable exceptions only where notification would place the child at risk of serious harm.

 “Exceptional circumstances” should be specified and subject to oversight rather than left to individual discretion. Parents are not bystanders. On a decision this significant, they should not be treated as optional.
So Should a parent be informed and have input?

Even the history of Britain's internal conflicts and the Irish struggle for independence demonstrates that many political and social conflicts have deep roots in historical grievances, economic inequality, discrimination, and the struggle to preserve national identity and sovereignty. The wounds left by these conflicts have not entirely healed in the collective memory of the Irish people.

Now, imagine that every country in the world, including European countries, surrounded its borders with high fences and refused entry to foreigners. Imagine that you, too, were denied entry to Britain or any other country, just as you advocate restricting the entry of others.

Under those circumstances, what practical skills, professional expertise, or economic and social solutions could you offer to serve the people of your own country and city?

Apart from opposing immigrants, what exactly do you propose to create jobs, increase incomes, strengthen industries, expand trade, improve public services, and solve the real problems facing ordinary citizens?

Opposing immigration, by itself, is not an economic, social, or development policy.

If you and your supporters genuinely care about the public interest, you should be able to explain how your proposed policies would improve people's lives and what consequences they would have for the economy, the labor market, and international relations.

Concern about immigration and the preservation of national culture is not necessarily racism. However, when fear, hatred, or prejudice against other people is exploited as a tool to attract attention, gain popularity, or pursue personal interests, it can seriously damage social cohesion and the public good.

My fundamental question to you is this: Is your real objective to serve the public and solve people's problems, or simply to gain attention and recognition by opposing immigrants?

In my view, anyone who claims to defend the interests of the people should be capable of presenting practical, measurable solutions based on economic and social realities.

Public service requires knowledge, responsibility, constructive ideas, and tangible results—not merely creating divisions between people to gain personal, social, or political influence.

text:
Artificial intelligence has not so far produced a clean story of mass unemployment. Aggregate employment in developed countries remains broadly stable, and recent assessments have found limited evidence that AI has shifted the headline numbers. But a troubling change may be hiding beneath the surface: the quiet weakening of the first rung of the career ladder.

The most worrisome evidence is showing up exactly where we should expect it first: in early-career hiring. A working paper released in November 2025 by the Stanford Digital Economy Lab found that workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations experienced a 16% relative decline in employment after the spread of generative AI, even after controlling for other factors that might affect firms’ employment decisions. An Anthropic report from March 2026 provides suggestive evidence for a similar conclusion.

More experienced workers in those same occupations did not suffer the same decline. Employment is also not declining in the entry-level jobs with low AI exposure. The concern is specific to early-career jobs that are exposed to AI.

That is not a minor signal. It suggests that firms may be using AI to substitute for the junior tasks through which people traditionally gain their first foothold—at least for those in jobs where generative AI is used extensively, like software developers, customer service representatives, computer programmers, and information systems managers.

The time is now to make changes in the way we train, prepare, and support young people who are about to enter the workforce. Educational institutions need to reorient for the era of an AI-augmented workforce. Governments must incentivize businesses to hire and train early-career workers. Businesses, in turn, need to recognize the importance of developing a long-term workforce experienced in AI—a process that begins with entry-level workers. And students themselves should take on the responsibility of not only becoming AI fluent but learning how to apply that knowledge in various fields.

In short, we must change the way we have traditionally thought of entry-level work.

This is especially true because the broader labor market for recent graduates is also softening. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported that in the fourth quarter of 2025, the unemployment rate for recent college graduates rose to 5.6%, while the underemployment rate (the share of graduates working in jobs that typically do not require a college degree) reached 42.5%, its highest level since the covid pandemic. No single statistic can prove that AI is the sole cause of that deterioration. Hiring in general is way down post-pandemic, and young people are particularly vulnerable to the slowdown. But it would be a mistake to ignore the possibility that AI is accelerating an already difficult transition from school to work.

Behind these statistics is a great deal of personal distress. Recent graduates today often submit hundreds of applications before they receive a single offer, and surveys consistently find elevated rates of anxiety, financial precarity, and burnout among young workers in extended job searches. If AI quietly closes the door on typical early jobs, people will pay the price in delayed independence, postponed family formation, and the sense that their first serious professional efforts have been refused.

It also matters because entry-level jobs are part of the economy’s training system. Junior analysts learn which numbers can be trusted. Young software developers learn how production systems fail. New marketers learn how customers behave outside the neat language of dashboards.

Early-career legal and financial staff learn how rules, judgment, deadlines, and human relationships actually interact. If AI absorbs more of the drafting, triage, coding, summarizing, and administrative preparation that once helped train entry-level workers, firms may become more efficient in the short run while society becomes less capable in the longer run.

The right way to improve the skills of young workers is not to tell them, “Learn to code.” That advice, which shaped more than a decade of federal initiatives and university expansion, rested on the premise that coding was a stable, scalable skill almost anyone could learn and parlay into a middle-class job. The premise no longer holds. The layer of work AI handles well—translating a specification into routine code, reproducing standard patterns, debugging predictable errors—is precisely the layer that “learn to code” programs were built around.

Supervising AI systems in their work is now a much more relevant skill. So understanding the outputs AI systems produce will become very important.

To help people develop such skills, we should require universities, community colleges, and professional programs to embed AI literacy, data literacy, prompt-based workflow skills, verification skills, and domain judgment into ordinary degrees. Every graduate should know how to use AI tools, check their output, understand their limits, and combine them with human expertise. This matters even for graduates entering occupations that look relatively safe from AI, such as those in health care. Almost every job contains tasks—drafting, summarizing, scheduling, research, basic data work, routine communication—for which AI is already a substantial productivity tool.

The competition most young workers will experience is not human versus machine but colleague versus AI-augmented colleague. For most young workers, the realistic path to making themselves valuable is not to avoid AI but to become fluent in the technology and combine that with domain judgment, contextual reasoning, and human relationship skills. To this end, schools should emphasize paid co-ops, apprenticeships, and employer-linked projects so students build judgment in real workplaces before they graduate.

Governments should also create targeted tax credits, wage subsidies, and training grants for employers that hire early-career workers into structured, AI-augmented roles. The architecture for this kind of conditional, behavior-linked subsidy already exists in US tax policy. What is missing is a version of these instruments built specifically around early-career AI-augmented work.

Firms, for their part, should stop making hiring decisions based only on short-run cost savings from AI. Young workers are not valuable only for the tasks they perform this quarter. Their value lies in learning, skill formation, institutional memory, and future productivity. Entry-level hiring is not just an expense. It is an investment in the future stock of judgment inside the firm. The most effective AI-augmented senior workforce of the late 2030s will be drawn overwhelmingly from the junior cohort of today. Firms that automate away the learning stage may improve their immediate margins but find themselves, a decade from now, without anyone who understands how their own AI-driven workflows actually behave.

Students graduating this spring and next face a tough labor market in transition. AI fluency is becoming a commodity. Domain expertise without AI fluency is being outpaced. The combination is what is genuinely scarce. The mechanical engineer with knowledge of manufacturing and AI proficiency; the software programmer with knowledge of financial services who is also a whiz at AI—these are the types of people who will be in demand.

Georgios Petropoulos is an assistant professor at the USC Marshall School of Business. His research focuses on the implications of information technologies for innovation, competition policy, and labor markets.

text:
Negative Feedback and Presence Controls

Negative feedback (NFB) affects tube amplifier gain, distortion, speaker damping, frequency response and playing feel.

Presence controls adjust high-frequency feedback, changing brightness and attack independently of preamp tone controls.

How negative feedback works

Part of the output-transformer’s signal returns to an earlier stage in opposing phase, reducing gain, distortion and output impedance.

Closed-loop gain:

A_CL = A/(1 + Aβ)

A = open-loop gain; β = feedback factor.

Example: A = 100, β = 0.05 gives ~16.7.

Feedback becomes less effective during clipping.

Speaker damping

Negative feedback lowers output impedance, increasing electrical speaker damping.

DF = Speaker impedance / Amplifier output impedance

With an 8-ohm speaker:

2-ohm output impedance = DF 4.

0.5-ohm output impedance = DF 16.

Greater damping generally produces tighter bass. Less feedback permits greater amplifier-speaker interaction.

Presence controls

Traditional presence controls reduce high-frequency negative feedback.

Turning presence up increases upper-frequency response, adding bite and perceived pick attack.

Turning it down reduces brightness.

Unlike treble controls, presence operates within the power amplifier’s feedback circuit.

What guitarists hear

Distortion - Reduced during clean operation.

Bass - Greater electrical damping.

Headroom - Changes in gain and clipping behavior.

Attack - Changes in transient response.

Playing feel - Less feedback can feel more open and responsive.

Six vintage amplifier examples

Fender 5F1 Champ - No global feedback

~5 W, 1 × 6V6GT, 5Y3GT. Local feedback only. Early breakup and responsive dynamics.

Fender 5E3 Deluxe - No global feedback

~12 W, 2 × 6V6GT, 5Y3GT. Thick overdrive, compression and less controlled response.

Fender 5F6-A Bassman - Global feedback and presence

~45 W, 2 × 5881, GZ34. Strong attack, substantial clean headroom and adjustable bite.

Marshall JTM45 - Global feedback and presence

~30-45 W, commonly 2 × KT66, GZ34. Dynamic overdrive, strong midrange and adjustable presence.

Vox AC30 - No conventional global feedback

~30 W, 4 × EL84, GZ34 in classic versions. Bright upper midrange and responsive overdrive. Its Cut control differs from presence.

Fender Twin Reverb AB763 - Global feedback

~85 W, 4 × 6L6GC, silicon rectification. Substantial clean headroom, firm bass and controlled response.

These characteristics reflect complete amplifier designs.

Amplifier stability

Frequency-dependent phase shifts can cause negative feedback to become effectively positive, producing oscillation or ringing.

Designers maintain stability through appropriate feedback levels, compensation and transformer design.

Vintage versus modern

Vintage amplifiers used fixed feedback networks, traditional presence controls or no global feedback.

Modern designs may offer adjustable feedback, presence and resonance/depth controls for additional frequency shaping.

Digital modeling can also simulate these interactions.

The essential distinction

Negative feedback reduces gain and distortion while improving speaker damping.

Presence controls reduce high-frequency feedback, increasing brightness and perceived attack.

The complete amplifier and speaker determine the sound.

text:
Rectifier Tubes Versus Solid-State Rectification

Rectifiers convert alternating current (AC) from a guitar amplifier’s power transformer into pulsating direct current (DC). Filter capacitors smooth this voltage to supply the amplifier’s tubes. Rectifier design influences headroom, compression, distortion and playing response, particularly when an amplifier is driven hard.

How rectification works

The rectifier produces pulsating DC, which filter capacitors, chokes and resistors smooth into the amplifier’s high-voltage supply (B+). Tube rectifiers generally produce greater voltage drop than silicon diodes, affecting supply voltage as current demand increases.

Three classic rectifier tubes

5Y3GT - Directly heated, 5 V, 2 A heater. Higher voltage drop, commonly used in smaller amplifiers such as the Fender Champ.

5U4GB - Directly heated, 5 V, 3 A heater. Higher current capability, used in larger amplifier power supplies.

GZ34/5AR4 - Indirectly heated, 5 V, 1.9 A heater. Lower voltage drop and substantial current capability. Used in Fender, Vox and Marshall amplifiers.

Silicon diodes - Semiconductor rectifiers requiring no heater power, with approximately 0.7-1.1 V forward drop per conducting diode.

Actual voltage drop depends on current and circuit design.

Understanding power-supply sag

Sag occurs when B+ voltage temporarily decreases as current demand increases. A strong guitar chord can increase output-stage current, causing voltage losses. As demand falls, voltage recovers.

Tube rectifiers can contribute to sag through their effective resistance. Silicon diodes generally produce less voltage drop, although their power supplies can still exhibit sag.

What guitarists hear

Breakup - Increasing signal produces audible distortion.

Headroom - Available clean output before significant clipping.

Compression - Reduced differences between signal peaks.

Harmonics - Additional frequencies from nonlinear amplification.

Pick attack - Response to playing dynamics.

Five classic amplifier examples

Fender 5F1 Champ - 5Y3GT

Approximately 5 W. Early breakup, compressed overdrive and responsive dynamics. Its single-ended output stage contributes substantially.

Fender 5F6-A Bassman - GZ34

Approximately 45 W. Strong clean output, dynamic overdrive and classic American blues-rock character.

Fender Deluxe Reverb - GZ34/5AR4

Approximately 22 W. Clean, articulate response with progressive overdrive when pushed.

Vox AC30 - GZ34

Approximately 30 W in classic tube-rectified versions. Bright upper midrange, harmonic complexity and responsive overdrive.

Fender Twin Reverb - Silicon Diodes

Approximately 85 W in blackface versions. Substantial clean headroom, firm bass and clear treble, particularly useful for clean guitar and pedals.

These characteristics reflect complete amplifier designs, not rectifiers independently.

Vintage versus modern

Vintage amplifiers frequently used tube rectifiers, although silicon rectification became established in classic designs.

Modern amplifiers often use silicon diodes for low voltage drop, reliability and reduced heater demand. Boutique designs may retain tube rectifiers or offer switchable rectification.

Interchangeability and safety

Rectifiers are not automatically interchangeable. Heater current, B+ voltage, transformer capacity and filter capacitor limits must be verified. Silicon replacements can significantly raise B+.

The essential distinction

Rectifiers do not amplify guitar signals. They shape the amplifier’s power supply.

The 5Y3, 5U4 and GZ34 have different voltage-drop and current-handling characteristics. Silicon diodes generally provide lower losses and firmer voltage.

The complete power supply, output stage, transformers and speaker ultimately determine the sound.

text:
Remember when the Biden administration, DOJ, and FBI repeatedly declared white supremacy the greatest terrorist threat facing America?

While Americans were being told whom to fear, the country was undergoing profound changes to its borders, culture, institutions, and national identity.

The question is no longer simply what government called a threat. It's who will be allowed to challenge what is happening without being branded one.

THE NARRATIVE

The statements were unmistakable.

In April 2021, Biden declared white-supremacist terrorism the most lethal terrorist threat to the homeland. In June, at Tulsa, he doubled down: "Not ISIS, not al Qaeda—white supremacists."

Attorney General Merrick Garland and FBI Director Christopher Wray also repeatedly identified racially motivated violent extremism as a major domestic security concern.

These were declarations from the highest levels of government. Their political consequences deserve serious scrutiny.

THE DANGEROUS DISTINCTION

There is a fundamental difference between violent extremism and defending America's borders, sovereignty, traditions, constitutional principles, and national interests.

Yet the progressive left increasingly blurs that distinction.

Question immigration policy? Far-right.

Demand assimilation? Xenophobic.

Defend traditional values? Extremist.

Prioritize American citizens? Nationalist—as though that were an accusation.

When political labels replace arguments, dissent itself becomes the target.

EUROPE'S WARNING

Look across the Atlantic. Britain, Ireland, and France offer important warnings about growing tensions surrounding immigration, national identity, cultural integration, and political dissent.

Different countries, different circumstances—but a common concern: expanding government discretion over protest and public expression.

When peaceful dissent becomes subject to increasingly broad restrictions, ordinary citizens have reason to be vigilant.

THE LABELING MACHINE

As Americans resist policies they believe threaten their culture, institutions, economic security, and national sovereignty, expect the familiar labels:

Racist. Xenophobic. White supremacist. Far-right. Domestic extremist.

The political objective is straightforward: portray resistance as intolerance rather than confront legitimate grievances. Discredit opposition, intimidate dissent, and make citizens think twice before speaking.

AMERICA FIRST IS NOT RACISM

American nationalism is a civic principle, not a racial test.

Our Constitution, laws, institutions, and shared national identity form the foundation of the Republic. Americans of every race and background have an equal stake in preserving them.

Citizenship carries responsibilities: loyalty to our constitutional order, respect for the rule of law, and commitment to the country we share.

Religious freedom is protected by the Constitution. The oath of public office is to the Constitution, not a particular religious book. Our founding framework is the standard, regardless of faith.

THE LINE AMERICANS MUST NOT CROSS

The greatest danger is a country where citizens become afraid to defend their own national identity.

A government that treats peaceful opposition as extremism, patriotism as suspicion, and accountability as a threat ultimately undermines the freedoms it claims to protect.

America should recognize Europe's warning before it becomes our reality.

The right to disagree is protected by our Constitution, not granted by political parties, government agencies, or ideological movements.

text:
Is Indiana Becoming America's Next Frontier in Autonomous Warfare?
Rolls-Royce, Purdue University, and a New Drone Testing Network Could Be Building Something Much Bigger Than Anyone Realizes

November 18, 2026

While much of the world's attention is focused on Ukraine's increasingly sophisticated drone attacks deep inside Russia, something remarkable is taking shape in the American Midwest.

Indiana, better known for manufacturing, agriculture, and automobile racing, is quietly assembling many of the ingredients needed to become a major center for the next generation of autonomous aircraft.

And the interesting part?

Most of the pieces are already there.

Rolls-Royce, Purdue University, the U.S. military, and a newly established 224-mile drone testing corridor are creating an unusual concentration of aerospace research, manufacturing, and military testing capabilities.

The question is whether Indiana is simply benefiting from several independent developments or witnessing the beginnings of something far more significant.

The Ukraine Connection

The war in Ukraine has demonstrated something military planners can no longer ignore.

Unmanned aircraft are changing warfare faster than traditional military procurement systems can comfortably adapt.

Ukraine's domestically produced FP-1 long-range attack drones demonstrate how relatively inexpensive aircraft can threaten refineries, military installations, and industrial infrastructure hundreds of miles from the battlefield.

Meanwhile, jet-powered drones, autonomous navigation, electronic warfare, and increasingly sophisticated coordinated attacks are transforming the battlefield.

A weapon that works effectively today may encounter an entirely new countermeasure six months from now.

The pace of technological adaptation is becoming almost as important as the weapons themselves.

And the United States is paying attention.

Enter Rolls-Royce — In Indianapolis

In August 2026, Rolls-Royce celebrated the completion of a $1 billion investment in its Indiana manufacturing, assembly, and engine-testing facilities.

This was a decade-long modernization program, not a sudden response to the war in Ukraine.

But the timing of its completion is remarkable.

Rolls-Royce's Indianapolis operations manufacture advanced military propulsion systems, while its LibertyWorks division develops next-generation engine technologies.

In June 2026, the U.S. Air Force confirmed that Rolls-Royce LibertyWorks had received a contract to develop propulsion technology for autonomous military aircraft.

These aren't necessarily the inexpensive, disposable drones Ukraine is launching into Russia.

They're part of a developing class of larger autonomous combat aircraft that may accompany piloted fighter jets, perform reconnaissance, carry weapons, and operate in increasingly dangerous environments.

Rolls-Royce also supplies engines for the Navy's MQ-25 Stingray unmanned aerial refueling aircraft.

The company is already involved in unmanned military aviation.

And Indiana is where much of its American defense propulsion expertise is concentrated.

Purdue University: The Missing Piece?

Here's where the story becomes particularly interesting.

Rolls-Royce has a $75 million, 10-year research alliance with Purdue University involving advanced propulsion technology.

Purdue is also a major participant in Indiana's rapidly expanding unmanned-aircraft research network.

In January 2026, the Federal Aviation Administration designated Indiana as one of America's newest unmanned-aircraft test sites.

Then, on October 29, Indiana launched its Midwest UAS Test Site at Terre Haute Regional Airport.

The centerpiece is an extraordinary testing network.

A drone corridor extending 224 miles through Indiana, approximately 15 miles wide.

It connects the Terre Haute and West Lafayette areas with Camp Atterbury and the Muscatatuck military training facility.

This is not simply an open field where hobbyists fly quadcopters.

It is a coordinated network intended to support advanced aviation research, military testing, autonomous operations, and the integration of unmanned aircraft into American airspace.

Purdue has already demonstrated a Windracers ULTRA autonomous cargo aircraft operating beyond visual line of sight within the corridor.

And its researchers are working toward something potentially more significant.

Allowing a single operator to supervise multiple autonomous aircraft simultaneously.

Think about that for a moment.

Instead of requiring a separate pilot or operator for every drone, future systems could allow one person to oversee an entire group of aircraft, with artificial intelligence handling portions of navigation, coordination, and flight management.

That has implications far beyond delivering cargo.

The Military Is Building Its Own Testing Capabilities

Just one day before Indiana's drone corridor officially opened, the U.S. Army announced another important development.

Camp Atterbury and Muscatatuck were designated premier testing ranges under the Army's Permissive Test Range Expansion Initiative.

The purpose is to expand access for commercial developers testing unmanned systems, counter-drone equipment, and other emerging military technologies.

Muscatatuck offers a particularly unusual testing environment.

Its simulated urban infrastructure allows engineers to study how drones and counter-drone systems function around buildings, complicated terrain, and other obstacles.

Camp Atterbury provides extensive training grounds and restricted airspace.

Put these developments together and Indiana now has access to several important parts of the autonomous aviation development process.

Research, propulsion engineering, manufacturing, civilian flight testing, and military evaluation.

All within the same state.

The Next Industrial Revolution May Have Wings

For decades, building advanced military aircraft required enormous factories, highly specialized labor, long development cycles, and massive government contracts.

Those requirements haven't disappeared.

But autonomous aircraft are introducing new possibilities.

Some systems can be produced more quickly, at lower costs, and updated more frequently than traditional military aircraft.

Artificial intelligence could eventually shorten development cycles further by improving design, simulation, testing, and operational analysis.

Imagine a future in which engineers develop a new propulsion system in Indianapolis, researchers test autonomous flight software at Purdue, aircraft undergo operational evaluation along Indiana's drone corridor, and military systems receive additional testing at Camp Atterbury or Muscatatuck.

That isn't an announced, unified Rolls-Royce program.

But Indiana is developing the infrastructure that could make such cooperation increasingly practical.

And that's the opportunity.

Why Rolls-Royce Matters

The economics of autonomous warfare could eventually create demand for enormous numbers of engines.

Not every drone needs a Rolls-Royce turbine.

Ukraine's inexpensive propeller-driven attack drones demonstrate that perfectly well.

But larger, faster, more capable autonomous aircraft require different propulsion technologies.

Range matters.

Fuel efficiency matters.

Thrust matters.

Cost matters enormously when military planners begin considering fleets of hundreds or thousands of aircraft.

Rolls-Royce is already developing propulsion systems for these emerging requirements.

Its Indianapolis manufacturing capabilities and Purdue research relationship provide a foundation for competing in that market.

There is an important distinction, however.

Rolls-Royce has confirmed autonomous-aircraft propulsion work, but there is no publicly confirmed contract connecting the company directly to Indiana's new drone corridor.

Nor is there evidence yet that the corridor itself will produce substantial additional revenue for Rolls-Royce.

The opportunity is real. The eventual financial payoff remains to be demonstrated.

Is Indiana at the Cutting Edge?

Indiana isn't the only state pursuing autonomous aviation.

Texas, North Dakota, New York, Alaska, and others have established important drone-testing and aerospace research operations.

But Indiana now possesses an unusually interesting combination of capabilities.

A major international aircraft engine manufacturer.

A world-class engineering university.

A federally designated drone-testing network.

Extensive military training and evaluation facilities.

An established industrial workforce.

And a growing relationship between civilian researchers and the defense industry.

These are not guarantees of future success.

They are, however, the foundations on which important aerospace industries can develop.

The Bigger Picture

Ukraine is teaching the world that autonomous warfare is not some distant science-fiction possibility.

It's already here.

The next question is which countries, companies, and regions will be capable of turning today's battlefield lessons into tomorrow's military systems.

Will they be the ones designing the aircraft?

Manufacturing the engines?

Developing the artificial intelligence?

Providing the testing environments?

Or somehow bringing all those capabilities together?

Indiana now has a foothold in every one of those areas, either through existing industry or its expanding research partnerships.

And Rolls-Royce is sitting squarely in the middle of an important part of that emerging ecosystem.

Perhaps the most interesting aspect of this story is that no single announcement explains it.

The FAA designation came in January.

The Rolls-Royce autonomous propulsion contract surfaced in June.

The company's billion-dollar modernization was completed in August.

The Army expanded its Indiana testing facilities in October.

And Purdue demonstrated autonomous flight in the new corridor before the month was over.

Each development has its own explanation.

Together, they tell a much larger story about the direction of American aerospace technology.

The future of military aviation may not be defined exclusively by the most advanced fighter jet.

It may also depend on which industrial centers can design, manufacture, test, and continuously improve enormous numbers of intelligent unmanned aircraft.

And Indiana is positioning itself to be part of that future.

The Hoosier State may be better known for building engines than flying drones.

It might soon be known for doing both.

text:
A 14-year-old in Mississippi can't vote, can't drink, can't sign a phone contract, but she can sign for life in prison like she's renewing a subscription. That's American justice doing mathematics without logic. 

She turned down 40 years like it was a lowball offer, and the jury gave her life instead.

Carly Gregg understood the assignment better than the adults did. Pew pew hidden behind her back like a prop. Camera stuffed inside the fridge like a director hiding a continuity error. Then the text to her stepdad: Are you almost home, honey? No panic, just stage direction. 

A generation raised on plot twists thinks real life needs a cliffhanger too. She even had a catchphrase ready: I put three in my mom and I got three more waiting for my stepdad. Catchphrase first, conscience later.

Then her lawyer stood up and blamed the antidepressant. Not the pew pew under the mattress. Not the three bullets. Not the fake honey text. The pill did it. If pills can do all that, pharmacies should come with prison warnings.

The jury watched the whole production and decided childhood ends the moment the crime gets scary. We don't rehabilitate children anymore, we warehouse them. We call it accountability because redemption sounds expensive.

She cried at guilty. She nodded at life. The performance was over. The audience had gone home.

text:
Gulf Shores Airport Gains 5 New Direct Flights From Allegiant Airline

Allegiant Travel Company, alongside Sun Country Airlines, has announced five new nonstop routes connecting Gulf Shores International Airport at Jack Edwards Field (GUF) to major destinations across the country. Scheduled to launch ahead of the summer travel season, Allegiant will offer direct service to Wichita, Kansas (ICT); Indianapolis, Indiana (IND); Little Rock, Arkansas (LIT); and Shreveport, Louisiana (SHV) beginning May 20, 2027. Additionally, Sun Country Airlines will begin nonstop service to Minneapolis-Saint Paul (MSP) on April 16, 2027. With introductory one-way fares starting as low as $49, these new connections significantly broaden options for travelers seeking convenient, low-cost access to Alabama’s white-sand beaches.

Fueling the Local Tourism Boom

The expansion of commercial service has served as a primary catalyst for the region’s tourism economy. Since commercial flights launched at Gulf Shores International Airport, approximately 176,000 total passengers have traveled through the terminal. Traffic reached historic highs, highlighted by June 2026 setting an all-time monthly record with over 34,000 passengers.

Passenger surveys indicate that 43% of travelers using the airport had never visited Alabama’s beaches prior to the arrival of commercial flights. By replacing grueling 14+ hour round-trip drives from key feeder markets with flights under 75 minutes, the airline has successfully introduced a new wave of visitors to the coast while helping establish Gulf Shores as a year-round destination.

Supporting Growth with a $15 Million Airport Expansion

To accommodate the rapid rise in flight volume and passenger traffic, Gulf Shores International Airport is undergoing a $15 million terminal expansion. Slated for completion to coincide with the new route launches, the upgraded terminal facility is engineered to process two simultaneous commercial aircraft operations.

Key enhancements to the passenger experience include:

Two initial operational gate areas.
An outdoor patio beyond security screening.
A dedicated mothers’ nursing room.
Expanded baggage claim carousels and larger curbside drop-off zones.
Upgraded retail, food, and beverage amenities, featuring local favorites such as Lucy Buffett’s LuLu’s.
Making Rental Cars and Short-Term Stays More Viable

Beyond air travel, Allegiant’s bundled vacation model has made ground transportation and local lodging far more accessible for visitors. By offering direct vacation packages combining flights, rental cars, and hotel deals through its booking platform, short-term hotel stays and quick weekend getaways have become increasingly viable for budget-conscious travelers.

To support seamless ground transit, the airport has partnered with major rental car providers, including Hertz and Dollar, operating on-site to handle growing passenger demand directly from the expanded queuing areas.

**Shop Mendoza too.** In superflex, a third starting QB is real currency. Some 2-QB teams with a hurt or benched starter will pay more for him than for any of your bench RBs. Mendoza plus an RB should land you a strong WR. Only do it if you're fine with Rodgers as your QB2 and no backup behind him.

**Hold Adams.** He's on IR with a ruptured hamstring. McVay said Adams underwent surgery on his hamstring and is expected to return "on the shorter end" of his six-to-10 week estimated timeline. That points to either November 25 against the Green Bay Packers or December 3 against the Kansas City Chiefs, right before your playoffs. He's free WR depth for the stretch run, and other managers will offer you almost nothing for him now. Keep him.

**Don't panic on Bowers.** The Raiders do not believe Brock Bowers suffered a major ankle injury, Ian Rapoport said, and Mike Florio reported that Bowers is expected to be able to play against the Denver Broncos in Week 11. Keep starting him. His floor is a lot lower than usual right now, so a cheap TE2 thrown into a bigger deal would be nice insurance.

**What to target.** Go after a WR on a team that throws a lot and has good playoff matchups in Weeks 15 to 17. Don't take a TD-dependent deep threat. McMillan, Collins and Tyson are all fine, but none of them is a weekly WR1. One proven target hog would turn your 4th-place team into a real contender.

If you send me the other managers' rosters, or tell me which WRs you're eyeing, I'll put together specific offers.

text:
Banning Israel’s Enemies 

It barely made the news, and I’m sure most people reading this don’t even know it occurred. Last week, France barred Yossi Dagan, head of the Samaria Regional Council, from entering the country because of his role in establishing settlements and his advocacy for Jewish communities in areas from which Israel withdrew in 2005. Dagan himself was evicted from his home by Israeli soldiers in 2005 and advocated, and successfully returned, to rebuild his town. Israeli authorities answered the next day by denying entry to Jean-Luc Mélenchon and Mathilde Panot, two French politicians whose public statements on Israel have included accusations that Israeli officials characterize as blood libels. 
Every sovereign state retains the authority to decide who may cross its borders, and that authority flows from the elementary duty of a government to shield its territory and its people from individuals it judges likely to produce disorder or lasting harm. Governments exercise this power daily through visa rules, watch lists, and border decisions that rarely attract attention until a high-profile case arises.
Countries invoke this power on concrete grounds. One argument in favor of selective bans holds that a government may refuse entry to people whose arrival would heighten domestic tensions or embolden groups that have already carried out attacks against local residents, particularly when the visitors have previously endorsed such violence or refused to condemn it. Another argument observes that a state may decline to host individuals who arrive with the announced purpose of manufacturing hostile coverage that weakens its security position or its standing with allies, since the obligation to maintain open borders does not extend to providing a platform for predetermined campaigns against the host country itself. These considerations appear in ordinary practice when nations limit entry for those linked to organized crime, extremist networks, or efforts to stage provocations that later circulate as evidence of official misconduct.
Arguments against routine bans also carry force in ordinary relations between states. One holds that excluding elected officials can convert ordinary policy disagreements into personal disputes that later complicate practical cooperation on intelligence sharing, trade, or joint military exercises among countries that otherwise maintain close ties. Another notes that selective exclusions risk appearing arbitrary when a government continues to admit other visitors who express equally sharp criticism, thereby inviting the charge that decisions rest on political convenience rather than any consistent standard applied to all comers. Diplomatic custom often favors allowing entry and then restricting activities inside the country, yet that approach fails when visitors design their programs precisely to generate conflict at the border or in sensitive areas.
Israel has applied these considerations unevenly in recent years and has repeatedly allowed entry to American politicians whose itineraries concentrated almost entirely on gathering material that casts Israeli actions in the most negative light available. Representative Ro Khanna traveled to the region and declined repeated offers from Israeli officials to meet families of hostages still held in Gaza or survivors of the October 7 massacre, electing instead a schedule built around visits to Palestinian communities in Judea and Samaria. During that visit his group was briefly stopped by local residents near a village in the southern hills, after which Khanna described the delay as a detention by armed settlers supported by soldiers, an account Israeli sources contested and that immediately generated headlines critical of Israeli policy. The episode supplied the material he sought, and the refusal to engage Israeli victims beforehand made the outcome predictable.

text:
Collapse Before Maturity: The Eight Cracks China Cannot Hide and Its Invisible Apocalypse
Mir Kamil Kashgarli
This article is about 17,000 words, too long for one reply, so here is the first part. I can continue with the rest in further messages.

Introduction: The Dark Twin of a Three-Thousand-Year-Old Strategy

The formula sealed in the first chapter of Sun Tzu’s Art of War forms the backbone of three thousand years of global strategic literature: “War is the art of deceit. When strong, appear weak; when weak, appear strong; when near, appear far; when far, appear near.” This sentence is not merely the title of an ancient book of war. It is a summary of the strategic wisdom of Chinese civilisation and remains the operational scaffolding of Beijing’s 21st-century foreign policy. From Mao’s “Long March” to Deng’s “hide your light, bide your time” doctrine, from Xi Jinping’s “Chinese Dream” rhetoric to the Belt and Road Initiative, at every stage we see different costumes of the same doctrine: conceal your intent, display your power out of proportion, package your weakness as strategy.

But at the very center of the doctrine lies a dark twin that it never states, even in its own sentences. A state that must constantly package weakness as strength is, over time, crushed under two exhausting burdens. The first is the energy spent actually covering up the weakness. The second is the permanent paranoia born of the worry that the weakness will one day be exposed. The more a country has to hide, the larger a memory, the broader a surveillance apparatus and the deeper a censorship infrastructure it must build. Backstage begins to consume more labour than the stage. The cunning player who cannot play an open game loses his breath under the weight of his own concealment.

The central claim of this article is that China today stands at exactly this threshold. On the surface, it is a dragon: the second-largest economy, the world’s largest navy, infrastructure projects spread across more than 140 countries under the Belt and Road. At its core it is a structure full of demographic, financial, institutional and spiritual cracks. None of these cracks is a catastrophe on its own. But when all of them move at the same time, feeding one another, an equation of rupture without precedent in history emerges.

China’s internal fracture matrix must be read along eight axes: demographic execution, the real estate bubble, epistemic crisis, the DNA of institutional corruption, the loneliness of the palace, asabiyyah fault lines on the periphery, Guangdong’s silent sense of separation, and the overextension trap. Each axis alone is a strategic limitation. But the eight working together produce for Beijing an equation that perhaps even Sun Tzu could not have foreseen: a civilisation suffocating on its own greatness.

The Law of Civilisations’ Collapse from Within: Ibn Khaldun, Bennabi and Three Historical Precedents

To understand China’s present, we need to stop at a crossroads where two thinkers join hands: Ibn Khaldun and Malik Bennabi.

When Ibn Khaldun wrote the Muqaddimah in 1377, the picture he saw around him was simple: Andalusia was melting away, Mamluk Egypt was tiring, and Tunisian dynasties were following one another. From this scene he formulated perhaps the boldest sociological law in human history. The decline of civilisations begins not with foreign invasion but with the unravelling of the inner fabric he called asabiyyah. Literally, asabiyyah means “feeling of solidarity,” but in Ibn Khaldun’s usage it is far broader: a society’s shared memory, its sense of common purpose, the moral bond between generations, the invisible glue that makes the word “we” truly meaningful.¹

When a society’s asabiyyah dissolves, collapse is inevitable, however high its outer walls, however numerous its army, however vast its economy. The external enemy is in fact a mechanical tool that clears the wreckage of a structure already rotted from within. It is not the one who “defeats” but the one who “empties.” This is why Ibn Khaldun says dynasties do not outlive three generations. The founding generation comes from the desert with its asabiyyah, the second generation manages prosperity, and the third is born into prosperity and loses asabiyyah. By the third generation, the smallest external blow is enough to trigger destruction.

Five hundred and seventy years later, in Algeria in 1948, Malik Bennabi wrote a modern variant of this diagnosis. In The Conditions of Civilisation, Bennabi asked a startling question: “Why are some peoples colonised while others resist?” The radicalism of the question was that colonisation is not done by the outside power, but is made possible by internal fragility. Bennabi called this fragility colonisabilité (colonizability).² When a people falls into intellectual fatigue, its institutions rot, and the bond between generations is broken, and only then do outside colonisers come. Colonialism is not a cause but a result, the external manifestation of an internal disease.

If we pause where the two diagnoses meet and look at history, three precedents offer a mirror image of China’s present position and a measure of the speed of decay.

The first precedent is Late Rome and the Severan Dynasty (AD 193–235). Under the Severans, Rome was at its peak externally: borders stretching from Britain to Mesopotamia, the world’s strongest army, the denarius as a global reserve currency. But the internal dissolution had already begun. The denarius’s silver content had been cut from 50% to 5%, which in today’s terms is like the Federal Reserve cutting the dollar’s value to a tenth at once. The mercenary class had seized political decision-making, and provincial asabiyyah had severed ties of loyalty to the center. From the assassination of Severus Alexander in 235 to Rome’s final collapse in 476, about three centuries passed.³

The second precedent is the last half-century of the Sasanian Empire (590–651). When Khosrow Parviz took the throne, the Sasanian state was at the peak of four centuries of hegemony: it took Jerusalem in 614 and Alexandria in 619. But the founding alliance between Persian and Parthian elites was slowly dissolving.⁴ In February 628, Khosrow Parviz was killed by his own son Kavad II. In the following fourteen years, twelve different rulers sat on the throne, most of them assassinated within months. When Khalid ibn al-Walid entered Ubulla in 633, and when Sa’d ibn Abi Waqqas scattered the Persian army at Qadisiyyah in 636, the Islamic armies were carrying away the wreckage of a structure already dissolved from within. From the threshold of collapse to final collapse took only 14 years.

The third precedent is the Late Qing Dynasty (1839–1912). On the eve of the Opium Wars, the Qing was at the peak of the world in population, economy and territory. But it had been rotting from within for a century. The ossified examination system of the Confucian bureaucracy had turned talented cadres into windbags, and the drain of silver reserves through the opium trade had dried up the treasury. When British ships came to Canton, they technically did not fight China. They settled the final account of a structure already dissolved from within. Collapse time: 73 years.

The speed scale these three precedents offer is this: Rome 300 years, Sasanian 14 years, Qing 70 years. These durations are not coincidental. The time from a civilisation’s internal decay to its final collapse is directly proportional to the “feedback speed” of its era. In Rome, news from Britain took weeks to reach the capital. In the Qing, it took months by ship. Today, global finance moves in seconds, capital flows in minutes, and a spark on social media becomes a fire overnight. The calendar of an internal dissolution cycle at 21st-century speed is closer to the Sasanian side than to Rome’s.

China today stands not at the beginning but in the middle of an internal dissolution cycle in which Ibn Khaldun’s and Bennabi’s diagnoses operate simultaneously. Each of the eight axes below is a separate channel of this cycle.

Still to translate: the eight axes (demographics, real estate, epistemic crisis, corruption, the palace, the periphery, Guangdong, overextension), the synthesis, the “Five Strategic Axes for the Turkic World” and the footnotes. Tell me which part to do next, or whether you’d prefer a short brief of the whole article instead.

This is an analytical and opinion piece with many statistics and predictions that I have only translated, not verified. If you publish any of the figures, check them against the sources in the footnotes.

text:
‘Steve Jobs ruined everything with the iPhone’: Tech billionaire Palmer Luckey gets real on what really killed the 10,000-hour rule | Nick Lichtenberg, Fortune

Palmer Luckey has a complaint about the iPhone, and he took it to Steve Jobs’s biographer.

“Steve Jobs ruined everything with the iPhone,” Luckey, the Oculus inventor and Anduril cofounder, tells Walter Isaacson in an episode of Isaacson’s podcast The Builders airing Tuesday, an excerpt of which was shared exclusively with Fortune. “We’re still suffering the impacts of his incredible product design.”

Luckey, worth an estimated $5.9 billion according to Forbes, offered an argument about skill: the iPhone made technology so easy to learn that there’s nothing left to get good at, and every product since has copied it. Luckey founded Oculus in 2012, and Facebook bought it in 2014 for more than $2 billion. He left in 2017 to found Anduril, a defense company last valued at $61 billion. Last year, Anduril and Meta teamed up to build augmented- and virtual-reality gear for the U.S. Army, and Luckey recently partnered with the dire wolf and woolly mammoth-cloning entrepreneur Ben Lamm to breed genetically engineered clone dogs for military use, via a company called Warhound.

The 10-minute ceiling

Isaacson opened with a theory that the greatest advances in tech come at the human-machine interface, from Doug Engelbart’s mouse through the graphical interface and Jobs, “maybe culminating with Neuralink and chips in our brain.”

Before the iPhone, Luckey responded, “there was an understanding that technology was something that could multiply your output.” He pointed to Jobs’s own line about the computer as a “bicycle for the mind.” But the iPhone turned out to be a self-operating bicycle of sorts, problematically so, in Luckey’s opinion.

“The problem with the iPhone is that it simplified everything to a degree where, yes, you could learn to use it in less than a minute,” Luckey said. In his telling, you learn everything it can do in about 10 minutes, and then you hit the ceiling on skill and productivity.

He held up an unlikely alternative. “A keyboard requires weeks or months of consistent, focused training in order to be able to achieve a high rate of speed, a high rate of accuracy,” he said, down to the key macros for running Excel. The payoff: “I get a superhuman input device where I can put words into the computer as fast as I can speak wordlessly and with an extremely high level of accuracy.”

Everything became the iPhone

“The problem is that everything has become the iPhone,” he said. “Every application is now the iPhone. Every product is the iPhone. Every virtual reality headset is the iPhone.” Products are built to be learned in one minute and mastered in 10, and “there is no provision made for the man who will spend 1,000 hours, 10,000 hours, 50,000 hours learning his art.”

The number will sound familiar. Malcolm Gladwell made the “10,000-hour rule” famous in Outliers in 2008, the year after the iPhone went on sale. It came from a 1993 study by psychologist Anders Ericsson of violin students at a Berlin music academy, where the best had averaged about 10,000 hours of practice by age 20. Ericsson spent years objecting to the slogan. The number was an average, he wrote with coauthor Robert Pool, and “there is nothing special or magical about ten thousand hours.” What mattered was deliberate practice: focused training at the edge of what you can do, something like Luckey’s keyboard.

Other studies are dubious of the idea that practice makes perfect. A 2014 meta-analysis of 88 studies led by Brooke Macnamara, then at Princeton, found practice accounted for about 12% of differences in performance overall, and less than 1% in professions.

There is hard evidence for the shape of what Luckey describes, and it comes from the newest interface, not the iPhone. A study by economists Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li and Lindsey Raymond tracked 5,179 customer support agents given a generative AI assistant. The number of issues resolved per hour rose 14% on average, including 34% for novice and low-skilled workers, but with “minimal impact on experienced and highly skilled workers.”

The iPhone bargain applied to work suggests that the beginner gets much better fast, and the expert gains little. Luckey doesn’t mention AI in the podcast excerpt, but he takes the same shot at brain-computer interfaces like Neuralink. “Everybody wants a magical human-to-computer interface where you can use it and you don’t have to train, you don’t have to learn,” he said. “Do we need to use this wondrous technology to have a different way of clicking a few buttons and operating an iPhone interface?”

All of these warnings recall Solow’s Productivity Paradox, or the famous observation from Robert Solow in 1987 that “you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.” U.S. labor productivity grew 3.3% a year from 1997 to 2005, then 1.4% a year from 2005 to 2018, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. BLS estimates the slowdown cost $10.9 trillion in lost output, or about $95,000 per worker.

The iPhone can’t take the blame on that evidence. University of Chicago economist Chad Syverson dates the slowdown to 2004, three years before the iPhone. He found it hit dozens of countries regardless of how heavily they used information technology, and that the value of free digital goods the statistics miss covers less than a third of the gap. The 2008 financial crisis also falls inside the period.

Why easy won

The reason products went the iPhone’s way is the money. A device anyone can master in 10 minutes can reach billions of people, and it remains Apple’s biggest business: the iPhone brought in $254.1 billion of the company’s $478.8 billion in revenue in fiscal 2026, which ended in September, according to Apple. That’s up from $209.6 billion a year earlier.

Workplace versions of the bargain are older than the iPhone. In 1974’s Labor and Monopoly Capital, Harry Braverman argued managers cut the skill out of jobs as a strategy of control, and the iPhone sold a version of that bargain to consumers.

Luckey’s own customer may test his theory. Anduril says it won a $159 million Army prototyping contract to build augmented-reality systems with Meta for the Soldier Borne Mission Command program, successor to Microsoft’s troubled IVAS headset, and it is developing its own EagleEye headset on its own dime. The Army isn’t expected to move its top choice into production until 2028, if it picks one at all.

Soldiers train for a living, about as close to the 10,000-hour user as anyone. But MIT Technology Review reported that the vision has them speaking to the interface in plain language, with eye movements and taps eventually replacing speech. RAND’s Jonathan Wong told the outlet the system has “got to be pretty seamless.”

Luckey was kinder to Apple three years ago. When the Vision Pro was unveiled in 2023, he said Apple “did basically everything right,” according to Road to VR. He said he’s “got some ideas” for interfaces that take years to master, and didn’t say what they are.

“I’m hoping it comes back around someday,” he told Isaacson.

The Builders is produced by Kaleidoscope and distributed by iHeartPodcasts.

Dave, you ask whether I've learnt anything from pointless wars. Yes, I have. And the most important lesson is that those who start them must be held responsible for the consequences.

Who ordered Russian troops into Ukraine in February 2022? Putin. Who sent forces towards Kyiv, attacked Ukrainian cities and attempted to impose Russia's will on a sovereign country? Putin. Who subsequently declared four Ukrainian regions annexed to Russia? Putin. Yet throughout this exchange, you continue to portray Moscow as the injured party, forced into war by circumstances beyond its control.

You accuse me of refusing to consider contrary evidence. But I've acknowledged NATO's mistakes, American interference in Ukrainian politics, Russia's security concerns and the failures surrounding Minsk. What I refuse to accept is your insistence that these matters made Russia's invasion unavoidable.

On the 14,000 deaths, I'll accept your clarification that you meant deaths rather than civilian deaths. But the UN figures include Ukrainian soldiers, Russian-backed fighters and civilians on both sides. They do not establish that Kyiv was solely responsible for those deaths. Nor do they justify Russia invading the rest of Ukraine.

You also object to the term "full-scale invasion", apparently because Russia deployed fewer troops than Germany did against France in 1940. That's an extraordinary argument. Russia attacked Ukraine from multiple directions, including Belarus, attempted to take Kyiv and launched military operations across a substantial part of the country. The size of Hitler's army eighty years earlier has no bearing on whether Russia launched a full-scale invasion.

And why do you repeatedly describe it as a "special military operation"? That is the Kremlin's preferred terminology. It doesn't change what happened.

You ask what evidence would change my mind. Evidence that Ukraine posed an imminent military threat to Russia, that an invasion was genuinely unavoidable, or that Moscow had exhausted all peaceful alternatives would certainly warrant serious examination. You have provided none of those things.

You also claim that Russia has no wider territorial ambitions. Yet Putin has annexed Crimea and subsequently claimed four more Ukrainian regions, including territory Russia did not fully control. Those are territorial ambitions demonstrated by actions, not Western speculation.

As for your proposed peace settlement, elections and negotiations deserve consideration. But since you place such importance on elections, perhaps we should examine Russia's own record. Alexei Navalny died in a Russian prison after years of persecution. Other opposition figures have been imprisoned, driven into exile or barred from standing. Russia's elections offer little genuine political competition.

And you expect Ukrainians to trust Moscow to respect their democratic choices? Elections held under occupation, intimidation or without adequate security cannot provide a credible democratic mandate. Nor can any settlement offer lasting peace if Russia retains the right to invade whenever it considers its interests threatened.

You ask whether I've learnt anything from pointless wars. I would ask you to consider the lesson of allowing powerful states to seize their neighbours' territory by force. Putin started this invasion. Ukrainians are fighting because their country was attacked. That fundamental distinction seems to disappear every time you explain the conflict from Moscow's perspective.

We agree that the killing must end. But you still haven't explained why Russia's fears should override Ukraine's right to exist as an independent country. And until you answer that, we are simply going round in circles.

text:
If I could pair two characters from the entire Harry Potter universe, including characters who never had a romantic storyline together, I would choose Neville Longbottom and Luna Lovegood.

And I actually think there’s a meaningful case to be made for them beyond the fact that they were both considered odd by their peers.

Look at their individual journeys in the books.

Neville spent much of his early years struggling with confidence. 

He was constantly underestimated, frequently bullied, and often felt overshadowed by the expectations placed on hi but underneath that awkwardness was someone incredibly courageous. 

His journey from a boy who struggled to stand up for himself to the person who stood against Voldemort in the Battle of Hogwarts is one of the most satisfying character developments in the entire series.

Then there’s Luna she was comfortable being herself in a world that constantly dismissed her,people laughed at her, called her names and treated her beliefs as ridiculous but she rarely allowed their opinions to dictate who she was. 

She possessed an emotional intelligence that many of the supposedly more sensible characters lacked.

What makes this pairing interesting to me is what they could have offered each other.

Neville could have given Luna a sense of belonging without expecting her to change who she was. Luna, in turn, could have helped Neville recognise that he didn’t need to become someone else to be worthy of respect. 

She could have appreciated the courage in him long before the rest of the wizarding world recognised it.

There’s also something beautiful about the fact that both characters understood what it meant to be underestimated. 

Neville was living with the trauma of what happened to his parents, while Luna had experienced the loss of her mother at a young age. Neither had an entirely easy childhood and both developed a remarkable capacity to keep going despite their circumstances.

Their involvement in Dumbledore’s Army and their willingness to fight in the Battle of the Department of Mysteries and the Battle of Hogwarts also show that their courage was never dependent on popularity or recognition.

To be clear, the books never establish a romantic relationship between them Luna eventually marries Rolf Scamander, while Neville marries Hannah Abbott i’m not suggesting Rowling secretly intended them to end up together.

I’m saying that, as an alternative pairing,i think there was genuine potential worth exploring.

Sometimes the most interesting couples aren’t necessarily the ones who are most alike, but the ones who understand parts of each other that the rest of the world overlooks.

Neville and Luna would have been a beautiful example of that.
